**Sūrat al-Anfāl**

Madaniyyah, except for verses 30 to 36, which are Makkī. It has 75 verses and was revealed after al-Baqarah.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿They ask you about the spoils (al-anfāl). Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger. So fear God, set right what is between you, and obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger. So fear God, set right what is between you, and obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers.﴾.

Know that His saying, ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾, requires investigation of five matters: the questioners, the one questioned, the reality of *nafl* (extra gift), whether this question concerned some ruling or other, and what the exegetes (*mufassirūn*) explained *al-anfāl* to mean.

As for the first investigation: who were the questioners? We say that His saying, ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾, is a report about people who had not been mentioned before, and this is fitting here, because at the time of revelation the questioners of this question were known and specific, so the expression is directed toward them. Undoubtedly they were groups who had an interest in the spoils and the *anfāl*, and they were groups among the Companions (*ṣaḥābah*).

As for the second investigation: who was the one questioned? Undoubtedly he was the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for the third investigation: what are *al-anfāl*? We say: al-Zuhrī said: *al-nafl* and *al-nāfilah* are whatever is an addition over the original. The spoils were called *anfāl* because the Muslims were distinguished by them over the other nations to whom spoils were not lawful. Voluntary prayer is *nāfilah* because it is an addition to the obligatory prayer, which is the original. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an extra gift (*nāfilah*)﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 72], meaning as an addition to what he asked for.

As for the fourth investigation: concerning which ruling of the *anfāl* was the question? We say: on this there are two views.

The first: although the wording of the question is vague, the specifying of the answer shows that the question was about that specific matter. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. From this it is known that it was a question about a ruling among the rulings of menstruation and orphans, and that ruling was not specified, but the answer was specific, because He, exalted is He, said concerning menstruation: ﴿Say: it is an injury; so keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222]. This answer indicates that the question was about mixing with women during menstruation. And concerning orphans He said: ﴿Say: setting things right for them is best; and if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. This specific answer indicates that the specific question was about dealing with their property and mixing with them in eating. Also He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isrā’: 85]. This answer indicates that the question was about whether the Spirit is created or eternal. Likewise here, when He said in answer to the question about the spoils: ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, this indicates that they asked him about how the spoils are to be disposed of and who is entitled to them.

The second view: His saying, ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾, means "from the spoils," and the intended meaning of this question is begging (*istiʿṭā’*), as is related in a report that they used to say: "O Messenger of God, give me such-and-such, give me such-and-such." And it is not far-fetched to put *ʿan* in place of *min*. This is the view of ʿIkrimah. And Abdullah recited it as: ﴿They ask you for the spoils﴾.

The fifth investigation: an explanation of the statements of the exegetes concerning what is meant by *al-anfāl*. We say: the *anfāl* about which they asked indicates that there had occurred among them dispute and rivalry over them, and this is shown by several considerations:

First: His saying, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, indicates that the purpose of mentioning it is to restrain the people from quarreling and contending.

Second: His saying, ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾, indicates that they asked about this only after a dispute had arisen between them.

Third: His saying, ﴿And obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾, indicates this.

Having understood this, we say: it is possible that what is meant by these *anfāl* is the spoils (*ghanā’im*), namely the wealth taken from the disbelievers by force; and it is possible that what is meant is other than them.

As for the first: there are several points.

One: he (ﷺ) divided what they seized on the day of Badr among those who were present and among groups who were also not present. They were three of the Emigrants (*muhājirūn*) and five of the Helpers (*anṣār*). As for the Emigrants, one of them was Uthmān, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, left him in charge of his daughter, because she was ill; and Ṭalḥah and Saʿīd ibn Zayd, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, had sent them to spy out news of the caravan, and they went out along the road to Syria. As for the five of the Helpers: one of them was Abū Lubābah Marwān ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) left in charge of Madinah; ʿĀṣim, whom he left in charge of al-ʿĀliyah; al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib, whom he sent back from al-Rawḥā’ to ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf because of something that reached him about him; al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ṣimmah, who fell ill at al-Rawḥā’; and Khawwāt ibn Jubayr. These did not take part, yet the Prophet (ﷺ) set aside for them a share in those spoils, and some others disputed over this, so this verse was revealed on account of it.

Two: it is related that on the day of Badr the young men killed and took captives, while the elders stood with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the battle lines. The young men said: "The spoils are ours, because we killed and routed." The elders said: "We were a reserve for you, and if you had been routed, you would have retreated to us. So do not take away the spoils without us." Dispute arose on this account, and the verse was revealed.

Three: al-Zajjāj said: the *anfāl* are the spoils, and they asked about them only because they had been forbidden to those before them. This view is weak, because on this interpretation the purpose of the question would be only to seek the ruling of God, exalted is He, and we have already shown by proof that this question was preceded by dispute and contention.

As for the second possibility, that what is meant by *al-anfāl* is something other than the spoils, then on this interpretation there are also several views regarding the explanation of *al-anfāl*:

One: Ibn ʿAbbās said in some reports: what is meant by *al-anfāl* is whatever strayed from the polytheists to the Muslims without fighting, such as a beast, a slave or goods; it belongs to the Prophet (ﷺ), who places it wherever he wills.

Two: *al-anfāl* is the fifth (*khums*) which God assigned to the people of the fifth, and this is the view of Mujāhid. He said: the people only asked about the fifth, so the verse was revealed.

Three: *al-anfāl* is the *salab* (the spoils of a slain enemy's gear), which is given to the fighter in addition to his share of the booty, to encourage him to fight, as when the Imam says: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, he shall have his spoils," or says to a detachment: "Whatever you take is yours," or says: "For you is half of it, or a third, or a quarter." And the extra gift (*nafl*) is not subjected to the fifth. And on the authority of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who said: My brother ʿUmayr was killed on the day of Badr, so I killed in return Saʿd ibn al-ʿĀṣ and took his sword, which pleased me. I came with it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "God, exalted is He, has healed my breast from the polytheists, so give me this sword." He said: "This is neither mine nor yours; throw it in the place where the spoils were put." So I threw it, with what God knows in me of grief for my brother and loss of my spoils. I had not gone far before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to me, for the Sūrat al-Anfāl had been revealed, and he said: "O Saʿd, you asked me for the sword, and it was not mine; now it has become mine, so take it." The judge (al-Qāḍī) said: all these views are admitted by the verse, and there is no proof in it favoring some of them over others.

If reports are authentic indicating a specific meaning, it is judged accordingly; otherwise all are possible. Just as each one of them is permissible, so too is it permissible to intend all of them together, for there is no contradiction among them. The closest view is that what is meant by this is what he, peace be upon him, had the right to give to others from the total of the spoils, both before they were obtained and after they were obtained, because it is permissible for him to do so as an incitement to jihad and a strengthening of souls, like what he used to give to one person at the start of the battle so that he would press harder in the fighting, or at the time of the return, or to give him the spoils of the slayer, or to give a portion to some of those present and give him an extra gift from the fifth which he, peace be upon him, had as his own. On this interpretation, His saying, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, means the matter beyond what was due to the fighters.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, there are two investigations concerning it.

The first investigation: what is meant is that its ruling is specific to God and the Messenger, Whom God commands to divide it according to what His wisdom requires; the matter of its division is not left to anyone's opinion.

The second investigation: Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and al-Suddī said: it was abrogated (*mansūkh*, i.e., cancelled by later revelation) by His saying: ﴿And know that for God is a fifth of it, and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfāl: 41]. This is because His saying, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, implies that all the spoils belong to the Messenger; so God abrogated it with the verses of the fifth. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbās in some reports. It has been answered in several ways:

The first: His saying, ﴿Say: the spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾, means that the ruling concerning them belongs to God and the Messenger, and this meaning remains, so it cannot become abrogated. Then God decreed that four-fifths of it be the property of the fighters.

The second: the verse of the fifth indicates that the spoils are the property of the fighters, while the *anfāl* here are explained not as the spoils but as the *salab*, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, gives it as an extra gift to some people for one of the public interests.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾. Concerning this there are two investigations:

The first investigation: its meaning is: fear the punishment of God, do not proceed to disobey God, leave off disputing and contending because of these circumstances, and be content with what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has ruled.

The second investigation: concerning His saying, ﴿and set right what is between you﴾, that is, set right what is between you of words. And since the words were occurring between them, it was called *dhāt al-bayn* (what is between), just as secrets, since they were hidden in the breasts, were called *dhāt al-ṣudūr* (what is in the breasts).

Then He said: ﴿And obey God and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, forbade them from opposing the ruling of the Messenger by His saying: ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾. Then He emphasized this by commanding them to obey the Messenger in His saying: ﴿And obey God and His Messenger﴾. Then He intensified this emphasis, saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾. The meaning is that the faith to which the Messenger has called you and which you desire cannot be completed except by holding fast to this obedience, so beware of departing from it. Whoever says that abandoning obedience causes the loss of faith argues from this verse, and its reasoning is that what is conditioned upon something by the word "if" is absent when that thing is absent; here faith is conditioned upon obedience by the word ﴿if﴾, so the absence of faith follows the absence of obedience. The full treatment of this issue is mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisā’: 31]. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ ﴿Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them.﴾ ﴿Those are the believers in truth. For them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and an honorable provision.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾, and this required that faith entails obedience, He explained this in this verse with greater explanation and detail, and clarified that faith is not attained except when these acts of obedience are present, so He said: ﴿The believers are only﴾ and so on. Know that this verse indicates that faith is not attained except when five matters are present:

The first: His saying: ﴿Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: it is said wajila yawjalu wajalan, so he is wajil, and awjala, when he fears. The poet said:

By your life, I do not know, and indeed I am apprehensive, over which of us death will first overtake.

The meaning is that the believer is only a believer if he is fearful of Allah. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23], and His saying: ﴿Those who are fearful out of awe of their Lord﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 57], and His saying: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 2].

The people of realities (ahl al-haqa'iq) said: fear is of two kinds: fear of punishment, and fear of majesty and magnificence. As for fear of punishment, it belongs to the disobedient. As for fear of majesty and magnificence, it does not leave the heart of any created being, whether he is a near angel or a sent prophet. This is because He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, independent of all existing things, and everything other than Him among existing things is in need of Him. The one in need, when he presents himself before the self-sufficient king, reveres him and fears him; and that reverence is not from punishment, but merely his knowledge that He is independent of him and that he is in need of Him necessitates that reverence and that fear.

Having known this, we say: if the meaning of trembling is the first kind, then that does not arise from the mere mention of Allah, but arises from the mention of Allah's punishment, and this is what is fitting for this place, because the aim of this verse is to obligate the people of Badr to obey Allah and obey the Messenger regarding the distribution of the spoils. As for if the meaning of trembling is the second kind, then that necessarily follows from the mere mention of Allah, and there is no need for any supposition in the verse.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, said here: ﴿their hearts tremble﴾, and in another verse He said: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts are reassured by the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 28]. So how is the reconciliation between them? Also, He said in another verse: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23]. We say: tranquility comes only from the solidity of certainty and the expansion of the breast through knowledge of tawhid, while trembling comes only from fear of punishment, and there is no contradiction between these two states. Rather, we say: these two attributes are combined in one verse, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23]. The meaning: the skins shiver from fear of Allah's punishment, then their skins and hearts soften at the hope of Allah's reward.

The second attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾, and it is like His saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say: "Which of you has this increased in faith?"﴾ [At-Tawbah: 124]. Then in it are issues:

The first issue: the increase of faith, which is affirmation (tasdiq), is in two respects:

The first respect: this is what the majority of scholars hold, as related by al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him: that whoever has more and stronger proofs is greater in faith, because when there is abundance and strength of proofs, doubt disappears and certainty strengthens. To this refers the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "If the faith of Abu Bakr were weighed against the faith of the people of the earth, it would outweigh it," meaning that his knowledge of Allah was stronger.

One may say: the intended increase is either the strength of the proof or the abundance of proofs. As for the strength of the proof, it is invalid, because every proof is necessarily composed of premises, and those premises are either held with a certainty that excludes the opposite or not. If the certainty excluding the opposite is present in all premises, it is impossible on this explanation for some proofs to be stronger than others, because certainty that excludes the opposite does not admit of degrees. And if the certainty excluding the opposite is not present, either in all or in some, then that is not a proof but a sign (amara), and the conclusion drawn from it is not knowledge but opinion. Thus it has been established from what we have mentioned that variation in proofs by strength is impossible. As for variation by abundance of proofs, the matter is the same, because the certainty arising from a single proof, if it excludes the opposite, is not a proof but a sign, and the conclusion would not be known but merely presumed. Thus it is established that this interpretation is weak.

Know that it is possible to say: the intended increase is persistence and non-persistence, because some who reason do not have the proof and the thing proven present in their minds except for a single moment, while others are constant in that state, and between these two extremes are various intermediate levels and differing ranks. This is what is meant by increase.

The second respect of the increase of affirmation: they affirm everything that is recited to them from Allah. Since the obligations were successive and consecutive in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, at the arrival of each obligation they increased in affirmation and acknowledgment. It is known that whoever affirms a person in two matters has a greater affirmation of him than one who affirms him in one matter. His saying: ﴿And when

Page 97
His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ means that whenever they heard a new verse, they brought a new acknowledgment, and that was an increase in faith and affirmation.

There is a third respect in the verse: that the perfection of Allah's power and wisdom is known only through the traces of His wisdom in His creatures, and this is a sea without shore. Whenever the human intellect stops at the traces of Allah's wisdom in the creation of one thing, it moves from it to seeking His wisdom in the creation of another thing, and so it has moved from one rank to another rank higher, more noble and more perfect. Since these ranks have no end, there is necessarily no end to the ranks of manifestation, unveiling and knowledge.

The second issue: they differed as to whether faith admits of increase and decrease or not. As for those who said that faith is a combination of belief, verbal affirmation and action, they argued from this verse in two ways:

The first: His saying, ﴿they increase them in faith﴾, indicates that faith admits of increase, and if faith were merely knowledge and affirmation, it would not admit of increase.

The second: when He, exalted is He, mentioned these five matters, He said of those described by them: ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾, and this indicates that all those qualities are included in the designation of faith. It is related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith." They also argued from this verse that faith is a combination of the three pillars, saying: because the verse is explicit that faith admits of increase, and knowledge and affirmation do not admit of variation, it is necessary that faith be a combination of affirmation, belief and action, such that by the entry of variation into action, variation appears in faith. This argument is weak, for we have shown that variation by persistence and non-persistence occurs in belief and affirmation, and this amount suffices for the occurrence of variation in faith. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾, its apparent sense implies that those verses are what effect the increase in faith. This is not the case, for the verses themselves do not necessitate the increase; rather, if it must be attributed, the cause is hearing those verses, or knowing those verses produces an increase in knowledge and affirmation. And Allah knows best.

The third attribute of the believers: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon their Lord they rely.﴾ Know that the attribute of believers is that they are confident in the truthfulness of His promise and His threat, and that they say "Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly," and that their speech is not like the speech of the hypocrites: ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 12]. Then we say: this statement conveys restriction, and its meaning is that they rely only upon their Lord. This state is a lofty rank and a noble degree, namely that a person reaches the point where he has no reliance in any matter except upon Allah.

Know that these three attributes are arranged in the best order of arrangement: the first rank is trembling from Allah's punishment; the second rank is submission to the stations of the obligations to Allah; the third rank is complete severance from all other than Allah, and complete reliance upon the bounty of Allah, indeed complete independence from all other than Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth and fifth attributes: His saying: ﴿Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them.﴾ Know that the three preceding ranks are states regarded in the hearts and inner being; then He moved from them to attending to the states of the outward; and the chief and head of the outward acts of worship is the giving of oneself in prayer and the giving of wealth for the pleasure of Allah, which includes zakat, charity, kinship gifts, and spending in jihad, and spending on mosques and bridges. The Mu'tazilah said: He, exalted is He, praised the one who spends from what Allah has provided him, and the community has agreed that spending from what is unlawful is not permitted, and that indicates that what is unlawful is not a provision (rizq). This statement has been mentioned before many times.

The second: when He, exalted is He, mentioned these five matters, He said of those described by them: ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾, and this indicates that all those qualities are included in the designation of faith. It is related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith." They also argued from this verse that faith is a combination of the three pillars, saying: because the verse is explicit that faith admits of increase, and knowledge and affirmation do not admit of variation, it is necessary that faith be a combination of affirmation, belief and action, such that by the entry of variation into action, variation appears in faith. This argument is weak, for we have shown that variation by persistence and non-persistence occurs in belief and affirmation, and this amount suffices for the occurrence of variation in faith. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾, its apparent sense implies that those verses are what effect the increase in faith. This is not the case, for the verses themselves do not necessitate the increase; rather, if it must be attributed, the cause is hearing those verses, or knowing those verses produces an increase in knowledge and affirmation. And Allah knows best.

The third attribute of the believers: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon their Lord they rely.﴾ Know that the attribute of believers is that they are confident in the truthfulness of His promise and His threat, and that they say "Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly," and that their speech is not like the speech of the hypocrites: ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 12]. Then we say: this statement conveys restriction, and its meaning is that they rely only upon their Lord. This state is a lofty rank and a noble degree, namely that a person reaches the point where he has no reliance in any matter except upon Allah.

Know that these three attributes are arranged in the best order of arrangement: the first rank is trembling from Allah's punishment; the second rank is submission to the stations of the obligations to Allah; the third rank is complete severance from all other than Allah, and complete reliance upon the bounty of Allah, indeed complete independence from all other than Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth and fifth attributes: His saying: ﴿Those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them.﴾ Know that the three preceding ranks are states regarded in the hearts and inner being; then He moved from them to attending to the states of the outward; and the chief and head of the outward acts of worship is the giving of oneself in prayer and the giving of wealth for the pleasure of Allah, which includes zakat, charity, kinship gifts, and spending in jihad, and spending on mosques and bridges. The Mu'tazilah said: He, exalted is He, praised the one who spends from what Allah has provided him, and the community has agreed that spending from what is unlawful is not permitted, and that indicates that what is unlawful is not a provision (rizq). This statement has been mentioned before many times.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned these five attributes, He affirmed three matters for those who are described by them:

The first is His saying: ﴿Those are the believers truly.﴾

The first question: With what does His saying ﴿truly (haqqan)﴾ connect? There are two opinions:

One: It connects with ﴿they are the believers﴾, meaning: they are believers in reality.

The second: The sentence is complete at ﴿Those are the believers﴾, and then a new statement begins: ﴿Truly, for them are degrees...﴾

The second question: They mentioned several views on the grammatical case (intisab) of ﴿haqqan﴾:

First: al-Farra' said: The estimate is, "I inform you of that truly," that is, an informing that is true. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Those are the disbelievers truly﴾ [al-Nisa': 151].

Second: Sibawayh said: It is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing an omitted verb that the context indicates. The estimate is: "What they did was indeed truth and sincerity."

Third: al-Zajjaj said: The estimate is: "Those are the believers; that is truly due (uhiqqu dhalika haqqan)."

The third question: They agree that a believer may say, "I am a believer," but they differ as to whether a man may say, "I am a believer truly" or not. The companions of al-Shafi'i (Shafi'is) said: It is better for a man to say, "I am a believer, God willing (in sha' Allah)," and not to say, "I am a believer truly." The companions of Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) said: It is better to say, "I am a believer truly," and it is not permissible to say, "I am a believer, God willing."

As for those who said he should say, "I am a believer, God willing," they have two positions:

The first position: That this is due to doubt about the attainment of faith.

The second position: That the matter is not like that.

As for the first position, its explanation is this: For al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him), faith is a term for the whole of belief, verbal affirmation and action. There is no doubt that a person's performing righteous deeds is something uncertain, and doubt about one part of a reality (mahiyya) necessitates doubt about the attainment of that reality. So although the person is certain of having the belief and the verbal affirmation, since he is in doubt about the performance of the deeds, this degree necessitates that he is in doubt about attaining faith. As for Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him): since faith is a name for belief and utterance, and action lies outside the definition of faith, doubt about the performance of deeds does not entail doubt about faith. Thus it is established that whoever says faith is a term for the combination of the three matters necessarily incurs doubt about faith. At this point it becomes clear that the disagreement is only in terms.

As for the second position, which is that we say: His saying, "I am a believer, God willing," is not due to doubt. Then there are several views:

The first: That a man's being a believer is the most noble of his attributes and the most known of his qualities and states. So when he says, "I am a believer," it is as if he praised himself with the greatest praise, and therefore he should say, "God willing," so that this becomes a cause for the heart's humbling and the removal of vanity. It is related that Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) said to Qatada: "Why do you make an exception (istithna') in your faith?" He said: "Following Abraham (peace be upon him) in his saying:"

page 99

﴿And He who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82], and in his saying: ﴿Did you not believe? He said: Yes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. I say: Qatada could have answered and said that after he said, "Yes," he said, "But that my heart may be at rest," so he sought greater tranquility. This indicates that there must be a saying of "God willing."

The second: God, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse that a man is not a believer unless he is described by the five attributes: fear of God, sincerity in the religion of God, reliance upon God, and the performance of prayer and zakat for the sake of God, exalted is He. He mentioned at the beginning of the verse what indicates restriction (hasr), namely His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who...﴾ and [they are] such-and-such. And at the end of the verse He mentioned His saying: ﴿Those are the believers truly﴾, and this also indicates restriction. Since this verse indicates this meaning, and since a person cannot be certain of himself that these five attributes are present in him, it is therefore better for him to say, "God willing." It is related that al-Hasan was asked by a man, "Are you a believer?" He said: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in God, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, then I am a believer. But if you are asking me about His saying: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾, then by God I do not know whether I am one of them or not."

The third: The Great Qur'an indicates that everyone who is a believer is among the people of Paradise. So certainty that someone is a believer necessitates certainty that he is among the people of Paradise, and that is not possible. Thus this is likewise. It is related from al-Thawri that he said: "Whoever claims that he is a believer in God truly, but does not testify that he is among the people of Paradise, has believed in only half of the verse." The point is that just as there is no way to be certain that he is among the people of Paradise, likewise there is no way to be certain that he is a believer.

The fourth: Faith is an expression for the heart's assent and for knowledge. On this basis, a man is only truly a believer when this assent and this knowledge are present in the heart and present in consciousness. But when this meaning is absent, he is a believer only according to God's ruling, while in reality he is not.

Once you know this, it is not far-fetched that what is meant by His saying "God willing" refers to the continuance of the designation of faith and the constant presence of its meaning, without heedlessness or forgetfulness of it. This meaning is possible.

The fifth: The adherents of the doctrine of muwafah (the view that faith is tied to a final state at the moment of death) say: The condition for being a believer at present is the attainment of faith at the end (muwafah 'ala al-iman), and this condition is not fulfilled except at death, and it is unknown. What depends on the unknown is itself unknown. For this reason it is good to say, "I am a believer, God willing."

The sixth: That one says, "I am a believer, God willing," at the time of death, and the intent is to direct this exception to the final outcome and the end. For even if a man is a believer at present, if that faith does not remain at the end, its existence is like its non-existence, and no benefit has been achieved at all. So the purpose of mentioning this exception is this meaning.

The seventh: That mentioning this expression does not contradict the attainment of certainty and conviction. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God has certainly fulfilled the vision for His Messenger in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, God willing, secure﴾ [al-Fath: 27], and He, exalted is He, is far above doubt and suspicion. Thus it is established that He mentioned that only to teach His servants this meaning. Likewise here, it is better to mention this expression, which indicates the entrusting of affairs to God, so that by the blessing of this expression the continuance of faith may be attained.

The eighth: That a group of the early generations (salaf) mentioned this expression, and we found for them support in the Book of God, which is His saying: ﴿Those are the believers truly﴾. They are the believers in the knowledge and judgment of God. That indicates the existence of a group who are believers, and the existence of a group who are not like that. So the believer says, "God willing," so that God, by the blessing of this expression, places him in the first category and not in the second.

As for those who say it is not permissible to mention this expression, they have argued for the soundness of their view with several proofs:

The first: A moving thing may say, "I am moving," but may not say, "I am moving, God willing." The same applies to the standing and the sitting. Likewise here, the believer must be a believer and must not say, "I am a believer, God willing." Just as the body's ceasing to be moving in the future does not prevent a judgment that it is moving while the motion is present in it, likewise the possibility of the loss of faith in the future does not impair his being a believer in the present.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the believers truly﴾, so He has ruled that they are believers truly. Therefore, saying "God willing" would introduce doubt about what God has affirmed as attained, and that is not permissible.

The answer to the first: The difference between describing a person as a believer and describing him as moving lies in the many aspects we mentioned, and when a difference exists, the comparison becomes impossible.

The answer to the second: God, exalted is He, ruled upon those described by the mentioned attributes that they are believers truly, but that condition is uncertain, and doubt about a condition necessitates doubt about the conditioned thing. This strengthens the very position of ours. And God knows best.

The second ruling

Among the rulings which God, exalted is He, affirmed for those described by the five attributes is His saying: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾. The meaning: for them are ranks, some of which are higher than others.

Know that the mentioned attributes are of two kinds. The first three are the attributes of the heart and spiritual states: fear, sincerity and reliance. The last two are outward acts and characteristics (akhlaq). There is no doubt that these acts and characteristics have effects in purifying the heart and illuminating it with divine knowledge. There is no doubt that the stronger the influence, the stronger its effects, and vice versa. Since these characteristics and acts have degrees and ranks, the knowledges also have degrees and ranks. That is what is meant by His saying: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾. The reward attained in Paradise is also determined according to the measure of these states. Thus it is established that the ranks of spiritual felicities before death and after death, and the ranks of the felicities attained in Paradise, are many and varied. For this reason He said: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾.

If it is said: Does not the lesser one, when he knows that the higher degrees are attained by the superior one and he is deprived of them, feel pain in his heart and his life becomes embittered? And does that not undermine the reward being a "generous provision" (rizq karim)?

The answer: The absorption of each one in his own particular felicity prevents him from acquiring rancor and envy. In sum, the states of the Hereafter do not resemble the states of this world except in name.

The third and fourth rulings

His saying: ﴿And forgiveness and a generous provision﴾. What is meant by forgiveness is that God passes over their misdeeds, and by the generous provision is the bliss of Paradise. The theologians (mutakallimun) said: As for it being a generous provision, this points to those benefits being pure, lasting, and joined with honour and exaltation, and the whole of that is the definition of reward. The gnostics (arifun) said: What is meant by forgiveness is the removal of the darknesses caused by occupation with other than God, and by the generous provision are the lights that arise from being absorbed in the knowledge and love of God. Al-Wahidi said: The people of language said: "Karim" is a comprehensive term for everything that is praised and admired, and "karim" is one who is praised in what one needs. God, exalted is He, is described as karim, and the Qur'an is described as karim. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29], and He said: ﴿of every noble pair﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 7], and He said: ﴿and We will admit you to a noble entrance﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], and He said:

page 101

﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. So the generous provision is the noble, excellent and good. Hisham ibn 'Urwa said: It means what God has prepared for them in Paradise of delicious foods and drinks and pleasant life. I say: It is necessary here to explain that spiritual pleasures are more perfect than bodily pleasures, and we have mentioned this meaning in this book in many places. At this point it becomes clear that the generous provision is the spiritual pleasures, which are the knowledge of God, His love, and absorption in His worship.

If someone says: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that whoever is described by these five matters is judged as saved from punishment and granted success with reward, and that would imply that there is no obligation (taklif) upon the servant regarding anything other than these five. But that is false by the consensus of the Muslims, for fasting, pilgrimage, and the performance of all the other obligations are necessary.

We say: He, exalted is He, began with His saying: ﴿Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾, and all the obligations (taklif) fall under these two statements. However, He specified, from among the inner qualities, reliance upon God (tawakkul) by name specifically, and from among the outward deeds, prayer (salah) and almsgiving (zakah) by name specifically, as a reminder that the most noble of the inner states is tawakkul, and the most noble of the outward deeds is salah and zakah.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 5–6:**

The Exalted said: ﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth, although a group of the believers were averse.﴾ ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become clear, as though they were being driven to death while they watch.﴾ In these verses there are several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah):

**The First Issue:** Know that His saying ﴿As your Lord brought you out﴾ requires that something be likened to this bringing out, and they have mentioned several interpretations of it.

The first: When the Prophet ﷺ saw the large number of polytheists on the day of Badr and the small number of Muslims, he said: "Whoever kills an enemy, his spoils are his, and whoever takes a captive, he will receive such and such," in order to encourage them to fight. When the polytheists were routed, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said: "O Messenger of Allah, a group of your companions and your people ransomed you with their own selves. They did not hold back from fighting out of cowardice, nor out of stinginess in giving up their lives, but they feared for you lest you be assassinated. So if you give these men what you named for them, a group of the Muslims will be left with nothing." Then Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], to dispose of them as He wills. So the Muslims refrained from pursuit, and some of them felt a measure of aversion. Likewise, when the Messenger ﷺ went out to fight on the day of Badr, they were averse to that fighting, as we will explain the state of that aversion. So when He said: ﴿Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾, the implied meaning was that they accepted this ruling concerning the spoils even though they were averse to it, just as [they were averse when] your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth to fight, though they were averse to it. This is the best of the interpretations mentioned here.

The second: The implied meaning is that the ruling was established that the spoils belong to Allah even though they disliked it, just as Allah's ruling to bring you out to fight was established even though they disliked it.

The third: When He said: ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾, the implied meaning is: the ruling that they are believers is true, just as Allah's ruling that He brought you out of your house to fight is true.

The fourth: al-Kisa'i said: the particle "al-kaf" (as) is connected to what follows it, namely His saying: ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth﴾, and the implied meaning is:

[Page 102]

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth﴾ despite the aversion of a group of the believers, so too they dislike fighting and argue with you about it. And Allah knows best.

**The Second Issue:** His saying ﴿from your house﴾ means his house in Medina, or Medina itself, because it is the place of his migration (hijrah) and residence. ﴿With the truth﴾ means: a bringing out accompanied by wisdom. The correct reading is that ﴿and indeed a group of the believers were averse﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He brought you out while they were averse.

It is narrated that the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria, carrying great wealth, and with it forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan and 'Amr ibn al-'As, and other people. Gabriel informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he informed the Muslims. They liked the idea of intercepting the caravan because of the abundance of goods and the small number of its guards. When they resolved and set out, news of their departure reached the people of Mecca. Abu Jahl called out from atop the Ka'bah: "O people of Mecca, rescue! Rescue! Upon every swift and slow mount! If Muhammad takes your caravan, you will never prosper!" The sister of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib had seen a vision and said to her brother: "I have seen a marvel. I saw as if an angel descended from heaven, took a rock from the mountain, then flew with it, and no house in Mecca remained but that a stone from that rock struck it." Al-'Abbas related it, and Abu Jahl said: "Are their men not content with prophethood, so that their women now claim prophethood?" Abu Jahl then set out with all the people of Mecca, and they were the nafir (the mobilized host). There was a well-known proverb: "Neither with the caravan nor with the nafir." It was said to him: "The caravan has taken the coastal road and escaped, so return to Mecca with the people." He said: "No, by Allah, that will never happen until we slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls and musical instruments play at Badr, so that all the Arabs will hear of our march. Muhammad has not seized the caravan." So he proceeded to Badr with his people. Badr was a place where the Arabs gathered once a year for their market. Gabriel descended and said: "O Muhammad, Allah has promised you one of the two groups, either the caravan or the nafir of Quraysh." The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions and said: "What do you say? The people have come out of Mecca upon every swift and slow mount. Which do you prefer, the caravan or the nafir?" They said: "Rather, the caravan is dearer to us than meeting the enemy." The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed, and he said: "The caravan has passed along the seashore, and this is Abu Jahl who has approached." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, take the caravan and leave the enemy." Then, at the Prophet's ﷺ anger, Abu Bakr and 'Umar stood and spoke well. Then Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah stood and said: "Proceed to what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. By Allah, if you were to travel to Aden, not one man of the Ansar would stay behind from you." Then al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr said: "O Messenger of Allah, proceed to what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. We will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Musa: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Rather we say: go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are fighting along with you, as long as there is an eye among us that blinks." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed, then said: "Set out in the blessing of Allah. By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall." When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished with Badr, some said: "Go after the caravan!" Al-'Abbas called out to him while he was in his bonds, "It is not right!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Why?" He said: "Because Allah promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised."

Having known this story, we say: the aversion to fighting was present in some of them, not in all of them, as is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed a group of the believers were averse﴾. The truth they argued about with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was meeting the nafir, because they preferred the caravan. His saying ﴿after it has become clear﴾ means: the Messenger of Allah had informed them that they would be victorious. Their argument was their saying: "Our departure was only for the caravan. Why did you not tell us, so that we could prepare and get ready for battle?" That is because they disliked fighting. Then He likened their state, in the extremity of their fear and terror, to the state of one who is dragged to be killed and driven to death, while he watches its causes and sees its inevitable outcomes. In sum, His saying ﴿while they watch﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for certainty and conviction. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever disowns his son while he looks at him," meaning he knows that he is his son. And His saying: ﴿On the day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Naba': 40] means: knows.

[Page 103]

Know that their fear was due to several matters:
One of them: the small number.

The second: they were on foot; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them.

The third: the scarcity of weapons.

**The Third Issue:** It is narrated that he ﷺ went out from his house by his own choice. Then Allah attributed that going out to Himself, saying: ﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth.﴾ This indicates that the act of the servant is by the creation of Allah, either directly or through the mediation of the capacity (qudrah, power) and the motive (da'iyah, impulse), which together necessitate the act, as is our position. Al-Qadi said: its meaning is that this going out occurred by the command of Allah and His obligation, so it was attributed to Him.

We say: there is no doubt that what you have mentioned is figurative (majaz, non-literal usage), while the principle is to take speech in its literal meaning (haqiqah).

Then Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah stood and said: "Proceed to what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. By Allah, if you were to travel to Aden, not one man of the Ansar would stay behind from you." Then al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr said: "O Messenger of Allah, proceed to what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. We will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Musa: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Rather we say: go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are fighting along with you, as long as there is an eye among us that blinks." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed, then said: "Set out in the blessing of Allah. By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall." When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished with Badr, some said: "Go after the caravan!" Al-'Abbas called out to him while he was in his bonds, "It is not right!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Why?" He said: "Because Allah promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised."

Having known this story, we say: the aversion to fighting was present in some of them, not in all of them, as is shown by His saying: ﴿And indeed a group of the believers were averse﴾. The truth they argued about with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was meeting the nafir, because they preferred the caravan. His saying ﴿after it has become clear﴾ means: the Messenger of Allah had informed them that they would be victorious. Their argument was their saying: "Our departure was only for the caravan. Why did you not tell us, so that we could prepare and get ready for battle?" That is because they disliked fighting. Then He likened their state, in the extremity of their fear and terror, to the state of one who is dragged to be killed and driven to death, while he watches its causes and sees its inevitable outcomes. In sum, His saying ﴿while they watch﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for certainty and conviction. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever disowns his son while he looks at him," meaning he knows that he is his son. And His saying: ﴿On the day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Naba': 40] means: knows.

[Page 103]

Know that their fear was due to several matters:
One of them: the small number.

The second: they were on foot; it is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them.

The third: the scarcity of weapons.

**The Third Issue:** It is narrated that he ﷺ went out from his house by his own choice. Then Allah attributed that going out to Himself, saying: ﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house with the truth.﴾ This indicates that the act of the servant is by the creation of Allah, either directly or through the mediation of the capacity (qudrah, power) and the motive (da'iyah, impulse), which together necessitate the act, as is our position. Al-Qadi said: its meaning is that this going out occurred by the command of Allah and His obligation, so it was attributed to Him.

We say: there is no doubt that what you have mentioned is figurative (majaz, non-literal usage), while the principle is to take speech in its literal meaning (haqiqah).

The Almighty's words: ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours, and you wished that the one without the thorn of arms would be yours, while God wished to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the remnant of the disbelievers﴾ ﴿so that He might establish the truth and nullify falsehood, even though the guilty dislike it﴾.

Know that His words ﴿idh﴾ (when) are in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: "remember." ﴿Annaha lakum﴾ (that it would be yours) is in apposition (badal) to ﴿iḥdā al-ṭā'ifatayn﴾ (one of the two groups). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: a parallel is His words: ﴿Do they await anything but the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly?﴾ Here ﴿an﴾ (that) is in the accusative position, just as it governs ﴿al-sā'ah﴾ (the Hour). Also His words: ﴿And if not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them﴾, where ﴿an﴾ is in the nominative position after ﴿lawlā﴾ (if not for).

The two groups are the caravan (ʿīr) and the army (nafīr). The one "without the thorn" is the caravan, because in it there were only forty riders, whereas the thorn (shawka) was in the army because of its number and equipment. Shawka means sharpness, used metaphorically from the singular of "thorn" (shawk). It is said "shawk al-qanā" (the thorn of the spear) for its point, and from this comes the saying "shākī al-silāḥ" (armed with weapons). That is, you wished that the caravan would be yours, because it is the group that has neither sharpness nor strength. You did not want the other group, but God willed that you turn toward the other group, ﴿so that He might establish the truth by His words﴾.

Here there are questions.

The first question: Is not His words ﴿and God wills to establish the truth by His words﴾, followed afterward by His words ﴿so that He might establish the truth﴾, pure repetition?

The answer: there is no repetition here, because what is meant by the first is the cause of what He promised in this event of victory and triumph over the enemies, and what is meant by the second is the strengthening of the Qur'an and the religion and the support of this law. For what happened at Badr between the believers and the disbelievers was a cause of the might and strength of the religion. For this reason He coupled it with His words ﴿and nullify falsehood﴾, which is polytheism, in contrast to ﴿the truth﴾, which is the religion and faith.

The second question: Truth is true in itself, and falsehood is false in itself. What is established for a thing in itself cannot be brought about by the making of a maker or the act of an agent. So what is meant by establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood?

The answer: what is meant by establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood is making manifest that this truth is truth and making manifest that this falsehood is falsehood. This happens sometimes by displaying the proofs and clear signs, and sometimes by strengthening the leaders of the truth and subduing the leaders of falsehood.

[Page 104]

Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) relied, in the question of the creation of acts, on His words: ﴿so that He might establish the truth﴾. They said: it must be understood to mean that the truth exists and comes to be. The truth is nothing but the religion and belief. This shows that true belief is not attained except by God's bringing it into existence. They said: it is not possible to understand the establishing of the truth as the manifestation of its effects, because that manifestation occurs through the act of servants, so it is also impossible to ascribe that manifestation to God. Nor can it be said that what is meant by its manifestation is placing the proofs upon it, because this meaning is present in relation to the disbeliever and to the Muslim, and before this event and after it. Therefore, restricting this event to this meaning yields no benefit at all.

Know that the Mu'tazilah also relied on this very verse to support their doctrine. They said: this verse indicates that He does not will the establishing of falsehood or the nullifying of truth at all; rather, He, exalted is He, always wills the establishing of truth and the nullifying of falsehood. This refutes the view of one who says that there is no falsehood or disbelief except that God wills it.

Our companions answered that it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that the singular noun with the definite article (al) is restricted to the previously known referent (al-maʿhūd al-sābiq). So this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, willed the establishing of truth and the nullifying of falsehood in this particular instance. Why then do you claim that the matter is the same in all instances? Rather, we have shown by proof that this verse indicates the soundness of our position.

The meaning is that you wished for the caravan to gain wealth, while God, exalted is He, wished that you turn toward the army, because of what it contains of raising up the true religion and uprooting the disbelievers.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 8, verses 9–10:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another."﴾ ﴿Allah did not make it except as good news, and so that your hearts would be reassured by it. Victory is only from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise.﴾

Know that when the Exalted, in the first verse, explained that He establishes the truth and nullifies falsehood, He then explained that He gave them victory when they called for help. On this there are several issues.

**First issue:** The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿idh﴾ ("when") may be His words ﴿and nullify falsehood﴾, in which case the verse is connected to what precedes it. It may also be that the verse begins a new sentence, with the implied meaning "and remember when you sought help."

**Second issue:** Concerning His words ﴿when you sought help﴾, there are two opinions.

The first opinion is that this seeking of help came from the Messenger, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: Umar ibn al-Khattab narrated to me, saying: On the day of Badr, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, and at his companions, who were three hundred and a little more. He faced the qiblah, extended his hands, and was saying: 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this group perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth.' He kept on like this until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr picked it up, put it back on him, then embraced him and said: 'That is enough, O Prophet of Allah. Your pleading with your Lord is enough; He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.'" So this verse was revealed. And when the two sides lined up, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, whichever of us is more upon the truth, give him victory." The Messenger of Allah raised his hands in the supplication mentioned.

The second opinion is that this seeking of help came from the group of believers, because the reason that led the Messenger to seek help was present in them as well. Indeed, their fear was greater than the fear of the Messenger. So the more likely view is that he, peace be upon him, supplicated and pleaded, as has been narrated, and the people were saying "Amin" to his supplication, following him in supplicating in their own selves. Thus the supplication of the Messenger of Allah was transmitted because he raised his voice with it, whereas the supplication of the people was not transmitted. This is the way to reconcile the differing reports on this subject.

**Third issue:** His words ﴿when you sought help﴾ mean "when you asked for relief." One says: "The one who is in trouble: 'Relieve me (aghithni),' that is, 'remove [the distress] from me.'"

Know that when the Exalted related their seeking of help, He explained that He answered them, saying: ﴿that I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾. On this there are several issues.

**First issue:** His words ﴿that I will reinforce you﴾: the original is ﴿bi-anni mumiddukum﴾, and the preposition was deleted, so that "answered" (istajaba) governed it directly, putting its place in the accusative. It is reported from Abu 'Amr that he recited ﴿inni mumiddukum﴾ with a kasrah, either with the sense of "saying" implied, or by treating "answered" as if it were "said," because answering is a kind of speech.

**Second issue:** Nafi' and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, recited ﴿murdafin﴾ with a fathah on the dal, while the rest recited it with a kasrah. Al-Farra' said: ﴿murdifin﴾ means "following one another," one coming right behind another, like the people who ride behind one another on mounts. And ﴿murdafin﴾ means that this was done to them; its meaning is that the Exalted made the angels follow after the Muslims and strengthened them with them.

**Third issue:** The scholars differed over whether the angels fought on the day of Badr. Some said: Gabriel descended with five hundred angels on the right wing, where Abu Bakr was, and Michael with five hundred on the left wing, where 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was, in the form of men wearing white garments, and they fought. It was also said that they fought on the day of Badr but did not fight on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) or on the day of Hunayn. It is reported from Abu Jahl that he said to Ibn Mas'ud: "From where was the voice that we used to hear without seeing a figure?" He replied: "It was from the angels." Abu Jahl said: "They defeated us, not you." And it has been reported that "a man from the Muslims, while he was pursuing a man from the polytheists, heard the sound of a whip-strike above him; he looked at the polytheist, and he had fallen flat on his back with his face split open. The Ansari related this to the Messenger of Allah, and he said: 'You have spoken the truth; that was help from the heavens.'"

Others said: They did not fight; they were only increasing the numbers and strengthening the believers. Otherwise, one angel is sufficient to destroy the whole world, for Gabriel destroyed the cities of the people of Lot with one feather from his wing, and he destroyed the land of Thamud and the people of Salih with a single cry. The discussion of the manner of this reinforcement is given in full in Surah Al 'Imran.

What indicates the correctness of the view that the angels did not descend for fighting is His words: ﴿Allah did not make it except as good news﴾. Al-Farra' said: the pronoun refers back to the reinforcement, and the meaning is: "Allah did not make the reinforcement except as good news." Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah did not make the ones who follow after one another except as good news," and this is better, because reinforcement by the angels was achieved through good news. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on the day of Badr in the arish (a booth or shelter), sitting and supplicating, and Abu Bakr was sitting at his right, with no one else with him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ dozed off briefly, then struck his right hand on the thigh of Abu Bakr and said: 'Rejoice in the victory of Allah; I have seen in my dream Gabriel leading the horses.'" This indicates that the only purpose of their descent was the attainment of this good news, and that negates their engaging in combat.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Victory is only from Allah.﴾ The intended purpose is to alert that although the angels descended in support of the believers, it is obligatory for the believer not to rely upon that; rather, his reliance must be upon the help, victory, guidance and sufficiency of Allah, because Allah is the Almighty (al-'Aziz), the Victor who is not overcome, the Dominant who is not subdued, and the Wise (al-Hakim) in what He sends down of support, placing it in its proper place.
