﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it, to remove from you the defilement of Satan, to strengthen your hearts, and to make your feet firm thereby.﴾ ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks and strike every fingertip of them."﴾ ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, indeed Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: the position of ﴿idh﴾ (when) is in the accusative (naṣb), in the sense of ﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings﴾, "at that time." It is also permissible that the implied meaning is: "Remember when He covered you with drowsiness as a security."

The second issue: There are three readings of ﴿yughashshīkum﴾:

The first: Nafi' read it with a damma on the yā' (ي), a sukūn on the ghayn (غ), and a lightened shīn (ش), i.e., *yughshīkum*, and *an-nu'ās* (النُّعاسَ) in the accusative (naṣb).

The second: *yaghshākum* (يَغْشاكم), with an alif, a fatḥa on the yā', and a sukūn on the ʿayn, and *an-nu'āsu* (النُّعاسُ) in the nominative (raf'). This is the reading of Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir.

The third: the rest read *yughashshīkum* with a shadda on the shīn and a damma on the yā', from *taghshiya* (covering), and *an-nu'āsa* in the accusative, meaning "He clothes you with sleep."

Al-Wahidi said: the first reading is from *aghshā*, the second from *ghashiya*, and the third from *ghashshā*. As for whoever reads *yaghshākum*, his evidence is His saying ﴿security, drowsiness﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:154), meaning: just as the verb there is attributed to the drowsiness and to the security which is the cause of drowsiness, so it is in this verse. And whoever reads *yughshīkum* or *yughashshīkum*, the meaning is one. The revelation has come with both forms in His saying ﴿So We covered them, and they cannot see﴾ (Yā-Sīn 36:9), and He said ﴿Then it covered them with what covered them﴾ (al-Najm 53:54), and He said ﴿as if their faces had been covered﴾ (Yūnus 10:27). On this basis, the verb is attributed to Allah.

The third issue: When He mentioned that He answered their supplication and promised them victory, saying ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾, He then mentioned the aspects of victory, and they are six kinds:

The first: His saying ﴿When He covers you with drowsiness as a security from Him﴾, meaning from the side of Allah.

[Page 107]

Know that every sleep and drowsiness only occurs from the side of Allah, the Most High. So singling out this drowsiness as being from Allah, the Most High, must have some added benefit. They mentioned several aspects of this:

One: when the one who fears his enemy fears greatly for his own self and his family, sleep does not overtake him. When those who fear sleep, they feel secure. So the occurrence of sleep for them at a time of intense fear indicates the removal of fear and the attainment of security.

Two: They feared from many directions:

One: the small number of the Muslims and the large number of the disbelievers.

Two: the equipment, weapons, and provisions of the disbelievers, and the scarcity of these for the believers.

Three: intense thirst. Had this drowsiness and rest not occurred, so that they were able to fight on the second day, the victory would not have been completed.

The third aspect of explaining that this drowsiness was a blessing for them: they did not sleep a deep sleep by which the enemy could overpower them. Rather, it was a drowsiness by which the weariness and exhaustion left them, while they were in a state where, if the enemy had approached them, they would have known of his arrival and would have been able to repel him.

The fourth aspect: this drowsiness covered them all at once despite their large number. The occurrence of drowsiness among a great multitude in intense fear is something extraordinary and against habit. For this reason it was said that this drowsiness was in the category of a miracle (muʿjiz).

If it is said: if the matter is as you have mentioned, why did they fear after that drowsiness?

We say: because it is known that Allah makes the army of Islam victorious and supported, and that does not prevent some of them from being killed.

If it is said: when ﴿yughshīkum﴾ is read with lightening and with shadda and with *an-nu'āsa* in the accusative, the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ﴿amanatan﴾ is the object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu). But when it is read *yaghshākumu an-nu'āsu* (the drowsiness covers you), how is it possible to make His saying ﴿amanatan﴾ an object of purpose, given that the object of purpose must be an action of the doer of the verb it explains?

We say: His saying *yaghshākum*, although apparently attributed to the drowsiness, is in reality attributed to Allah, the Most High. So this explanation is valid when considering the meaning. The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: it is also read *amanatan* with a sukūn on the mīm, and its parallel is *amina amanatan* like *ḥayiya ḥayatan*, and its parallel is *amina amanatan* like *raḥima raḥmatan*. Ibn ʿAbbas said: drowsiness during fighting is a security from Allah, and drowsiness during prayer is a whisper from Satan.

The second kind of Allah's blessings mentioned in this context is His saying: ﴿and He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it and to remove from you the defilement of Satan.﴾ There is no doubt that what is meant by it is rain. It is reported that the people had reached the place of water first and taken control of it, and for this reason they hoped to have the upper hand. The believers were thirsty and afraid, and water for drinking and purification was scarce. Most of them had become junub (in a state of major impurity), and in addition, that place was sand in which feet sink and much dust rises. Fear was present in their hearts because of the large number of the enemy and the abundance of their weapons and tools. When Allah, the Most High, sent down that rain, it became a sign of the attainment of help and victory, and the blessing became great in several ways:

One: the removal of thirst. It is narrated that they dug a place in the sand, and it became like a large pool, and water gathered in it until they drank from it, purified themselves, and took provisions.

Two: they bathed with that water, and the state of junub was removed from them. It is known by habit that the believer almost loathes himself when he is junub, and grieves when he cannot bathe, and his heart is troubled because of this. Therefore, the Most High and Most Holy counted the enabling of their purification among the blessings He bestowed upon them.

[Page 108]

Three: when they became thirsty and did not find water, then slept and became junub, their need for water doubled. Then the rain fell, so that calamity and trial were removed from them, and the goal was achieved. In this state there is what may be taken as evidence of the removal of hardship, the arrival of ease, and joy.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: what is meant by it is the wet dream (iḥtilām), because that is from the whisperings of Satan.

The second: when the disbelievers camped by the water, Satan whispered to them and frightened them of destruction. When the rain fell, that whispering ceased. It is narrated that when they slept and most of them had a wet dream, Iblis appeared to them and said: "You claim that you are upon the truth, yet you pray in a state of junub, and you are thirsty. Had you been upon the truth, they would not have overcome you over the water." So Allah sent down the rain until the valley flowed, the Muslims made pools and bathed, and the sand became packed until feet could firmly stand upon it.

The third: what is meant by the defilement of Satan is everything that Satan calls to of disobedience and corruption.

If it is said: which of these three aspects is the most preferable?

We say: His saying ﴿li-yuṭahhirakum﴾ (to purify you) means to remove junub from you. So if we interpret His saying ﴿and remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾ as referring to junub, it would entail repetition, which is contrary to the original principle. It can be answered that what is meant by ﴿li-yuṭahhirakum﴾ is the attainment of legal purification (ṭahāra sharʿiyya), and what is meant by ﴿and remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾ is the removal of the substance of semen from their limbs, for it is something repugnant. Then we say: interpreting it as the removal of the trace of the wet dream is preferable to interpreting it as the removal of whispering. That is because the effect of water in removing a physical substance from a limb is a real effect, whereas its effect in removing whispering from the heart is a figurative effect, and interpreting the word literally is preferable to interpreting it figuratively. Know that if we interpret the verse in this way, it necessarily follows that semen is definitively the defilement of Satan, and this entails ruling that it is absolutely impure, based on His saying ﴿and the defilement, keep away from﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:5).

The third kind of blessings mentioned in this verse is His saying ﴿and to strengthen your hearts﴾. What is meant is that by the descent of this rain their hearts became strong, and fear and dread were removed from them. The meaning of *rabṭ* (binding) in language is tightening, and we have already mentioned this in His saying ﴿and be steadfast﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:200). It is said of everyone who endures a matter that he has bound his heart upon it, as if he restrained his heart from trembling. One says: "a man is *rābiṭ*," meaning restraining. Al-Wahidi said: it seems that *ʿalā* (upon) here is superfluous, and the meaning is "and to bind your hearts with victory." But what has been stated in its explanation seems not to be superfluous, because the word ʿalā indicates elevation. So the meaning is that the hearts were filled with that binding, as if it had risen over them and ascended above them.

The fourth kind of blessings mentioned here is His saying ﴿and to make your feet firm thereby﴾. They mentioned several aspects regarding it:

One: that rain moistened that sand and made it such that their feet did not sink into it, so they were able to walk on it as they wished. Had it not been for this rain, they would not have been able to do so. On this interpretation, the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ (thereby) refers to the rain.

Two: what is meant is that the binding of their hearts caused the firmness of their feet, because whoever has a weak heart flees and does not stand firm. When Allah strengthened their hearts, He certainly made their feet firm. On this interpretation, the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to the binding.

Three: it is reported that when the rain fell, the opposite of what happened to the believers happened to the disbelievers. This is because the place where the disbelievers had camped was a place of dust and mud, and when the rain fell, the mud became severe, which prevented them from walking as they wished. So His saying ﴿and to make the feet firm thereby﴾ indicates, by implication, that the condition of the enemies was contrary to this.

[Page 109]

Fifth type of blessing mentioned here: His saying, ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you"﴾. There are two discussions regarding this.

The first: al-Zajjaj said: ﴿idh﴾ (when) is in the accusative position, and the implied meaning is: "and so that He might bind your hearts and firm your feet by it, at the time when He revealed to the angels such-and-such," and it is permissible that it be upon the assumption of "remember" (udhkuru).

The second: His saying, ﴿I am with you﴾, has two aspects.

The first: that the intended meaning is that He, Exalted, revealed to the angels, "I am with the believers, so support them and firm them up." This second view is preferred, because the purpose of this statement is to remove fear, and the angels were not afraid of the disbelievers; rather, it is the Muslims who were afraid.

Then He said: ﴿So firm up those who have believed.﴾ They differed about the manner of this firming up in several ways:

The first: they informed the Messenger (ﷺ) that Allah is the supporter of the believers, and the Messenger informed the believers of that; this is the firming up.

The second: just as Satan can cast whisperings into a human being, so too the angel can cast inspiration into him; this is the firming up in this regard.

The third: the angels would take the forms of men among their acquaintances, and they would aid them with victory, triumph and success.

The sixth type of blessing mentioned in this verse: His saying, ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾. This is among the great blessings, because the commander of the self is the heart. So when Allah, Exalted, explained that He had bound the hearts of the believers, meaning that He strengthened them and removed fear from them, He mentioned that He cast terror and fear into the hearts of the disbelievers. That was among the greatest of Allah's blessings upon the believers.

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: it is a command to the angels connected to His saying, ﴿So firm up﴾. It was said: rather, it is a command to the believers, and this is more correct, since we have explained that He did not send down the angels for the sake of fighting and warfare. Know that when He, Exalted, explained that all the requisites of victory and triumph had been realized for the Muslims, at this point He commanded them to fight against them.

Regarding His saying, ﴿So strike above the necks﴾, there are two views:

The first: that what is above the neck is the head, so this is a command to remove the head from the body.

The second: that His saying, ﴿So strike above the necks﴾, means: strike the necks.

Then He said: ﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾, meaning the extremities of the hands and feet. Then they differed: some said the intended meaning is that they strike them however they wish, because what is above the neck is the head, the noblest of the limbs, and the fingertip is an expression for the weakest of the limbs; so He mentioned the noblest and the lowest as an alert to all the limbs. Others said: rather, the intended meaning is either killing, which is striking what is above the necks, or cutting off the fingertips, because the fingers are the instruments for grasping swords, spears and all other weapons; so if their fingertips are cut off, they become unable to fight.

Know that when He, Exalted, mentioned these many aspects of blessing upon the Muslims, He said: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾. The meaning: He, Exalted, cast them into disgrace and punishment through these many aspects because they opposed Allah and His Messenger. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿shaqqu﴾ means they went to the side and became on a side other than the side of the believers; the shiqq is the side. And ﴿they opposed Allah﴾ is a metaphor, and the meaning is: they opposed the friends of Allah and the religion of Allah.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾. Meaning: what befell them on that day is a small thing compared with what Allah has prepared for them of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and the purpose of this is to deter from disbelief and to warn against it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That, so taste it; and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾. In it are two issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: ﴿That﴾ (dhalikum) is in the nominative case because it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the estimation is: the matter is that, so taste it. It is not permissible for ﴿dhalikum﴾ to be the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿fa-dhuquhu﴾ as its predicate, because what follows the fa' cannot be a predicate of the subject, except where the subject is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) or an indefinite noun described by a qualifier (nakira mawsufa), as in: "The one who comes to me, then for him is a dirham," and "Every man in the house, then he is honored." As for saying "Zayd, then he is departing," it is not permissible unless we make Zayd the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimation is: "This is Zayd, then he is departing," meaning, then he is departing.

The second issue: When Exalted is He stated that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, then Allah is severe in punishment, He then explained the nature of His punishment, and that it may be hastened in this world and may be deferred in the Hereafter. By His saying ﴿That, so taste it﴾ He drew attention to what is hastened, namely the killing and capture, indicating that this is slight in comparison with what is deferred for them in the Hereafter. Therefore He called it "taste" (dhawq), because tasting is only the recognition of the taste of a small amount so that by it the state of the large amount may be known. So what befell them of pains in this world is like a small taste in comparison with the great matter prepared for them in the Hereafter. His saying ﴿so taste it﴾ indicates that tasting occurs by a means other than perceiving the specific flavors, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I spend the night with my Lord, Who feeds me and gives me drink." This indicates the affirmation of tasting, eating and drinking by a spiritual means distinct from the physical means.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 15–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahfan), do not turn your backs to them.﴾ ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless it is a maneuver for battle (mutaharrifan li-qital) or withdrawing to join a company (mutahayyizan ila fi'ah), he has certainly earned anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Azhari said: The origin of zahf is for the child, which is that he crawls on his buttocks before he stands. The walking of the two groups, each going toward the other for battle, was likened to the crawling of the child, so each group walks slowly toward the other group before drawing close for striking. Tha'lab said: zahf is walking little by little toward a thing, and from it comes zihaf in poetry, where a letter falls out from between two letters so that one of them crawls toward the other.

Having understood this, we say: His saying, ﴿when you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahfan)﴾, meaning advancing upon one another, is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It may be a state of the disbelievers, and it may be a state of the addressees, who are the believers. Zahf is a verbal noun described by the attribute, like 'adl and ridan, and for this reason it is not made plural. The meaning: when you go toward them for battle, do not flee. The meaning of ﴿do not turn your backs to them﴾ is: do not make your backs face the side where they are. Then, when He, exalted is He, forbade this fleeing, He clarified that this fleeing is prohibited except in two situations:

One of them: that one should be maneuvering for battle (mutaharrifan li-qital), and what is meant by it is that one makes his enemy imagine that he is routing, then turns back upon him. This is one of the doors of the tricks and stratagems of war. It is said: taharrafa and inharafa when he moved away from the direction of straightness.

The second: His saying, ﴿or withdrawing to join a company (mutahayyizan ila fi'ah)﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: tahayyuz is withdrawal, and it has two forms: tahayyuz and tahawwuz. al-Wahidi said: its origin is hawz, which is gathering, it is said: I gathered it, so it withdrew, tahawwaza and tahayyaza, when it joined together and gathered. Then withdrawal was called tahayyuz, because the one who withdraws from a side separates from it and inclines to another.

Having understood this, we say: fi'ah means a group. So when this one withdrawing is like a lone individual, and among the disbelievers there is great number, and that lone individual is inclined to think that if he stands firm he will be killed without benefit, but if he withdraws to a group he would be hopeful of deliverance and eager against the enemy through numbers, it may then be obligatory for him to withdraw to this group, let alone that it be permissible. The conclusion is that fleeing from the enemy is forbidden except in these two situations.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, except in these two situations, ﴿has certainly earned anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

The second issue: The judge (al-Qadi) argued by this verse for the certainty of the threat against the sinful among the people of prayer (ahl al-salah), because the verse indicates that whoever flees, except in these two situations, deserves the anger of Allah and the fire of Hell. He said: The Murji'ah cannot carry this verse upon the disbelievers only, excluding the people of prayer, as they do with the rest of the verses of threat, because this threat is specific to the people of prayer.

Know that this issue we have discussed exhaustively in Surat al-Baqarah, and we mentioned that deriving proof from these apparent texts yields only conjecture (zann), and we also mentioned that they are opposed by the general promises, and we mentioned that preference lies with the general promises for many reasons, so there is no benefit in repetition.

The third issue: The exegetes differed as to whether this ruling is specific to the day of Badr or is general in application. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak that this ruling is specific to those who fled on the day of Badr. They said: The reasons for the specificity of the day of Badr to this ruling are several:

One of them: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was present on the day of Badr, and with his presence no other is counted in it, either because the other companies are not equated with him, rather he is more noble and higher than all, or because Allah, exalted is He, had promised him victory and triumph, so there was no need for them to withdraw to another group.

The second: that He, exalted is He, made the matter severe for the people of Badr, because it was the first jihad, and if a rout had occurred to the Muslims in it, a great disruption would have followed. For this reason it was obligatory upon them to be strict and exert themselves, and for this reason Allah forbade taking ransom from the captives on that day.

The second view: that the ruling mentioned in this verse is general in all wars, by the evidence that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve﴾ is general and therefore encompasses all battles. At most, it was revealed concerning the event of Badr, but the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

The fourth issue: They differed as to whether the permissibility of withdrawing to a company is forbidden when the army is large, or whether it is established only when there is lightness in the army. Some said: when the army is large, they do not have this withdrawal. Others said: rather, all are alike. And this is more fitting to the apparent meaning, because it did not distinguish.

The second: that He, exalted is He, made the matter severe for the people of Badr, because it was the first jihad, and if a rout had occurred to the Muslims in it, a great disruption would have followed. For this reason it was obligatory upon them to be strict and exert themselves, and for this reason Allah forbade taking ransom from the captives on that day.

The second view: that the ruling mentioned in this verse is general in all wars, by the evidence that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve﴾ is general and therefore encompasses all battles. At most, it was revealed concerning the event of Badr, but the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

The fourth issue: They differed as to whether the permissibility of withdrawing to a company is forbidden when the army is large, or whether it is established only when there is lightness in the army. Some said: when the army is large, they do not have this withdrawal. Others said: rather, all are alike. And this is more fitting to the apparent meaning, because it did not distinguish.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 17–18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw, that He might test the believers with a good test from Him. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ In it are several issues:

The first issue: Mujahid said: They disagreed on the day of Badr. One of them said, "I killed him," and another said, "I killed him." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse, meaning that this great defeat did not come about from you, but came about through the help of Allah. It is narrated that "when Quraysh appeared, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Here is Quraysh, who have come with their arrogance and their pride, denying Your Messenger. O Allah, I ask You for what You have promised me.' Then Jibril descended and said: 'Take a handful of dust and throw it at them.' When the two hosts met, he said to Ali: 'Give me a handful of dust from the pebbles of the valley,' so he threw it into their faces and said: 'May the faces be disfigured.' No polytheist remained except that he was occupied with his eyes, and they fled." The author of al-Kashshaf said: The fa' in His saying, ﴿So you did not kill them﴾, is the answer to an omitted condition, its estimate being: If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them, but Allah killed them.

Then He said: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, meaning that the handful of pebbles which you threw, you did not really throw, because your throwing does not reach its effect except what the throwing of the rest of mankind reaches. But Allah threw it when He made the parts of that dust penetrate and brought them to their eyes. So the form of the throwing proceeded from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and its effect proceeded from Allah. For this meaning, the negation and the affirmation are valid concerning it.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with this verse that the actions of servants are created by Allah, exalted is He. The manner of the inference is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾, and it is known that they were wounded, so this indicates that the occurrence of those actions came from Allah. Also, His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ affirmed that he, peace be upon him, was a thrower, and negated from him that he was a thrower, so it is obligatory to interpret it as meaning that he threw by acquisition (kasb), and did not throw by creation (khalq).

If it is said: As for His saying, ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that the killing of the disbelievers was only made easy by the help of Allah, His support and His strengthening, so this attribution is valid.

The second: that the wounding was by them, and the taking out of the soul was by Allah, exalted is He. The estimate is: "So you did not cause them to die, but Allah caused them to die."

As for His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾:
The judge (al-Qadi) said: In it there are several matters:

Among them: that a single throw does not necessitate the arrival of the dust into their eyes, and bringing the parts of the dust to their eyes was only by the bringing of Allah, exalted is He.

Among them: that the dust he threw was little, so it is impossible for that amount to reach the eyes of all of them. This indicates that He, exalted is He, added to it other parts of the dust and brought them to their eyes.

Among them: that at the time of his throwing, Allah, exalted is He, cast terror into their hearts, so what was meant by His saying: ﴿But it was Allah who threw﴾ is that He, exalted is He, threw their hearts with that terror.

The answer: Everything you have mentioned is a departure from the apparent meaning, and the basic principle in speech is its literal sense.

If they say: Rational proofs prevent the claim that the act of the servant is created by Allah, exalted is He, so we say: Far from it! The rational proofs are on our side, and the textual proofs are established in support of the correctness of our position, so you cannot depart from the apparent meaning to the figurative. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: It was read (wa-lakin-i Allahu qatalahum. Wa-lakin-i Allahu rama) with the lightening of wa-lakin and raising of what follows it.

The fourth issue: Regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse there are three opinions:

The first, which is the view of most of the exegetes, is that it was revealed on the day of Badr, and the meaning is that he, peace be upon him, took a handful of pebbles and threw them at the faces of the people and said, "May the faces be disfigured," so no polytheist remained except that some of it entered his eyes and nostrils, and that throwing was a cause of the defeat, and this verse was revealed concerning it.

The second: that it was revealed on the day of Khaybar. It is narrated that "he, peace be upon him, took a bow while he was at the gate of Khaybar and shot an arrow, and the arrow came until it killed Ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his horse," and so ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾ was revealed.

The third: that it was revealed on the day of Uhud, concerning the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf. That is because "he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said: 'O Muhammad, who will give life to this when it is decayed?' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'Allah will give it life, then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life, then He will cause you to enter the Fire.' Then he was taken prisoner on the day of Badr, and when he was ransomed he said to the Messenger of Allah: 'I have a horse which I feed every day a farq of maize, so that I may kill you on it.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Rather, I will kill you, if Allah wills.' When it was the day of Uhud, Ubayy came charging on that horse until he approached the Messenger, peace be upon him. Some men of the Muslims intercepted him to kill him, but he, peace be upon him, said: 'Withdraw!' and he struck him with a spear, breaking one of his ribs, so he was carried away and died on part of the way." It was concerning this that the verse was revealed. The most correct view is that this verse was revealed on the day of Badr, for otherwise an alien statement would enter into the course of the narrative, and that is not fitting. Rather, it is not far-fetched that all the other events fall under it, because the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not in the specificity of the occasion.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He might test the believers with a good test from Him﴾, this is conjoined to His saying: ﴿But it was Allah who threw﴾, and what is meant by this test is bounty, i.e., He bestows upon them a great blessing through victory, spoils, reward and recompense.

The judge said: Were it not that the exegetes agreed to interpret the trial here as bounty, it would have been possible to take it as a trial through obligation in what comes after it, namely the jihad, so that it might be said that what He, exalted is He, did on the day of Badr was the cause of the occurrence of a heavy obligation upon them in the raids that followed.

Then He, exalted is He, concluded this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, i.e., Hearing of your speech, Knowing of the states of your hearts. This runs in the manner of warning and admonition, so that the servant does not become deceived by the outward appearances of affairs, and knows that the Creator, exalted is He, is aware of everything in the inner thoughts and hearts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is so, and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿If you seek a decision, then indeed the decision has come to you. And if you desist, it is better for you. And if you return, We will return. And your company will not avail you anything, however numerous it is. And indeed Allah is with the believers.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (muwahhinu) with a shaddah on the ha' from al-tawhin (weakening), and kayda (plot) in the accusative. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read muwahhinu kayda in the genitive construction (idafah). The rest read muhinu with a light (unshaddah) ha', and kayda in the accusative. A similar case is His saying: ﴿removers of His harm﴾ [al-Zumar: 38], read with tanwin and with idafah.

The second issue: The discussion regarding this and its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is as in His saying: ﴿That is so, so taste it﴾.

The third issue: Allah's weakening of their plot takes place through several things: by informing the believers of their weak points ('awrat), by casting terror into their hearts, by dividing their word (unity), and by undoing what they had firmly determined, due to the difference in their resolutions. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He informs the Messenger of Allah and says: 'I have indeed weakened the plot of your enemy, until you have killed their best and taken their nobles captive.'"

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you seek a decision, then indeed the decision has come to you﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi, that it is addressed to the disbelievers. It is related that Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O Allah, give victory to the better of the two religions and the more deserving of it." It is also related that he said: "O Allah, whichever of us is more severing of kinship and more wicked, destroy him this morning." Al-Suddi said: When the polytheists prepared to go out to Badr, they took hold of the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O Allah, give victory to the higher of the two armies, the more guided of the two groups, the most noble of the two parties, and the better of the two religions." So Allah revealed this verse. The meaning: If you seek victory, i.e., seek help for the more guided of the two groups and the most noble of the two parties, then indeed victory has come to you. Others said: If you seek a judgment, then indeed judgment has come.

The second opinion: That it is addressed to the believers. It is related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw the polytheists and their great number, he sought help from Allah, and so did the Companions. He asked for what Allah had promised him of one of the two groups, and humbled himself before Allah. So He said: ﴿If you seek a decision, then indeed the decision has come to you.﴾ The meaning is that he asked for the help which had been promised beforehand, so indeed the decision has come to you, i.e., what you were promised has come about, so thank Allah and hold fast to His obedience. The qadi said: This opinion is preferable, because His saying ﴿then indeed the decision has come to you﴾ befits only the believers. As for if we take al-fath (the decision) to mean clarification, judgment and ruling, there is nothing preventing it from being meant for the disbelievers.

As for His saying: ﴿And if you desist, it is better for you﴾, the interpretation of this verse depends on what we have mentioned, namely whether His saying ﴿If you seek a decision, then indeed the decision has come to you﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers or to the believers.

If we say that this is addressed to the disbelievers, the interpretation of this verse is: If you desist from fighting the Messenger, his enmity and his denial, then it is better for you. As for religion, by deliverance from punishment and success with reward. As for this world, by deliverance from killing, captivity and plunder.

Page 115
Then He said: ﴿And if you return﴾, i.e., to killing, ﴿We will return﴾, i.e., We will give them power over you. You have indeed witnessed that on the day of Badr and you knew the effect of Allah's support for the believers over you. ﴿And your company will not avail you anything﴾, i.e., the multitude of your hosts, just as it did not avail on the day of Badr. As for if we say that this is addressed to the believers, the interpretation of this verse is: If you desist from disputing about the matter of the spoils (al-Anfal) and desist from seeking ransom for the captives, (then it is better for you), for there had occurred among them a dispute on the day of Badr regarding these matters, to the point that Allah rebuked them with His saying: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ [al-Anfal: 68]. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you desist﴾ from the like of it, ﴿it is better for you. And if you return﴾ to those disputes, ﴿We will return﴾ to abandoning your support, because the promise of Our support for you is conditional upon your continuing in obedience and abstaining from opposition. Then your company will not benefit you, for Allah is only with the believers who do not commit sins.

Know that most of the exegetes took His saying ﴿If you seek a decision﴾ to be addressed to the disbelievers, and they argued from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾, and they thought that this befits only fighting. We have already shown that this admits of being understood in terms of what we have mentioned concerning the conditions of the believers, so this preference falls away.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed Allah is with the believers﴾, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read ﴿wa-anna Allaha﴾ with a fatha on the alif of anna, while the rest read it with a kasra. As for the fatha, it is said that it is by supposition: "and because Allah is with the believers." It is also said that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to His saying: ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers.﴾ As for the kasra, it is because it is a new sentence (ibtida'). And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 20–22:

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, obey God and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾ ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being disinclined.﴾

Know that when God addressed the believers with His words, ﴿And if you cease, it is better for you; and if you return, We will return; and your company will not avail you at all﴾, He followed it with their discipline, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey God and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing.﴾ He did not specify what they were hearing, but since the discourse from the beginning of the surah up to this point concerned the jihad (holy struggle), it is known that the intended meaning of "while you are hearing" is hearing his call to jihad. Then, jihad involves two matters:

The first: risking one's life.

The second: gaining wealth.

Since risking one's life is extremely difficult for everyone, and leaving wealth after having the ability to take it is extremely difficult, God, exalted is He, emphasized the discipline in this regard, saying: ﴿obey God and His Messenger﴾ in responding to jihad, and in responding to leaving wealth when God commands its abandonment. The purpose is to affirm what we mentioned in the explanation of His words: ﴿Say, the spoils are for God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1].

If it is asked: Why did He say "and do not turn away from him," making the pronoun singular, when God and His Messenger were mentioned earlier?

We say: God commanded obedience to God and obedience to His Messenger. Then He said: ﴿and do not turn away,﴾ because turning away is only valid with regard to the Messenger, by turning away from him, from accepting his word, and from aiding him in jihad.

Then He said, emphasizing this: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ The meaning is that a person cannot accept and commit to a legal obligation except after hearing it. So He made hearing a kinaya (metaphor or allusion) for acceptance. From this is the saying "God hears whoever praises Him." The meaning is: do not be like those who say with their tongues, "We have accepted God's commands," while in their hearts they do not accept them. This is a description of the hypocrites, as God informed about them in His words: ﴿And when they meet those who have believed, they say, "We have believed"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾ They differed concerning "living creatures" (dawabb). It was said: He likened them to beasts because of their ignorance and their deviation from benefiting from what is said to them; therefore He described them as deaf, dumb, and as not reasoning. And it was said: rather, they are among the beasts, because the term refers to whatever crawls upon the earth, and He did not mention it in the context of comparison, but described them with an attribute suited to them in the manner of dispraise, as one says of someone who does not understand speech: "he is a shadow, a body, and a ruin," by way of dispraise.

Then He said: ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being disinclined.﴾ The meaning is that whatever exists, God must know it; so the absence of God's knowledge of its existence is a necessary consequence of its non-existence. Therefore it is fitting to express its non-existence in itself by God's not knowing its existence. The sense of the statement is: if good had existed in them, God would have made them hear the proofs and admonitions with the hearing of instruction and understanding; but if He had made them hear after He knew that there was no good in them, they would not have benefited from them, and they would have turned away while being disinclined.

It was said: The disbelievers asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) to bring back to life for them Qusayy ibn Kilab and others of their dead, so that they might inform them of the truth of his prophethood. So God made clear that if He knew good in them, namely their benefiting from the words of these dead, He would have revived them so that they could hear their speech. But God knew of them that they would say this only out of obstinacy and stubborn defiance, and that if God made them hear His speech, they would turn away from accepting the truth and would be averse to it.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾ They differed concerning "living creatures" (dawabb). It was said: He likened them to beasts because of their ignorance and their deviation from benefiting from what is said to them; therefore He described them as deaf, dumb, and as not reasoning. And it was said: rather, they are among the beasts, because the term refers to whatever crawls upon the earth, and He did not mention it in the context of comparison, but described them with an attribute suited to them in the manner of dispraise, as one says of someone who does not understand speech: "he is a shadow, a body, and a ruin," by way of dispraise.

Then He said: ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being disinclined.﴾ The meaning is that whatever exists, God must know it; so the absence of God's knowledge of its existence is a necessary consequence of its non-existence. Therefore it is fitting to express its non-existence in itself by God's not knowing its existence. The sense of the statement is: if good had existed in them, God would have made them hear the proofs and admonitions with the hearing of instruction and understanding; but if He had made them hear after He knew that there was no good in them, they would not have benefited from them, and they would have turned away while being disinclined.

It was said: The disbelievers asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) to bring back to life for them Qusayy ibn Kilab and others of their dead, so that they might inform them of the truth of his prophethood. So God made clear that if He knew good in them, namely their benefiting from the words of these dead, He would have revived them so that they could hear their speech. But God knew of them that they would say this only out of obstinacy and stubborn defiance, and that if God made them hear His speech, they would turn away from accepting the truth and would be averse to it.

[Page 116]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 20–22:

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, obey God and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾ ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being disinclined.﴾

Know that when God addressed the believers with His words, ﴿And if you cease, it is better for you; and if you return, We will return; and your company will not avail you at all﴾, He followed it with their discipline, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey God and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing.﴾ He did not specify what they were hearing, but since the discourse from the beginning of the surah up to this point concerned the jihad (holy struggle), it is known that the intended meaning of "while you are hearing" is hearing his call to jihad. Then, jihad involves two matters:

The first: risking one's life.

The second: gaining wealth.

Since risking one's life is extremely difficult for everyone, and leaving wealth after having the ability to take it is extremely difficult, God, exalted is He, emphasized the discipline in this regard, saying: ﴿obey God and His Messenger﴾ in responding to jihad, and in responding to leaving wealth when God commands its abandonment. The purpose is to affirm what we mentioned in the explanation of His words: ﴿Say, the spoils are for God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1].

If it is asked: Why did He say "and do not turn away from him," making the pronoun singular, when God and His Messenger were mentioned earlier?

We say: God commanded obedience to God and obedience to His Messenger. Then He said: ﴿and do not turn away,﴾ because turning away is only valid with regard to the Messenger, by turning away from him, from accepting his word, and from aiding him in jihad.

Then He said, emphasizing this: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ The meaning is that a person cannot accept and commit to a legal obligation except after hearing it. So He made hearing a kinaya (metaphor or allusion) for acceptance. From this is the saying "God hears whoever praises Him." The meaning is: do not be like those who say with their tongues, "We have accepted God's commands," while in their hearts they do not accept them. This is a description of the hypocrites, as God informed about them in His words: ﴿And when they meet those who have believed, they say, "We have believed"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.﴾ They differed concerning "living creatures" (dawabb). It was said: He likened them to beasts because of their ignorance and their deviation from benefiting from what is said to them; therefore He described them as deaf, dumb, and as not reasoning. And it was said: rather, they are among the beasts, because the term refers to whatever crawls upon the earth, and He did not mention it in the context of comparison, but described them with an attribute suited to them in the manner of dispraise, as one says of someone who does not understand speech: "he is a shadow, a body, and a ruin," by way of dispraise.

Then He said: ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being disinclined.﴾ The meaning is that whatever exists, God must know it; so the absence of God's knowledge of its existence is a necessary consequence of its non-existence. Therefore it is fitting to express its non-existence in itself by God's not knowing its existence. The sense of the statement is: if good had existed in them, God would have made them hear the proofs and admonitions with the hearing of instruction and understanding; but if He had made them hear after He knew that there was no good in them, they would not have benefited from them, and they would have turned away while being disinclined.

It was said: The disbelievers asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) to bring back to life for them Qusayy ibn Kilab and others of their dead, so that they might inform them of the truth of his prophethood. So God made clear that if He knew good in them, namely their benefiting from the words of these dead, He would have revived them so that they could hear their speech. But God knew of them that they would say this only out of obstinacy and stubborn defiance, and that if God made them hear His speech, they would turn away from accepting the truth and would be averse to it.

[Page 116]

In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** God has judged them to be turning away from the proofs and averse to the truth, and that they will never accept it or benefit from it at all. We say: it must be impossible for faith to proceed from them, because if faith did proceed from them, then either that faith would exist while this report remains true, or it would exist while the report turns into a lie. The first is impossible, because the existence of faith together with the report of the absence of faith is a combination of contradictories, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, because the reversal of God's true report into a lie is impossible, especially in a past time that has passed. The same applies to the reversal of God's knowledge into ignorance, and its demonstration has been given many times before.

**The second issue:** The grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) say that the particle ﴿ولو﴾ (*law*, "if/had") is used to indicate the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. So when you say, "Law ji'tani la-akramtuka" ("If you had come to me, I would have honored you"), it conveys that the coming did not occur and the honoring did not occur. Some jurists (al-fuqaha') said that it conveys only implication (al-istilzam), and does not convey the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. The evidence for this is the verse and the report. As for the verse, it is this verse. Its demonstration: if the word ﴿ولو﴾ conveyed what they said, then His saying ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ would imply that God did not know any good in them and did not make them hear. Then He said ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾, so its meaning would be that He did not make them hear and that they did not turn away. But the absence of turning away is one of the good things, so the beginning of the speech implies the negation of good, and its end implies the occurrence of good, and this is contradictory. It is thus established that the view that ﴿ولو﴾ conveys the negation of one thing because of the negation of another necessitates this contradiction, so it must not be adopted. As for the report, it is his peace be upon him saying: "How excellent a man Suhayb is; if he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." If the word "law" conveyed what they said, the meaning would become that he feared Allah and disobeyed Him, and that is contradictory. It is thus established that the particle ﴿ولو﴾ does not convey the negation of one thing because of the negation of another, but conveys only mere implication.
Know that this proof is the better one, but it is contrary to the view of the majority of the men of letters (jumhur al-udaba').

**The third issue:** God's objects of knowledge are of four kinds:

First: the totality of existing things.

Second: the totality of non-existing things.

Third: how each one of the existing things would be if it were non-existent.

Fourth: how each one of the non-existing things would be if it were existent.

The first two kinds are knowledge of what actually is, and the last two kinds are knowledge of the hypothetical, which is not actual. So His saying ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ is from the second kind, which is knowledge of hypotheticals, and it is not among the kinds of knowledge of actualities. A parallel to it is His, exalted is He, quoting the hypocrites: ﴿If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them, and if they are fought, they will not support them, and if they support them, they will surely turn their backs﴾ [al-Hashr: 12]. So God knows, regarding the non-existent, how it would be if it were existent. Also His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾; so He informs about the non-existent how it would be if it were existent.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life. And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.﴾ There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: Abu 'Ubayd and al-Zajjaj said that ﴿istajibu﴾ (respond) means ajibu (answer). And he cited the verse of the poet:

"So no answerer answered him at that time."

The second issue: Most jurists hold that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation (wujub), and they relied on this verse for the soundness of their position from two aspects:

The first aspect: Everyone whom Allah commands to an act has been called by Him to that act, and this verse indicates that there must be a response to everything Allah calls to.

If it is said: His saying, ﴿respond to Allah﴾ is a command. Why do you say that it indicates obligation? Is the dispute not precisely about this? So the outcome of this statement returns to proving that the command implies obligation on the basis that this command conveys obligation, and this requires proving a thing by itself, which is impossible.

The answer: It is known by necessity that everything Allah commands is recommended and encouraged. So if we take His saying, ﴿respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ in this sense, it would be like clarifying the obvious, and that would be futile. Therefore it must be taken to carry an additional benefit, namely obligation, in order to preserve this text from being rendered void. This is reinforced by the fact that His saying, exalted is He, after that, ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered﴾ functions as a threat and warning, and that is fitting only for obligation.

The second aspect: Regarding the use of this verse to establish this claim, what Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, reported: that "the Prophet ﷺ passed by the door of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and called to him while he was praying, so he shortened his prayer, then came and said: 'What prevented you from responding to me?' He said: I was praying. He said: 'Were you not informed in what was revealed to me: Respond to Allah and to the Messenger?' He said: 'Indeed, I will not, I will answer you whenever you call.'"

The argument from it is that when the Prophet ﷺ called him and he did not respond, he rebuked him for not responding, and he used this verse in establishing that rebuke. Were it not for this verse's indication of obligation, that inference would not be valid. And the claim of one who says that the issue of the command implying obligation is a definitive matter, so it is not permissible to rely on a solitary report in it, is weak, because we do not concede that the issue of the command implying obligation is a definitive matter; rather, according to us it is a speculative matter, because its purpose is action, and speculative proofs are sufficient for practical matters.

If they say: He did not command responding absolutely, but rather with a specific condition, namely His saying, ﴿when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾. Why do you say that this condition is present in all commands?

We say: The story of Ubayy ibn Ka'b indicates that this ruling is general and not restricted to a specific condition. Moreover, it is not possible to take "life" here to mean life itself, because giving life to the living is impossible. So it must be taken to mean something else, namely attaining reward. Everything Allah calls to and encourages includes a reward, so this ruling is general for all commands, and that yields the intended conclusion.

The third issue: They mentioned several interpretations of His saying, ﴿when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾:

The first: al-Suddi said: It is faith and Islam, and in it is life, because faith is the life of the heart and disbelief is its death. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ [Yunus: 31]. It was said: the believer from the disbeliever.

The second: Qatada said: It means the Qur'an, i.e., respond to what is in the Qur'an, for in it is life, salvation, and protection. The Qur'an was called life because the Qur'an is the cause of knowledge, and knowledge is life, so it is permissible to call the cause of life "life."

The third: Most scholars said: ﴿that which gives you life﴾ is jihad. Then, regarding the reason jihad is called life, there are several aspects:

One of them: The weakening of one of the two enemies is life for the second enemy, so the affair of the Muslims grows strong and becomes great only through jihad against the disbelievers.

The second: Jihad is a cause of attaining martyrdom, and martyrdom necessitates eternal life. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169].

The third: Jihad may lead to being killed, and being killed leads to the Hereafter, and the Hereafter is the source of life. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the [true] life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64], i.e., the eternal life.

The fourth view: ﴿that which gives you life﴾ means every truth and righteousness. On this interpretation, the Qur'an, faith, jihad, and all acts of righteousness and obedience are included. The intended meaning of His saying, ﴿that which gives you life﴾ is the good, eternal life, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

* * *

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾ — its interpretation differs according to the differences of people concerning predestination (jabr) and divine decree (qadar). As for those who hold the doctrine of compulsion (jabr), al-Wahidi related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak: He intervenes between the disbelieving man and his obedience, and intervenes between the obedient man and his disobedience. The happy one is one whom Allah makes happy, and the wretched one is one whom Allah misguides, and the hearts are in the hand of Allah, He turns them however He wills. So when the disbeliever wants to believe while Allah does not will his faith, He intervenes between him and his heart; and when the believer wants to disbelieve while Allah does not will his disbelief, He intervenes between him and his heart.

I say: We have demonstrated by rational proofs that the matter is indeed so, because the states of the heart are either beliefs or volitions and motives. As for beliefs: they are either knowledge or ignorance. As for knowledge, it is impossible for an agent to intend to acquire it unless he knows that it is knowledge, and he does not know that unless he knows that this belief corresponds to the known object, and he does not know that unless his knowledge of the object preceded it; and that necessitates the thing depending on itself. As for ignorance, a person absolutely does not choose or will it unless he supposes that this belief is knowledge, and this supposition arises only from a prior ignorance, and that too necessitates the thing depending on itself.

As for motives and volitions: their occurrence, if not by an agent, entails originating without an originator. If it is by an agent, that agent is either the servant or Allah, exalted is He. The first is invalid, for otherwise that intention would depend on another intention, which is impossible. So it is determined that the agent of beliefs, volitions, and motives is Allah, exalted is He. Thus the text of the Qur'an indicates that the states of the hearts are from Allah, and rational proofs indicate the same, so it is established that the truth is what we have mentioned.

As for those who hold the doctrine of divine decree (qadar), they said: It is not permissible that the meaning of this verse be what you have stated, and its clarification is by several aspects:

The first aspect: al-Jubba'i said: Whoever Allah prevents from faith is incapable, and commanding the incapable is folly. If that were permissible, then it would be permissible for Allah to command us to ascend to heaven. They have agreed that a paralyzed person is not commanded to pray standing; how then is that permissible for Allah, exalted is He? He, exalted, said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He said regarding one who makes his wife unlawful to himself (zihar): ﴿So whoever does not find [the means], then feeding sixty needy persons﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 4], thus He dropped the obligation of fasting from one who is unable to do it.

The second aspect: Allah, exalted is He, commanded responding to Allah and to the Messenger, and mentioned this statement in the context of reminder and warning against abandoning the response. If the meaning were what you have stated, that would be a strong excuse for abandoning the response, and it would not be a deterrent from abandoning the response.

The third aspect: He, exalted is He, sent down the Qur'an so that it would be a proof for the Messenger against the disbelievers, not so that it would be a proof for the disbelievers against the Messenger. If the meaning were what you have stated, this verse would become one of the strongest proofs for the disbelievers against the Messenger, and they would say: Since He, exalted is He, has prevented us from faith, how then does He command us to it? Thus it is established by these aspects that the verse cannot be taken to mean what the people of compulsion said.

They said: We too will mention several interpretations of the verse:

The first: Allah, exalted is He, intervenes between a person and benefiting from his heart by means of death. The meaning is: hasten to respond to what I have obligated upon you of jihad and other things before the death that is inevitable comes upon you, and it intervenes between you and obedience and repentance. The judge (al-Qadi) said: For this reason He, exalted is He, followed it with what indicates it, namely His saying: ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾, and the purpose of this verse is to urge obedience before the arrival of death, which prevents it.

The second: The meaning is that He, exalted is He, intervenes between a person and what he wishes and desires in his heart, for the term (ajal) intervenes between a person and his hope. It is as if He said: Hasten to righteous deeds and do not rely on what occurs in your hearts of expecting long life, for that is not to be trusted. The use of the word "heart" for the wishes arising in the heart is fine because naming a thing by the name of its container is permissible, as in the saying: "The valley flowed."

The third: The believers were fearful of fighting on the day of Badr, so it was as if it were said to them: Hasten to obedience and do not hold back from it because of the weakness and cowardice you find in your hearts, for Allah, exalted is He, changes those states, replacing weakness with strength and cowardice with courage, because He, exalted is He, is the Turner of hearts.

The fourth: Mujahid said: The intended meaning of "heart" here is the intellect, so the meaning is that He intervenes between a person and his heart, and the meaning is: hasten to the deeds while you are still reasoning, for you cannot be sure of the loss of the intellects, and when they are removed, obligation is voided. Making "heart" a metonym for the intellect is permissible, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37], i.e., whoever has intellect.

The fifth: al-Hasan said: The meaning is that Allah is a barrier between a person and his heart, and the meaning is that His nearness to His servant is greater than the servant's heart's nearness to him. The purpose of this is to alert that nothing is hidden from Him of what is within the servant's inner being and what is in his mind, and its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]. This is the total of the aspects mentioned in this chapter for the people of compulsion and the people of divine decree.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾, i.e., know that you will be gathered to Him, i.e., to Allah, and you will not be left neglected and idle. In this there is an intense encouragement to action and a warning against laziness and heedlessness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 25:

God the Exalted says: ﴿And guard yourselves against a trial which will not affect only those among you who have done wrong. And know that God is severe in punishment.﴾

Know that just as He warned man that He might come between him and his heart, so He also warned him against trials (fitan). The meaning is: beware of a trial which, if it befalls you, will not be confined to the wrongdoers alone, but will extend to all of you, reaching both the righteous and the wicked. From al-Hasan: it was revealed concerning Ali, Ammar, Talha and al-Zubayr, and it refers specifically to the Day of the Camel (yawm al-Jamal). Al-Zubayr said: "It was revealed about us. We recited it for a time, and we did not think that we were its people, but then we were the ones it was about." From al-Suddi: it was revealed concerning the people of Badr, who fought one another on the Day of the Camel. It is related that al-Zubayr was once conversing with the Prophet (ﷺ) when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) approached. Al-Zubayr smiled at him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How is your love for Ali?" He replied: "O Messenger of Allah, I love him as I love my son, or more." He said: "How will you be when you march against him and fight him?"

If it is asked: how is it permissible for the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) to enter the response to an imperative?

We say: there are two views on this.

The first: the response to the imperative came in the form of a prohibition, and when this is the case, it is good to add the emphatic nun to that prohibition, as when you say: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you (la tatrahak) or lest it throw you indeed (la tatrahannak)," and as in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you unknowingly﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

The second: the intended construction is: "Guard against a trial which will surely afflict those among you who have done wrong," but the prohibitive form was used for emphasis in negating the restriction of the trial to the wrongdoers, as if the trial had been forbidden from that restriction, and it was said to it: "Do not afflict only those who have done wrong." The purpose of this is emphasis on the non-restriction, by way of metaphor (isti'ara).

Then He said: ﴿And know that God is severe in punishment﴾. The purpose of this is to urge adherence to uprightness out of fear of God's punishment.

If it is asked: the sense of the verse is that He frightens them with a punishment which, if it descended, would encompass both the guilty and others. How is it fitting for the mercy of the All-Merciful, the All-Wise, to bring trial and punishment upon one who has not sinned?

We say: God may indeed send death, poverty, blindness and disability upon His servant from the outset, either because it is good for Him to do so by the right of absolute ownership (al-malikiyya), or because God knew that this contains some kind of benefit, according to the difference between the two schools. If this is permissible on either of these two grounds, then it is likewise here. And God knows best.

[Page 121]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 26–28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away, so He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help, and provided you with good things, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded them to obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and then commanded them to guard against disobedience, He confirmed this obligation with this verse. That is because He, exalted is He, explained that before the appearance of the Messenger (ﷺ) they were in the utmost fewness and humiliation, and after his appearance they became in the utmost honour and elevation, and that requires of them obedience and the abandonment of opposition. As for the explanation of the conditions they were in before the appearance of Muhammad, it is in several aspects:

The first of them: they were few in number.

The second of them: they were oppressed, meaning that others oppressed them. The meaning of this oppression is that they feared that people would snatch them away; the sense is that whenever they went out of their city, they feared that the Arabs would snatch them away, because they feared the polytheists of the Arabs on account of their proximity to them and the intensity of their enmity toward them. Then He, exalted is He, explained that after they had been in that state, those conditions were turned into happiness and goodness:

The first of them: that He sheltered them, and what is meant by it is that He, exalted is He, moved them to Medina, so they became safe from the evil of the disbelievers.

The second of them: His saying, ﴿and strengthened you with His help﴾, and what is meant by it is the existence of victory on the day of Badr.

The third of them: His saying, ﴿and provided you with good things﴾, which is that He, exalted is He, made the spoils lawful for them after they had been forbidden to those who were before this community.

Then He said: ﴿that perhaps you would be grateful﴾, i.e., We transferred you from hardship to ease, and from trial to blessings and favours, so that you would occupy yourselves with gratitude and obedience. How then is it fitting for you to occupy yourselves with disputing and quarrelling because of the spoils?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know.﴾ ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He provided them with good things, here He forbade them from betrayal. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: they differed concerning the meaning of that betrayal, in several sayings:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to the Banu Qurayzah when he besieged them, and his family and his children were among them. They said: "O Abu Lubabah, what do you think? Should we come down to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh concerning us?" Abu Lubabah pointed to his throat, meaning that it would be slaughter, so do not do it. So that was a betrayal by him of Allah and His Messenger.

The second: al-Suddi said: they used to hear something from the Prophet (ﷺ), then they would spread it and throw it to the polytheists, so Allah forbade them from that.

The third: Ibn Zayd said: Allah forbade them to betray as the hypocrites did, who show faith and conceal disbelief.

The fourth: from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: Abu Sufyan left Mecca, and the Prophet (ﷺ) learned of his departure and resolved to go towards him, so a man among the hypocrites wrote to him: "Muhammad intends to come upon you, so take your precaution," and Allah revealed this verse.

The fifth: al-Zuhri and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah when he wrote to the people of Mecca when the Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to go out against them; al-Asamm related it.

The sixth: al-Qadi said: the closer view is that the betrayal of Allah is other than the betrayal of His Messenger, and the betrayal of the Messenger is other than the betrayal of trusts, because conjunction requires difference.

Having known this, we say: He, exalted is He, commanded them not to betray the spoils, and made that a betrayal of Him, because it is a betrayal of His gift, and a betrayal of His Messenger, because he is the one in charge of dividing them. Whoever betrays them has betrayed the Messenger. These spoils the Messenger had made a trust in the hands of the warriors, and obliged them not to take any part of them for themselves, so they became a deposit, and a deposit is a trust in the hand of the depositor. So whoever among them betrays in them has betrayed the trust of the people, since betrayal is the opposite of trust. He said: It is possible that by trust he means everything by which one is made to worship, and on this reading the spoils and other things enter into it. So the meaning of the verse is: the obligation of performing all the duties in full completeness, without deficiency or neglect.
