**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 29:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, if you fear God, He will grant you a criterion (furqan), and will remove from you your misdeeds, and forgive you. And God is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned against the trial of wealth and children, He encouraged taqwa (God-consciousness), which necessitates abandoning inclination and desire in loving wealth and children. In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Someone may say: attaching a condition to a judgment is only appropriate for one who is ignorant of the outcomes of affairs, and that is not fitting for God, exalted is He.

The answer: Our saying "if such-and-such is the case, then such-and-such follows" only indicates that the condition necessitates the consequence. As for whether the occurrence of the condition is doubtful or known, that is not conveyed by this wording. Even if we grant that it conveys this doubt, He, exalted is He, deals with the servants regarding the consequence in the manner of one who doubts. On this reading comes His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and are patient﴾ [Muhammad: 31].

**The second issue:** This conditional proposition has one condition, which is fearing God, exalted is He, and this covers avoiding all major sins. We have restricted it to major sins because He, exalted is He, mentioned in the consequence the expiation of misdeeds, and the consequence must be different from the condition. So we took taqwa to mean avoiding major sins, and we took misdeeds to mean minor sins, so that the difference between the condition and the consequence becomes clear. As for the consequences that follow from this condition, they are three:

The first is His saying: ﴿He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾. The meaning is that He distinguishes between you and the disbelievers. Since the wording is unrestricted, it must be understood as covering all the distinctions that arise between believers and disbelievers. So we say: this criterion is either considered in the affairs of this world or in the affairs of the Hereafter. As for the affairs of this world, it is either considered in the states of the hearts, which are the inward states, or in the outward states. As for the states of the hearts, there are several matters:

The first: He specifically grants the believers guidance and knowledge.

The second: He specifically opens their hearts and breasts to expansion, as He said: ﴿So is one whom God has opened his breast to Islam, and he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22].

The third: He removes rancor, hatred and envy from their hearts, and removes deceit and treachery from their breasts, whereas the hypocrite and the disbeliever have hearts filled with these base states and blameworthy traits. The cause of these matters occurring is that when the heart becomes illuminated by obedience to God, exalted is He, all these darknesses depart from it, because knowledge of God is light, and these traits are darkness, and when light appears, the darkness must vanish.

As for the outward states, God, exalted is He, specifically grants the Muslims elevation, conquest, victory and triumph, as He said: ﴿And to God belongs honour, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], and as He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 33]. The condition of the wicked and the disbeliever is the reverse of that. As for the affairs of the Hereafter, there is reward, lasting benefits, and honour from God and the angels, and all these states are included in the criterion.

The second type of recompense that is consequent upon taqwa is His saying: ﴿and will remove from you your misdeeds﴾. We say: if we take His saying ﴿if you fear God﴾ to mean guarding oneself against disbelief, then what is meant by His saying ﴿and will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ is all the misdeeds that existed before disbelief. And if we take it to mean guarding oneself against major sins, then what is meant by this is the expiation of minor sins.

The third type is His saying: ﴿and forgive you﴾. Know that what is meant by the expiation of misdeeds is concealing them in this world, and by forgiveness is their removal on the Day of Resurrection, so that repetition does not follow. Then He said: ﴿And God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, and whoever is like this, when he promises something, fulfils it. We have said that the bounties of God are greater than the bounties of others, for several reasons:

The first: that everything other than the Truth does not bestow favour or do good except when there arises in its heart the motive to bestow favour and do good, and that motive is originated, so it does not arise except by God's creating it, exalted is He. At this point it becomes clear that the true bestower of favour is none but God, who created that motive which necessitates that act.

The second: that everyone who bestows favour gains from it some kind of perfection, either a return in wealth or a return in praise and commendation, or a return of another kind, which is the removal of the pain present in the heart due to natural tenderness. God, exalted is He, gives and bestows favour and seeks no return from it, because He is perfect in His essence, and what is attained by a thing through its essence is impossible for it to gain from another.

The third: that everyone who bestows favour upon another makes the recipient obligated to him, and that is repellent. As for the Truth, glory be to Him, He is the originator of the essence of every being with all its attributes, so no aversion arises from accepting His kindness.

The fourth: that whoever bestows favour upon another, the recipient does not benefit from that favour except when he has a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and a digestive stomach, so that he may benefit from that kindness. At this point it becomes clear that the true bestower of favour is God. Thus by these proofs the correctness of His saying is established: ﴿And God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 30:**

God the Exalted says: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you. They plot, and God plots. And God is the best of plotters.﴾

Know that when God the Exalted reminded the believers of His favours upon them by saying, ﴿And remember when you were few﴾, He likewise reminded His Messenger of His favour upon him, which was the repelling of the scheming of the polytheists and the deceit of the deceivers from him. This surah is Medinan. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and other exegetes said: The polytheists of Quraysh conspired in Dar al-Nadwa (the council house of Quraysh), and Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man, claiming that he was from the people of Najd. Some of them said: "Confine him, and let us wait for him to be struck by the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." Iblis said: "There is no benefit in this, for his people will become angry on his behalf, and blood will be shed for him." Others said: "Expel him from among you, and you will be relieved of his harm to you." Iblis said: "There is no benefit in this either, for he will gather a group around himself and fight you with them."

Abu Jahl said: "The opinion is that we gather one man from every tribe, and they strike him with their swords in a single blow. When they have killed him, his blood will be scattered among the tribes, so the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and they will accept the payment of blood-money." Iblis said: "This is the correct opinion." So God revealed this to His Prophet, and permitted him to leave for Medina, commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and permitted him to emigrate. He commanded ʿAli to sleep in his bed, and said to him: "Cover yourself with my cloak (bardah), for no harm that you dislike will reach you." They stayed watching, and when they awoke they rushed to his bed and saw ʿAli, and they were bewildered, and God frustrated their effort. [p. 125]

As for His saying ﴿to confine you﴾ (li-yuthbitūka): Ibn ʿAbbas said: "to bind you and tie you up. Whoever is tied up has been confined (utbita), because he cannot move. For this reason it is said of one whose illness or wound prevents him from moving: 'So-and-so has been confined, and he is confined (muthbat).'" It was also said: "to imprison you," and it was said: "to detain you," and it was said: "to confine you in a house," where the place is omitted because its meaning is clear. Some read (li-yuthabbitūka), with the shadda (doubling), and al-Nakhaʿi read (li-yubayyitūka), from al-bayāt (to spend the night, to plot at night). As for His saying ﴿or kill you﴾, this is what we have related from Abu Jahl, may God curse him. ﴿Or expel you﴾, that is, from Mecca. When God the Exalted mentioned these three categories, He said: ﴿They plot, and God plots. And God is the best of plotters.﴾ We have already discussed the meaning of plotting with respect to God the Exalted in surah Al ʿImran, in His saying: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted. And God is the best of plotters﴾ (Al ʿImran: 54).

The summary is that they devised schemes to nullify the affair of Muhammad, while God the Exalted supported and strengthened him, so their action was lost and the work of God the Exalted became manifest. The judge (al-Qadi) said: The story that Ibn ʿAbbas related agrees with the Qur'an, except for what it contains about Iblis, for he claimed that his form was similar to the form of humans, and that is false. For that transformation is either from God's doing or from Iblis's doing. The first is false, because it is not permissible for God the Exalted to do that in order to tempt the disbelievers in their plotting. The second is also false, because it does not befit the wisdom of God the Exalted that Iblis should be able to change the form of his own self.

Know that this dispute is strange. For since it is not far from God the Exalted to empower Iblis with various kinds of whisperings, how could it be far from Him to empower him to change the form of his own self?

If it is said: How could He say ﴿and God is the best of plotters﴾, when there is no good in their plotting?

We say: There are several answers to this.

The first: that the meaning is "the strongest of plotters," so the word ﴿best﴾ (khayr) is placed in the position of "strongest" and "most powerful," to alert that every plot is nullified in the face of the action of God the Exalted.

The second: that the meaning is "the best of plotters, if it were possible for their plotting to contain anything good and fine."

The third: that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿the best of plotters﴾ is not comparison. Rather, what is meant is that it is good in itself, as one says: "Tharid (a dish of bread and broth) is good" (al-thārīd khayr).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 31–32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Our verses are recited to them, they say: "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the myths of the ancients."﴾ ﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ ﴿And what is there for them that Allah should not punish them, while they bar access to the Sacred Mosque, and they were not its guardians? Its guardians are only the God-fearing, but most of them do not know.﴾

Page 126

Know that when He, exalted is He, related their scheming against the person of Muhammad, He related their scheming against the religion of Muhammad. It was narrated that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith went out to al-Hirah as a merchant and bought the tales of Kalilah wa Dimnah. He used to sit with the mockers and the dividers (al-muqtasimin), and he was one of them, and he would recite to them the myths of the ancients, claiming that they were like what Muhammad related of the stories of the ancients. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They say: "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the myths of the ancients."﴾

Here there is a point of inquiry. The basis for the Qur'an being a miracle is that the Prophet ﷺ challenged the Arabs to produce its like, and they did not produce it. This verse indicates that they did produce such a counterpart, and that would invalidate the proof on which we rely.

The answer: the word ﴿law﴾ (if/had) indicates the non-occurrence of one thing due to the non-occurrence of another. So His saying ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ indicates that they did not wish that speech and did not say it. Thus it is established that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith acknowledged that he did not produce a counterpart, and he only reported that if he wished, he could have produced it. This is weak, because the purpose is achieved only if one actually produces the counterpart; the mere statement of it has no benefit.

The second doubt for them is their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment,﴾ meaning, a different kind of punishment, more severe and more grievous for us than that.

If it is said: this statement raises a problem from two aspects.

Know that when the Exalted described these two objections, He did not mention the answer to the first objection, which is His saying: ﴿If We willed, we would have said the like of this﴾. But He did mention the answer to the second objection, which is His saying: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the explanation of the answer is that when the disbelievers went to extremes and said, "O Allah, if Muhammad is in the right, then rain down upon us stones from the sky," the Exalted stated that Muhammad, although he is in the right in what he says, nevertheless does not bring down stones upon his enemies and upon those who deny his prophethood, for two reasons:

The first: As long as Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, is present among them, Allah does not inflict this upon them, out of honour for him. This is also the custom of Allah with all the earlier prophets, for He did not punish the people of any town until their messenger had left them, as was the case with Hud, Salih and Lut.

If it is said: Since his presence among them prevents the descent of punishment upon them, how then does He say: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ (9:14)?

We say: What is meant by the first is the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal), and what is meant by the second is the punishment that results from warfare and fighting.

The second reason: His saying: ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ Concerning its interpretation there are several views:

The first: "Allah would not punish these disbelievers while among them there are believers who seek forgiveness." The wording is general, but what is meant is some of them, as one says, "The people of the quarter killed a man," and "The people of such-and-such town committed corruption," meaning some of them.

The second: "Allah would not punish these disbelievers, while He knows that they will have children who will believe in Allah and seek His forgiveness." So they were described by the attribute of their offspring and descendants.

The third: Qatadah and al-Suddi said: ﴿nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ means that if they had sought forgiveness, they would not have been punished. Thus the purpose of mentioning this statement is to call them to seeking forgiveness; that is, if they had busied themselves with seeking forgiveness, Allah would not have punished them.

For this reason some have held that seeking forgiveness here means Islam, and the meaning is that there were among them people whom Allah knew would embrace Islam, among them Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Hakim ibn Hizam, and a large number of others. The meaning of ﴿Allah would not punish them while you were among them﴾ is, even though Allah knows that among them are those whose affair will end in faith. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: This verse indicates that seeking forgiveness is a security and a safeguard from punishment. Ibn 'Abbas said: There were two securities among them: the Prophet of Allah and seeking forgiveness. As for the Prophet, he has passed away; as for seeking forgiveness, it remains until the Day of Resurrection.

Then He said: ﴿And why should Allah not punish them?﴾ Know that in the first verse the Exalted clarified that He would not punish them as long as the Messenger of Allah was among them, and in this verse He mentioned that He would punish them. So the meaning is that He would punish them once the Messenger had left from among them. Then they differed concerning this punishment. Some said: this promised punishment befell them on the day of Badr. Others said: rather, on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Ibn 'Abbas said: this punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, and the punishment which He negated from them is the punishment of this world.

Then the Exalted explained the reason for which He would punish them, saying: ﴿while they bar [access to] the Sacred Mosque.﴾ The reports have made clear how they barred access to it in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. He drew attention to the fact that they barred it because they claimed that they were its guardians. Then He showed the falsity of this claim by His saying: ﴿And they were not its guardians; its guardians are only the righteous﴾, those who guard themselves against prohibited deeds, unlike what they used to do at the House, namely al-mukaa' wa-t-tasdiyah (whistling and clapping). The point intended is to show that whoever is in this condition is not a guardian of the Sacred Mosque; therefore they were deserving of being put to the sword and fought. So Allah killed them on the day of Badr, and thereby exalted Islam, as its explanation has already passed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping. So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said concerning the disbelievers that they were not the guardians of the Sacred House, and said: ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, He then explained what it was that removed them from being the guardians of the House. It is that their prayer at the House, their drawing near, and their worship were only with *al-mukaʾ* (whistling) and *al-taṣdiyah* (clapping). The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-mukaʾ* is *fuʿāl* on the pattern of *al-nughāʾ* and *al-rughāʾ*, from *makā yamkū*, when one whistles. *Al-mukaʾ* is a whistle, and from it comes *al-mukkāʾ*, a bird that frequents the countryside, whose plural is *al-makākī*; it was so named for the abundance of its whistling. As for *al-taṣdiyah*, it is clapping; it is said: *ṣadda yuṣaddī taṣdiyatan* when he clapped his hands. Concerning its origin there are two opinions:

The first: it is from *al-ṣadā*, which is the sound that returns from a mountain.

The second: Abu ʿUbayda said: its original form is *taṣdidah*, and the *yāʾ* was substituted for the *dāl*. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When your people from it cry out﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 57], meaning they are unable. Some denied this statement, but al-Azhari affirmed the view of Abu ʿUbayda and said: *ṣadā* has the original form *ṣaddā*, so the *dāl*s multiplied and one of them was changed into a *yāʾ*.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Quraysh used to circumambulate the House naked, whistling and clapping.

Mujahid said: they would oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) in the circumambulation, mock him, whistle, and confuse his circumambulation and his prayer.

Muqatil said: when the Messenger (ﷺ) prayed in the mosque, they would stand on his right and left, whistling and clapping, so as to confuse his prayer.

According to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, the *mukaʾ* and *taṣdiyah* were a kind of worship for them, and according to the view of Mujahid and Muqatil, they were harm inflicted upon the Prophet (ﷺ). The first is closer to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾.

If it is said: whistling and clapping were not of the same kind as prayer, so how is it permissible to make them an exception from prayer?

We say: there are several answers:

The first: they believed that whistling and clapping were of the kind of prayer, so this exception came according to their belief.

The second: this is like your saying, "I loved the prince, so he made my estrangement my connection," meaning he put estrangement in the place of connection; so it is here too.

The third: the purpose is that whoever has whistling and clapping as his prayer, then he has no prayer, just as the Arabs say: "So-and-so has no fault except generosity," meaning whoever has generosity as his fault, then he has no fault.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning the punishment of the sword on the Day of Badr. It was also said: it will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the circumstances of these disbelievers regarding bodily acts of worship, He followed it with an explanation of their circumstances regarding financial acts of worship. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his spending of wealth on the war against Muhammad on the day of Uhud, for he had hired two thousand of the Ahabish (mercenaries) besides those whom he enlisted from the Arabs, and he spent on them forty ounces, and the ounce is forty-two mithqals. The first issue: The author of the *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: "﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾ means: say this statement for their sake, which is: ﴿If they desist, they will be forgiven﴾. Had it meant 'address them with it,' it would have been said: 'If you desist, you will be forgiven.'" Ibn Mas'ud also said it in this way.

The second issue: The meaning is that if these disbelievers desist from disbelief and hostility toward the Messenger, enter Islam and commit to its laws, Allah will forgive them what has passed of their disbelief and their hostility toward the Messenger. And if they return to it and persist in it, then the precedent of the former peoples has already passed. On this there are several views:

The first: What is meant is that the precedent of the former peoples has already passed concerning those among them whose scheming turned back upon them on the Day of Badr.

The second: The precedent of the former peoples has already passed, those who banded together against their prophets from the nations that have gone by. So let them expect the like of that if they do not desist.

The third: Its meaning is that when the disbelievers desist from disbelief and embrace Islam, what has passed of disbelief and sins is forgiven them. And if they return, then the precedent of the former peoples has passed, and it is His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail."﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21], ﴿And Our word has already preceded﴾ [al-Saffat: 171], ﴿And We have written in the Psalms after the Reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 105].

* * *

The third issue: The jurists (fuqaha) differed over whether the repentance of a zindiq (a heretic who conceals his disbelief while outwardly professing Islam) is accepted or not. The correct view is that it is accepted, for several reasons:

The first: this verse, for His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ encompasses all kinds of disbelief.

If it is said: The condition of the zindiq is not known, as to whether he has desisted from his heresy or not?

We say: The rulings of the Sharia are based on outward appearances, as he (ﷺ) said: "We judge by what is apparent." So when he returns, it is obligatory to accept his statement concerning it.

The second: There is no doubt that he is obligated to return, and there is no way for him to do so except by this repentance. So if it were not accepted, it would entail imposing what cannot be borne.

The third: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds﴾ [al-Shura: 25].

* * *

The fourth issue: The followers of Abu Hanifa used this verse as evidence that disbelievers are not addressed with the subsidiary rulings of the Sharia (furu' al-shara'i). They said: If they were addressed with them, then they would be addressed either while in disbelief or after disbelief has ceased. The first is invalid by consensus (ijma'), and the second is invalid, because this verse indicates that a disbeliever who becomes Muslim is not held accountable for anything that passed over him during the time of disbelief. And requiring the making up of those acts of worship contradicts the apparent meaning of this verse.

* * *

The fifth issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, used this verse as evidence that when an apostate (murtadd) embraces Islam again, he is not obligated to make up the acts of worship that he abandoned during the state of apostasy and before it. The line of evidence is clear.

The sixth issue: He (ﷺ) said: "Islam erases what came before it." So when a disbeliever embraces Islam, he is not obligated to make up any of the physical or financial acts of worship. Whatever crime he committed against a person or property is pardoned, and at the moment of his Islam he is as on the day his mother bore him. Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said regarding this verse: "The monotheism (tawhid) of one hour destroys the disbelief of seventy years, so how could the monotheism of seventy years not prevail over destroying the sin of one hour?"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 39–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah (persecution/strife) and religion is entirely for Allah. But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained that if these disbelievers desist from their disbelief, forgiveness is attained for them, and if they return, they are threatened with the way of the earlier peoples, He followed this by commanding that they be fought if they persist, saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah.﴾ ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr said: At the beginning of the call, the believers were being subjected to fitnah concerning the religion of Allah, so some of the Muslims were tempted away from it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia (al-Habasha). A second fitnah was this: when the Ansar pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the pledge of al-ʿAqabah, the Quraysh conspired to subject the believers in Mecca to fitnah concerning their religion, and great hardship befell the believers. This is what is meant by fitnah, so Allah, exalted is He, commanded that they be fought until this fitnah ceases.

There is also another interpretation, which is that people's exaggeration in their love of their religions is greater than their exaggeration in their love of their own souls. Thus the disbeliever always strives with the greatest kinds of effort to harm the believers, to cast doubts into their hearts, and to place them in trials and hardships. When fighting takes place, disbelief and hardship cease, Islam becomes pure, and those fitnahs are entirely removed.

The Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: He, exalted is He, commanded that they be fought, then explained the cause for which fighting them was made obligatory, saying: ﴿until there is no more fitnah﴾ and the religion, which is the religion of Allah, becomes purified from all other religions. This aim is achieved only when disbelief is entirely removed.

Having understood this, we say: Either the meaning of the verse ﴿And fight them﴾ is for the sake of this meaning being attained, or the meaning is ﴿And fight them﴾ with the purpose that this meaning be attained. If the meaning of the verse is the first, then this meaning must be attained through fighting, and so it must be that the meaning of ﴿and religion is entirely﴾ refers to the land of Mecca and its surroundings, because the aim was attained there. He, peace be upon him, said: "Two religions shall not coexist in the Arabian Peninsula" (Jazirat al-ʿArab). It cannot be applied to all lands, for if that were intended, disbelief would not remain anywhere despite the fighting that Allah commanded. But if the meaning of the verse is the second, namely His saying: "fight them" with the purpose that the religion be entirely for Allah, then under this assumption there is no impediment to applying it to the removal of disbelief from the entire world, because not everything that is a human's aim necessarily comes to pass. So the command to fight is for the sake of attaining this aim, whether or not it is actually attained.

Then He said: ﴿But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ The meaning: ﴿If they cease﴾ from disbelief and all other sins through repentance and faith, ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, Knowing, nothing hidden from Him, and He will convey to them their reward. ﴿And if they turn away﴾, meaning from repentance and faith, ﴿then know that Allah is your Protector﴾, that is, your Guardian who preserves you and removes calamity from you. Then He explained that He is ﴿an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ Whoever is under the protection of this Protector, and in His care and sufficiency, is safe from calamities and guarded from things that cause fear.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 8, verse 41:

﴿And know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer, if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down to Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day the two hosts met. And Allah has power over all things.﴾

He, exalted is He, said: Know that when He commanded fighting in His words, ﴿And fight them﴾, and it is known that spoils are usually obtained during fighting, Allah therefore mentioned the ruling on the spoils (ghanima). There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: al-ghunm means gaining something. It is said: ghanima yaghnamu ghunman, so he is ghanim. In the Sharia, al-ghanima (spoils of war) is what enters the hands of the Muslims from the property of the polytheists by way of force, with horses and camels.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ma" in His words, ﴿that whatever you acquire﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and His words ﴿from anything﴾ mean whatever it is, even a thread. ﴿Then indeed for Allah﴾: the predicate of "anna" is omitted, and its estimated form is: "then it is due and obligatory that for Allah is its fifth." Al-Nakha'i narrated from Ibn Umar "fa-inna li-Llahi khumusahu" with a kasra, and its estimate according to al-Nakha'i's reading is: "then for Allah is its fifth." The well-known reading is more emphatic and more firmly established for obligation, as if it were said: there must be the establishment of the fifth in it, and there is no way to neglect it. That is because when the predicate is omitted and it admits many estimated possibilities, such as your saying "established," "obligatory," "due," "binding," it is stronger in its obligation than explicitly naming one. It was also read "khumsahu" with a sukun.

The third issue: On the manner of distributing the spoils.

Know that this verse requires that one-fifth of it be taken, and regarding the manner of distributing that fifth there are two opinions:

The first opinion, which is the well-known one: that fifth is divided into five. One share is for the Messenger of Allah, one share for his near kin from the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, but not the Banu Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal, based on what was narrated "from Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im that they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: These are your kinsmen, the Banu Hashim, whose excellence cannot be denied because you are of them. Tell us, what about our kinsmen the Banu al-Muttalib? You gave them and deprived us, though we and they are in one rank." He, peace be upon him, said: "They have not separated from us in the Jahiliyya nor in Islam; the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib are one thing," and he interlaced his fingers. Three shares are for the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.

As for after the death of the Messenger ﷺ: according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of Allah, which is spent on what he used to spend it on for the interests of the Muslims, such as the equipping of the fighters with horses and weapons; one share for the near kin, from their rich and their poor, divided among them, the male receiving the equivalent of the portion of two females; and the remainder is for the three groups, who are: the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: after the death of the Messenger, peace be upon him, his share has lapsed due to his death; likewise the share of the near kin, and they are given only for their poverty, so they are like the rest of the poor, and their rich are not given, and it is divided among the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. Malik said: the matter of the fifth is entrusted to the opinion of the Imam; if he sees dividing it among these, he does so, and if he sees giving some of them and not others, he may do that.

Page 133

Know that the apparent meaning of the verse conforms to the opinion of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and is explicit in it, so it is not permissible to depart from it except by a separate proof stronger than it. And how, when He said at the end of the verse: ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾, meaning: if you have believed in Allah, then rule by this division. This indicates that whenever the ruling by this division is not implemented, faith in Allah is not realized.

The second opinion, which is the opinion of Abu al-Aliya: the fifth of the spoils is divided into six parts: one of them is for Allah, one for the Messenger of Allah, the third for the near kin, and the remaining three for the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. They said: the evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, made the fifth of the spoils for Allah, then for the five groups. Among those who hold this opinion, some said: the share of Allah is given to the Messenger; others said: it is spent on the upkeep of the Ka'ba. Some of them said: he, peace be upon him, used to put his hand into this fifth, and whatever he grasped of it he assigned to the Ka'ba, and that is what is named for Allah, exalted is He.

Those who hold the first opinion answered this: that His words ﴿for Allah﴾ do not intend to establish a share for Allah, since all things are Allah's possession and dominion; rather, what is intended is to open the speech by mentioning Allah in a manner of glorification, as in His words: ﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. Al-Qaffal argued for the soundness of this opinion with what was narrated "from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said to them regarding the spoils of Khaybar: 'I have nothing from what Allah has granted you except the fifth, and the fifth is returned to you.'" So his words "I have nothing except the fifth" indicate that the share of Allah and the share of the Messenger are one. And on the combined reading, his share would be a sixth, not a fifth; and if we say that the two shares are for the Messenger, his share becomes more than a fifth. Both opinions contradict the apparent meaning of his words: "I have nothing except the fifth."

This is the discussion on the division of the fifth of the spoils. As for the remainder, which is four-fifths of the spoils, it belongs to the warriors who took part, because they are the ones who gained it and acquired it, just as grass is acquired by cutting and birds by hunting. The jurists derived from this verse many issues mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

The fourth issue: The verse indicates that it is permissible to divide the spoils within the territory of war, as is the saying of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. The evidence for this is that His words ﴿then indeed for Allah is its fifth, and for the Messenger, and for the near kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ require that ownership is established for these in the spoils, and when ownership has been established for them in it, the permissibility of division must follow, because there is no meaning to division in this case except transferring ownership to its owner, and that is permissible by consensus.

The fifth issue: They differed regarding the near kin. It was said: they are the Banu Hashim. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: they are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, and he cited the report we have related. It was said: the family of Ali, Ja'far, Aqil, the family of Abbas, and the descendants of al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and this is the opinion of Abu Hanifa.

The sixth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf related from al-Kalbi that this verse was revealed at Badr. Al-Waqidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the fifth was (instituted) at the expedition of Banu Qaynuqa', one month and three days after Badr, on the middle of Shawwal, at the twentieth month after the Hijra.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾, and the meaning is: know that the fifth of the spoils is spent on these five categories, so cut off your greed for it and be content with the four-fifths. ﴿if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down to Our servant﴾, meaning: if you have believed in Allah and in what was sent down to Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day of Badr. "Al-jam'an" (the two hosts): the two groups of Muslims and disbelievers. What is meant by it is the signs that were sent down to him, the angels, and the victory on that day. ﴿And Allah has power over all things﴾, that is, He is able to grant you victory when you were few and humbled. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When you were on the near side of the valley, and they were on the far side, and the caravan was lower than you. And had you made a mutual appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment. But [it was] so that Allah might accomplish a matter already decreed, that those who perished might perish upon clear evidence, and those who lived might live upon clear evidence. And indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning His saying, ﴿When you were on the near side of the valley﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them: it is connected to an implied verb whose meaning is: "Remember when you were such-and-such," as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-Anfal: 26].

The second: that His saying ﴿when﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of the Criterion" (yawm al-furqan).

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "bil-'idwah" with a kasra on the ayn in both instances, while the rest read it with a damma. Both are dialectal forms. Ibn al-Sikkit said: 'udwat al-wadi and 'idwatuhu are its side, and its plural is 'uda and 'idan. Al-Akhfash said: the kasra is the speech of the Arabs; nothing else has been heard from them. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the damma in 'udwah is the more common of the two dialects. The author of al-Kashshaf related the damma, the fatha and the kasra, and said: they were all read, and also "bil-'idyah" by changing the waw into a ya' because between it and the kasra there is a weak barrier, as in al-fityah. As for "al-dunya", it is the feminine of al-adna, and its opposite is "al-quswa", which is the feminine of al-aqsa. Everything that withdraws from something has become distant (qasa), and al-aqsa and al-quswa are like al-akbar and al-kubra.

If it is said: both are of the fu'la pattern from the waw category, so why did one come with a ya' and the other with a waw?

We say: the analogy is to change the waw into a ya', as in al-'ulya, but al-quswa has come irregularly, and most of its usage is upon its original form.

The third issue: What is meant by "the near side of the valley" (al-'udwah al-dunya) is the side adjacent to Madinah, and by "the far side" (al-quswa) is the side adjacent to Makkah. The water was on the side where the polytheists had camped, and their advantage from this direction was greater. "And the caravan" (al-rakb) is the caravan (al-'ir) for which they had set out, and it was in a place ﴿lower than you﴾, toward the seashore. ﴿And had you made a mutual appointment﴾, you and the people of Makkah, for battle, you would have differed among yourselves because of your fewness and their multitude. ﴿But so that Allah might accomplish a matter already decreed﴾, meaning: Allah strengthens you and gives you victory, so that He may accomplish a matter already decreed, obligatory to come into being. His saying ﴿so that those who perished might perish﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿so that He might accomplish﴾. Concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: There is no doubt that the army of the Messenger, peace be upon him, at the outset were in the utmost fear and weakness because of their small number and lack of preparation. They camped far from the water, and the land in which they camped was sandy, in which their feet sank. As for the unbelievers, they were in the utmost strength because of their great numbers and the availability of equipment and tools; for they were near the water, and the land in which they camped was suitable for walking; and the caravan was behind their backs, and they were expecting reinforcement from the caravan moment by moment. Then He, Exalted is He, reversed the situation and inverted the affair, and made the victory for the Muslims and the destruction upon the unbelievers. Thus this became among the greatest miracles and the most powerful proofs of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he reported from his Lord concerning the promise of help, conquest and triumph.

So His saying ﴿so that those who perished might perish upon clear evidence﴾ points to this meaning: that those who perished perished only after witnessing this miracle, and the believers who remained alive witnessed this overpowering miracle. By "clear evidence" is meant this miracle.

The second issue: The lam in His saying ﴿so that Allah might accomplish a matter already decreed﴾ and in His saying ﴿so that those who perished might perish upon clear evidence﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad). Its apparent meaning requires explaining the acts and rulings of Allah by purposes and interests, but we turn this statement away from its apparent meaning by the well-known rational proofs.

The third issue: His saying ﴿so that those who perished might perish upon clear evidence﴾ apparently requires that He, Exalted is He, intended for all knowledge, recognition, goodness and righteousness, and this conflicts with the saying of our companions that He, Exalted is He, willed disbelief from the disbeliever. But we leave this apparent meaning by the known proofs.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and those who lived might live upon clear evidence﴾. Nafi', Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, and Nusayr from al-Kisa'i read "man hayiya" with the two ya's made clear. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir by the narration of al-Qawwas, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read it with a shaddah on the ya' by idgham. As for the idgham, it is because the vowel is obligatory on the second, so it follows the pattern of radda; for in the Mushaf it is written with one ya'. As for the clear pronunciation, it is because idgham is impermissible in its present-tense form from "yahya", so it follows its pattern. Some Kufan grammarians permitted idgham in "yahya".

Then He, Exalted is He, concluded the verse with His saying ﴿And indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears your supplication, knows your need and your weakness, and so He sets right your affairs.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When God showed them to you in your dream as few; and had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter, but God saved you. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾

Know that this is the second kind of the blessings with which God favoured the people of Badr. It contains two issues.

The first issue: ﴿When God showed them﴾ is in the accusative by the implied verb "remember" (udhkur), or it is a second substitute (badal) for "the Day of the Criterion," or it is connected to His saying ﴿Hearing, Knowing﴾, meaning: He knows the interests when He makes them few in your eyes.

The second issue: Mujahid said: God showed the Prophet ﷺ the disbelievers of Quraysh in his dream as few, and he informed his Companions of that. They said: "The vision of the Prophet is true, and the people are few." So that became a cause of their boldness and the strengthening of their hearts.

If it is said: seeing the many as few is an error, so how is it permissible for God, exalted is He, to do that?

We say: Our school holds that He, exalted is He, does what He wills and decrees what He desires. Also, perhaps God showed it to some and not to others, so the Messenger judged, regarding those whom he saw, that they were few. It is also reported from al-Hasan that this showing was while awake. He said: the meaning of "dream" is the eye, which is the place of sleep.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had He shown them to you as many﴾, you would have mentioned it to the people, and had they heard that, they would have lost heart and disputed. The meaning of mutual dispute over the matter is the disagreement by which each one tries to pull the other away from what he is upon. The meaning is: your affair would have been thrown into disorder and your word would have differed. ﴿But God saved﴾, that is, He saved you from opposition among yourselves. It has been said: God preserved their affair for them until He made them victorious over their enemy. It has also been said: He saved them from defeat on the day of Badr. The more apparent view is that what is meant is: but God saved you from disputing. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, He knows what arises within them of boldness and cowardice, of patience and impatience.

God's words: ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you, when you met [in battle], as few in your eyes and made you appear few in their eyes, that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done. And to Allah are [all] matters returned.﴾

Know that this is the third type of favour which Allah manifested to the Muslims on the Day of Badr. The meaning is that the few [enemy] whom they saw in the sleep was confirmed by their being seen while awake. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: "﴿And when He showed them to you﴾: the two pronouns are objects, meaning [that He made you see them], that is, 'when He caused you to see them with your eyes.' And 'qalilan' (few) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl)."

Know that Allah made the number of the polytheists appear few in the eyes of the believers, and He also made the number of the believers appear few in the eyes of the polytheists. The wisdom in the first diminishing is to confirm the vision of the Messenger (ﷺ), and also to strengthen their hearts and increase their boldness against them. The wisdom in the second diminishing is that when the polytheists considered the number of the Muslims to be small, they did not exert themselves in preparation, readiness and caution, and so that became a cause for the believers to gain mastery over them.

If it is said: How is it permissible that He would show them the many as few?

We say: As for what we have said, that is permissible, because Allah the Exalted created perception for some and not for others. As for the Mu'tazilah, they said: Perhaps the eye was prevented from perceiving all of them, or perhaps most of them were at an extreme distance, so they were not actually seen.

Then He said: ﴿that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾.

If it is said: He mentioned this statement in the previous verse, so mentioning it here is pure repetition.

We say: The purpose of mentioning it in the previous verse is that He, the Exalted, did those acts so that the Muslims would gain mastery over the polytheists in a way that would be a miracle indicating the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). The purpose of mentioning it here is not that meaning; rather, the purpose is that He, the Exalted, mentioned here that He made the number of the believers appear few in the eyes of the polytheists, and so He explained here that He did that only so that it would be a cause for the disbelievers not to exert themselves in preparation and caution, and thus it would become a cause for their defeat.

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah are [all] matters returned﴾. Its purpose is to draw attention to the fact that the conditions of this world are not sought for their own sakes; rather, what is meant by them is what may serve as provision for the Day of Return.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet a company (fi'ah), stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may prosper.﴾ ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.﴾ ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes insolently and to be seen by people, and who averted [others] from the way of Allah. And Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the kinds of His blessings upon the Messenger and upon the believers on the day of Badr, He taught them two kinds of etiquette when they meet a fi'ah (a company of combatants):

The first: thabat (steadfastness), which is that they prepare themselves for the encounter and do not let their souls entertain the thought of turning back.

The second: that they remember Allah much. Regarding the interpretation of this remembrance there are two views:

The first view: that they remember Allah in their hearts and with their tongues. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah commanded His friends to remember Him in their most difficult circumstances, as a reminder that a person may not leave his heart and tongue empty of the remembrance of Allah. Even if a man were to come from the west to the east spending wealth generously, and another from the east to the west striking with his sword in the way of Allah, the one who remembers Allah would have the greater reward.

The second view: that what is meant by this remembrance is supplication for victory and triumph, because that is not attained except by the help of Allah, exalted is He.

Then He said: ﴿that you may prosper﴾. That is because if fighting the disbeliever is for the sake of obeying Allah, exalted is He, then it is like giving up the soul in seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, and this is the greatest station of servanthood. If he overcomes the adversary, he succeeds with reward and spoils; and if he becomes overcome, he succeeds with martyrdom and high ranks. As for if the fighting is not for Allah but for the sake of praise in this world and seeking wealth, that is not a means to success and triumph.

If it is said: This verse makes steadfastness obligatory in every circumstance, and this gives the impression that it abrogates the verse on taharruf (maneuvering) and tahayyuz (withdrawing to a position).

We say: This verse makes steadfastness obligatory in general, and what is meant by steadfastness is earnestness in fighting. The verse on taharruf and tahayyuz does not conflict with the attainment of steadfastness in fighting; rather, steadfastness in this objective could not be attained except by that taharruf and tahayyuz.

Then He, exalted is He, said, emphasizing this: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in all that He commands, because jihad benefits only together with adherence to all the acts of obedience.

[Page 138]

Then He said: ﴿And do not dispute with one another, lest you lose heart and your strength depart﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: God, exalted is He, made clear that dispute necessitates two things.

One of them: it necessitates the emergence of cowardice and weakness.

The second is His words: ﴿and your strength depart﴾. On this there are two opinions.

The first: by "strength" (*rih*) is meant good fortune (*dawla*). Good fortune is likened to the wind at the time it takes effect and its affairs proceed, and to its blowing. It is said, "the winds of so-and-so blew," when good fortune submitted to him and his command took effect.

The second: there has never been victory except by a wind that God sends. In a hadith: "I was made victorious by the east wind (*al-Saba*), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (*al-Dabur*)."

The first opinion is stronger, because God made their dispute the cause of the departure of the wind, and it is known that their disagreement does not affect the blowing of the east wind. Mujahid said: "***and your strength depart***" means your victory. And the strength of the Companions of Muhammad departed when they disputed on the Day of Uhud.

The second issue: those who deny analogical reasoning (*qiyas*, the method of deducing a ruling by analogy) have argued from this verse. They said: the position of analogy leads to dispute, and dispute is forbidden; therefore this verse requires that acting upon analogy be unlawful. The connection is established by observation, for we see that the world has been filled with differences because of analogies. That dispute is forbidden is shown by His words: ***"And do not dispute."*** Also, those who hold that a text may not be specified by analogy have relied on this verse, and said: His words, ***"And obey God and His Messenger,"*** are explicit in requiring obedience to God and His Messenger in everything they have stipulated. Then He followed it with: ***"And do not dispute, lest you lose heart."*** It is known that whoever relies on an analogy that specifies a text has abandoned obedience to God and obedience to His Messenger, and has adopted an analogy that leads to dispute and cowardice, and all of that is forbidden. Those who uphold analogy have answered the first point by saying that not every analogy leads to dispute.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ***"And be patient. Indeed, God is with the patient"***. The intended meaning is that the perfection of the matter of jihad rests upon patience, so He commanded them to be patient, as He said in another verse: ***"Be patient, endure, and stand firm"*** [Al-'Imran: 200]. And He made clear that He is with the patient. There is no doubt that by this "being with" is meant support and help.

* * *

Then He said: ***"And do not be like those who came out of their homes insolently and to be seen of people, and who bar from the way of God."*** The exegetes said: the reference is to Quraysh when they set out from Mecca to protect the caravan. When they reached al-Juhfa, al-Haqqaf al-Kinani, who was a friend of Abu Jahl, sent to him gifts with a son of his. When the son came to him he said: "My father sends you his greetings and says to you: If you wish, I will send you men to reinforce you, and if you wish, I will march to you with those of my relatives who are with me, and I will do so." Abu Jahl said: "Tell your father: may God and kinship reward you with good. If we were fighting God as Muhammad claims, then by God we have no power against God. But if we are fighting people, then by God we have strength over the people. By God, we will not turn back from fighting Muhammad until we reach Badr, and drink wine there, and singing girls will play for us there, for Badr is a season of the seasons of the Arabs and one of their markets, so that the Arabs will hear of this event." The exegetes said: they arrived at Badr and drank the cups of death instead of wine, and mourning women wailed over them instead of singing girls.

Know that God described them with three things:

The first: *al-bataru* (insolence). Al-Zajjaj said: *al-bataru* is overweening in blessing. The truth is that when blessings from God multiply upon a servant, if he directs them toward God's pleasure and recognizes that they come from God, exalted is He, that is gratitude. But if he uses them to boast over his peers and to outdo the people of his time, that is insolence.

The second: His words, ***"and to be seen of people."*** *Ri'a'* is an expression for intending to display what is good while its inner reality is ugly. The difference between it and hypocrisy (*nifaq*) is that hypocrisy is displaying faith while concealing disbelief, whereas *ri'a'* is displaying obedience while concealing disobedience. It is related that when he (ﷺ) saw them at the place of Badr he said: "O God, Quraysh has come with its arrogance and its pride, to oppose Your religion and to fight Your Messenger."

The third: His words, ***"and who bar from"***

[Page 139]

***"the way of God."*** This is a present-tense verb, and coordinating a verb with a noun is not good. Al-Wahidi mentioned three aspects of this:

The first: that His words, ***"and who bar from the way of God,"*** should be in the sense of "barring" (*sadd*, as an active participle).

The second: that His words, ***"insolently and to be seen,"*** should be in the sense of "they act insolently and they seek to be seen."

I say: none of these aspects satisfies the need, because he sometimes places a verb in the position of a noun and sometimes places a noun in the position of a verb, so that the word may be coordinated with its own category. It was incumbent on him to mention the reason why he expressed the first two with the verbal noun (*masdar*) and the third with the verb. I say: Shaykh Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani mentioned that the noun indicates permanence and continuity, while the verb indicates renewal and occurrence. He said: an example of the noun is His words, ***"and their dog stretching out its forelegs at the threshold"*** [Al-Kahf: 18], and that indicates that this state is fixed and established. An example of the verb is His words, ***"Say: who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?"*** [Yunus: 31], and that indicates that He, exalted is He, delivers provision to them moment by moment. This is what Shaykh Abd al-Qahir mentioned.

Given this, we say: Abu Jahl, his clan and his followers were disposed to insolence, boasting and self-admiration. As for their barring from the way of God, it occurred at the time when Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, claimed prophethood. For this reason He mentioned insolence and *ri'a'* in the form of the noun, and mentioned barring from the way of God in the form of the verb. And God knows best.

The summary of the matter: God commanded them, when they met the enemy, to stand firm and to occupy themselves with the remembrance of God, and forbade them from letting insolence and *ri'a'* be what moves them to that steadfastness. Rather, He made it obligatory upon them that what moves them to it should be the seeking of servanthood to God.

Know that the whole of the Qur'an, from its beginning to its end, is a call of creation away from preoccupation with creation, and a command to them to exert effort on the path of servanthood to the Real. Disobedience accompanied by humility is closer to sincerity than obedience accompanied by pride. Then He concluded this verse with His words: ***"And God is encompassing of what they do."*** The intended meaning is that a person may often display that what moves him and prompts him to a particular act is seeking God's pleasure, while in reality the matter is not so. So God, exalted is He, made clear that He knows what is within the depths of hearts. This is a warning and a deterrent against *ri'a'* and affectation.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 8, verse 48:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector." But when the two hosts came in sight of each other, he turned on his heels and said, "I am free of you. I see what you do not see. I fear Allah, and Allah is severe in punishment."﴾

Know that this is among the blessings with which the people of Badr were specially favored. Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The governing element (al-'amil) in "idh" (when) has several possibilities. It is said that its implied sense is "Remember when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them." It is also said that it is coordinated with what came earlier about reminding them of blessings, so the implied sense is: "And remember when He showed them to you and when Satan made their deeds seem fair." And it is said that it is coordinated with His saying, "They went out insolently and to be seen by people," so the implied sense is: "Do not be like those who went out from their homes insolently and to be seen by people, and when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them."

[Page 140]

**The second issue:** Concerning how this making-fair (tazyin) took place, there are two views.

The first: Satan made it fair through his whispering, without taking the form of a human being. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Asamm.

The second: He appeared in human form. They said: When the polytheists intended to march to Badr, they feared the Banu Bakr ibn Kinana, because they had killed one of them, so they were not secure that the Banu Bakr would attack them from behind. Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, who was of the Banu Bakr ibn Kinana and one of their nobles, accompanied by a host of devils, and he carried a banner. He said: "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector (mujir) against the Banu Kinana." When Iblis saw the angels descending, he turned on his heels. It is also said that his hand was in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham, and when he turned back, al-Harith said to him: "Will you abandon us in this situation?" He said: "I see what you do not see," and he pushed al-Harith in the chest, and they fled. In this story there are questions:

**The first question:** What is the benefit in changing Iblis's form into the form of Suraqa?

The answer: In it there is a great miracle for the Messenger (peace be upon him). For when the disbelievers of Quraysh returned to Makka, they said: "Suraqa defeated the people." This reached Suraqa, and he said: "By Allah, I did not know of your march until your defeat reached me." At that point it became clear to the people that the figure was not Suraqa but a devil.

If it is said: Then Iblis came to fight the believers, and it is known that he is at the height of strength. Why did they not defeat the armies of the Muslims?

We say: Because he saw Jibril in the army of the Muslims with a thousand angels, and for this reason he feared and fled.

If it is said: Then according to this line of reasoning, all the armies of the Muslims should have been defeated, since he takes on the form of a human, attends, assists the mass of the disbelievers and defeats the hosts of the Muslims. The summary is: if he is capable of this, why does he not do so in all the other battles of the Muslims? And if he is not capable of it, how can you attribute this act to him in the event of Badr?

The answer: Perhaps He, exalted is He, changed his form into the form of a human only in that event; as for the other events, He does not make that change.

**The second question:** When He changed his form into the form of a human, he no longer remained a devil but became a human.

The answer: A human is human by the essence of his rational soul, and the souls of devils differ from the souls of humans. Therefore changing the form did not entail changing the reality. This matter is one of the transmitted (sam'i) proofs that a human being is not human by virtue of his outward structure and particular form.

**The third question:** What is the meaning of Satan's saying ﴿No one among the people can overcome you today﴾, and what is the benefit of this statement, given that they were many and dominant?

The answer: Although they were many in number, they were witnessing that the state of Muhammad (peace be upon him) was growing and increasing every day. Also, whatever Muhammad reported about something, it came to pass, so for this reason they were extremely afraid of the people of Muhammad (ﷺ). Iblis said this statement to remove fear from their hearts. It is possible that what was meant is that he would secure them especially from the evil of the Banu Bakr ibn Kinana, since he had appeared in the form of one of their leaders, and he said: ﴿and I am your protector﴾. The meaning is: If I and my people are a supporter for you, then no one among the people will overcome you. The meaning of "jar" (protector) here is the one who defends his companion from all kinds of harm, just as a neighbor defends his neighbor. The Arabs say: "I am your protector (jar) from so-and-so," meaning: I guard you from his harm, so that no harm from him reaches you.

[Page 141]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But when the two hosts came in sight of each other﴾, meaning the two groups met such that each saw the other. ﴿He turned on his heels﴾. Nukus (turning back) is withdrawing from something, and the meaning is that he returned. He said: ﴿I see what you do not see﴾, and concerning this there are several views.

The first: He is a spiritual being, so he saw the angels and feared them. It is said that he saw Jibril walking in front of the Prophet (peace be upon him), and it is said that he saw a thousand angels following in succession.

The second: He saw the signs of victory and triumph on behalf of the Prophet (peace be upon him), so he knew that if he stood his ground, an affliction would befall him.

Then he said: ﴿I fear Allah.﴾ Qatada said: He was truthful in his saying ﴿I see what you do not see﴾, and he lied in his saying ﴿I fear Allah.﴾ It is also said: When he saw the angels descending from the sky, he feared that the time at which he had been reprieved had arrived, so he said what he said out of concern for himself.

As for His saying ﴿and Allah is severe in punishment﴾, it may be part of the remainder of Iblis's speech, and it may be that his speech ends at his saying "I fear Allah," and then God, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿and Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

**The commentary of Al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 8, verse 49:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "Their religion has deluded these people." And whoever relies upon Allah, then indeed Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾

Within this are several issues:

**The first issue:** The conjunction الواو (*wāw*, "and") does not appear in His saying ﴿إذْ يَقُولُ﴾ ("when [they] say"), but it does appear in His saying ﴿وإذْ زَيَّنَ لَهُمُ﴾ ("and when [Satan] made their deeds appear attractive to them"). This is because His saying ﴿وإذْ زَيَّنَ﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) with this adornment of their state and their going out in insolence and to be seen. As for here, His saying ﴿إذْ يَقُولُ المُنافِقُونَ﴾, there is no coordination of this statement with what precedes it. Rather, it is a new, independent statement, disconnected from what came before. The governing element of the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*, the inflectional analysis of words) of إذْ ("when") in it has two possibilities:

The first: the implied sense is, "And Allah is severe in punishment when the hypocrites say..."

The second: "Remember when the hypocrites say..."

**The second issue:** As for the hypocrites (*al-munāfiqūn*), they are a people from the Aws and the Khazraj. As for those in whose hearts is a disease, they are a people from Quraysh who had embraced Islam, but whose Islam had not become firm in their hearts, and they did not emigrate. Then, when Quraysh set out to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, those people said: "We will go out with our people. If Muhammad has a large force, we will go out to him; and if he has a small force, we will remain among our people." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "Then all of these were killed alongside the polytheists on the day of Badr."

As for His saying ﴿غَرَّ هَؤُلاءِ دِينُهُمْ﴾ ("their religion has deluded these people"), Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is that [Muhammad] went out with 313 men to fight a thousand men, and this was only because they relied upon their religion. It has also been said that the intended meaning is: these people strive toward the killing of themselves, hoping that they will be made alive after death and will be rewarded for this killing.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then indeed Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾ That is: whoever entrusts his affair to Allah, trusts in His bounty, and depends upon the beneficence of Allah, then indeed Allah is his protector and his helper, because He is Exalted in Might, nothing overcomes Him; Wise, He conveys the punishment to His enemies and mercy and reward to His allies.

[Page 142]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 8, verses 50–52:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs, [saying], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward, and because Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the conditions of these disbelievers, He then explained their condition at death and the punishment that reaches them at that time. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Amir alone read ﴿tatawaffa﴾ (إذْ تَتَوَفّى) with a *ta'* (تاء), in accordance with the feminine form of the word *al-mala'ikah* (the angels) and its plurality. The rest read it with a *ya'* (ياء), in accordance with the meaning.

**The second issue:** The answer to *law* (لَوْ, "if") is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "You would see a dreadful scene, a terrible matter, and a severe punishment."

**The third issue:** ﴿Wa law tara﴾ means "and if you were to witness and observe," because *law* (لَوْ) turns the present tense into the past, just as *in* (إنْ) turns the past into the present.

**The fourth issue:** *al-mala'ikah* (the angels) is the subject (marfu') of the verb. ﴿Yadribuna﴾ (they strike) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to them. It is also permissible that in His saying ﴿yatawaffa﴾ there is a pronoun referring to Allah, exalted is He, and *al-mala'ikah* is then the subject of an inchoative sentence (mubtada'), with ﴿yadribuna﴾ as its predicate (khabar).

This is clear proof that the human being is something distinct from this body.

So Allah requited them in kind at the time of the soul's extraction.

Because of his disbelief, he sees nothing in the world of the Hereafter except darkness. Because of his intense love for corporeal things, and his separation from them, he obtains nothing from his distance from them except pains and regrets. Thus, because of his separation from the world, pains after pains and regrets befall him, and because of his turning toward the Hereafter while lacking light and knowledge, he passes from darkness to darkness. These two aspects are what is meant by His saying ﴿yadribuna wujuhahum wa adbarahum﴾.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Wa dhuqu 'adhaba al-hariq﴾ ("and taste the punishment of the burning"). In it there is an omission, and the implied meaning is: "and We say: Taste the punishment of the burning." Its like in the Qur'an is abundant. Al-Wahidi said: The correct view is that the angels say this to them in the Hereafter.

I say: As for the physical punishment, it is true and genuine. As for the spiritual punishment, it is also true, because reason indicates it. That is because we have explained that when the ignorant person departs from the world, he experiences intense grief because of separation from the beloved world, and intense fear because of the accumulation of darknesses upon him in the world of fear and grief. Both fear and grief necessitate spiritual burning and spiritual fire.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾. It has been said: This is a report of the angels' saying. In it there are issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Wahidi said: It is permissible that *dhalika* (that) be a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His saying ﴿bima qaddamat aydikum﴾ (for what your hands have sent forward). The reason for this figurative usage is that the hand is the instrument of action, and power is what effects action, so it is good to make the hand a metonymy for power.

Know that the truth is that the human being is one substance: he is the doer, he is the perceiver, he is the believer, he is the disbeliever, he is the obedient, and he is the disobedient. **The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿dhalika bima qaddamat aydikum﴾ indicates that this punishment is like a matter that issues from the action that proceeded from him. You have known that punishment only arises from the false beliefs that a person acquires and from the firmly established dispositions that a person acquires. Thus this statement agrees with what is rationally understood.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾. In it there are issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding the position of *anna* (أنَّ) there are two possibilities:

This indicates that if that advancing had not proceeded from him, Allah, exalted is He, would have been unjust in this punishment. So if the originator of disbelief and disobedience were Allah and not the servant, it would necessarily follow that Allah is unjust. Also, this verse indicates that He is capable of injustice, for if it were not possible for Him, there would be no benefit in praising Him by negating it.

Know that this issue has already been discussed in detail in Surah Al 'Imran, so there is no benefit in repeating it. And Allah knows best.
