**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 65:**

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, rouse the believers to fighting. If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.﴾

Know that when Allah promised him victory against the deception of the enemies in the previous verse, He promised him victory and triumph in this verse unconditionally, under all circumstances. On this understanding, there is no repetition, because the meaning of the first verse is: if they intend to deceive you, Allah will suffice you against their affair. The meaning of this verse is general, covering everything that is needed in religion and in worldly life.

This verse was revealed at al-Bayda' during the expedition of Badr, before the fighting. By His saying ﴿and those of the believers who follow you﴾ is meant the Ansar. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that it was revealed concerning the conversion of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Thirty-three men and six women embraced Islam with the Prophet (ﷺ), then 'Umar embraced Islam, and then this verse was revealed." The commentators said: according to this view, this verse is Meccan, though it was placed within a Medinan surah by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

There are two views concerning the verse:

The first: the meaning is, "Allah is sufficient for you and sufficient for those of the believers who follow you." Al-Farra' said: the kaf in *ḥasbuka* is in the genitive position, and *man* is in the accusative position, and the meaning is: Allah suffices you, and suffices those who follow you. The poet said:

*When battle rages and the staff is split, then sufficient for you, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, is a sword of Indian steel.*

He (al-Farra') said: it is not common in their speech to say *ḥasbuka wa-akhāka* ("sufficient for you and your brother"); rather, the usual form is *ḥasbuka wa-ḥasbu akhīka* ("sufficient for you, and sufficient for your brother").

The second: the meaning is that Allah has sufficed you and your followers among the believers have sufficed you. Al-Farra' said: this is the better of the two views. It may be argued in support of the first view that whoever has Allah as his helper, his condition cannot increase or decrease because of the help of others than Allah. Also, attributing the judgment to the group may give the impression that one individual of that group is not sufficient for achieving that important matter, and Allah is far exalted above that. It may be answered that all comes from Allah, but among the kinds of help is that which is not obtained through the familiar and customary causes, and among them is that which is obtained through the familiar and customary causes. Because of this distinction, He took account of the help of the believers. Then He made clear that, although Allah suffices you with His help and the help of the believers, it is not obligatory for you to rely on that unless you rouse the believers to fighting. Allah suffices you with sufficiency only on condition that they give of themselves and their wealth in striving. So He said: ﴿O Prophet, rouse the believers to fighting.﴾

*Al-taḥrīḍ* (rousing, urging) in the language is like *al-taḥḍīḍ* (urging), and it means urging someone toward a thing. Al-Zajjaj mentioned another, distant derivation, saying: *al-taḥrīḍ* in the language means that a person urges another toward something with such urging that it is known from him that if the other person holds back from it, he would be *ḥāriḍan* (one who is near ruin). *Al-ḥārid* is one who has approached destruction. By this he indicated that if the believers held back from fighting after the urging of the Prophet (ﷺ), they would be *ḥāridūn*, that is, ruined. Thus, according to him, *al-taḥrīḍ* is derived from the word *al-ḥārid* and *al-ḥaras*.

Then He said: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred.﴾ The purpose of this is not a report but a command, as if He said: "If there are twenty of you, then let them be steadfast and strive in fighting until they overcome two hundred." The following points show that the purpose of this statement is not a report:

First: if it were meant as a report, it would follow that two hundred of the disbelievers never overcame twenty of the believers, and it is known that this is false.

Second: He said, ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾ (8:66), and abrogation (*naskh*) is more appropriate to a command than to a report.

Third: His saying afterward, ﴿And Allah is with the steadfast﴾ (8:66), which is an encouragement to steadfastness in striving. Thus it is established that the purpose of this statement is a command, even though it comes in the form of a report. This is like His saying: ﴿The mothers shall suckle their children for two full years﴾ (2:233), and ﴿Divorced women shall keep themselves in waiting﴾ (2:228). On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve﴾. Its essential meaning is the obligation for one to stand firm against ten. What is the benefit of departing from this concise expression to those long words?

Its answer: this statement came in accordance with the actual event. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would send out detachments (*sarāyā*), and generally those detachments did not number fewer than twenty nor exceed a hundred. For this reason, Allah mentioned these two numbers.

**The second issue:** Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *in takun* with *tā'* (the feminine form), and likewise the following one, *wa-in takun minkum mi'atun ṣābirah*. Abu 'Amr read the first with *yā'* and the second with *tā'*, and the rest read both with *yā'*.

**The third issue:** Allah clarified the reason for this victory, which is His saying: ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾. The explanation of this statement is according to several aspects:

**The first aspect:** Whoever does not believe in Allah and does not believe in the Hereafter, for him the utmost happiness and joy is nothing but this worldly life. Whoever holds this belief is stingy with this life and does not expose it to loss. As for one who believes that there is no happiness in this life, and that happiness is attained only in the Abode of the Hereafter, he does not care for this worldly life, does not attend to it, and gives it no weight. He therefore advances to striving with a strong heart and a sound resolve. When the matter is so, a single man of this kind can withstand a large number of the first kind.

**The second aspect:** The disbelievers rely only on their strength and their might, while the Muslims seek help from their Lord through supplication and humble entreaty. Whoever is like this, victory and success are more fitting and more deserved for him.

**The third aspect:** This is an aspect known only to the people of spiritual disciplines (*riyāḍāt*) and unveilings (*mukāshafāt*). It is that every heart that is singled out for knowledge and recognition, its owner is awe-inspiring in the eyes of creation. For this reason, when a learned man is present among a group of strong, ignorant, fierce people, those strong, fierce, ignorant people stand in awe of that scholar, respect him, and serve him. Indeed, we say that strong beasts, when they see a human being, stand in awe of him and turn away from him, and that is only because the human being, by means of the light of intellect that is in him, is awe-inspiring. Moreover, when the wise man is overtaken by the light of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, his limbs grow strong and his members become firm, and perhaps when manifestation (*tajallī*) appears in his heart, he becomes capable of actions he was unable to perform before that time.

Having understood this, when the believer advances to striving, it is as though he has given himself and his wealth in seeking the good pleasure of Allah. He is then in this state like one who witnesses the light of the majesty of Allah, so his heart becomes strong, his soul is perfected, and he is able to do what others cannot. These are states from the category of unveilings, which indicate that the believer must be stronger in power than the disbeliever. If this does not occur, it is because the appearance of this manifestation happens only rarely, and to one individual after another. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 66:**

*Allah's words: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness among you. So if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾*

[Page 155]

In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to send ten men against a hundred. He sent Hamzah with thirty riders toward a people before Badr. Abu Jahl met them with three hundred riders and they wanted to fight them, but Hamzah prevented them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also sent Abdullah ibn Unays to Khalid ibn Sufyan al-Hudhali, who was with a group. Abdullah hastened and said, "O Messenger of Allah, describe him to me." He said: "When you see him, you will remember Satan and you will feel a shudder in yourself. It has reached me that he has gathered [people] against me. So go out to him and kill him." He said: "I went toward him, and when I drew near to him I felt the shudder. He said to me, 'Who is the man?' I said to him, 'An Arab. I have heard of you and of your gathering.' I walked with him until I got close enough to him, then I killed him with the sword and hastened to the Messenger (ﷺ) and mentioned that I had killed him. He gave me a staff and said: 'Keep it, for it will be a sign between me and you on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Then this obligation was hard upon the Muslims, and Allah removed it from them by this verse. ʿAtaʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbas: When the first obligation was revealed, the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) complained and said, "O Lord, we are hungry while our enemy is full; we are in exile while our enemy is in his homeland; we have been expelled from our homes, our wealth and our children, while our enemy is not so." The Helpers (al-Ansar) said, "We are occupied with our enemy and we comfort our brothers." So the lightening was revealed.

ʿIkrimah said: The man was commanded to be steadfast against ten, and the ten against a hundred, at the time when the Muslims were few. When they increased, Allah the Exalted lightened [the burden] for them. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Whoever flees from three has not fled, but whoever flees from two has fled."

The sum is that the majority (al-Jumhur) of scholars claimed that His words ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ abrogate (naskh) the preceding verse. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani (Abu Muslim al-Isfahani) denied this abrogation. The explanation of his view is that Allah the Exalted said in the first verse: ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾. Grant that we take this statement as a command, nevertheless this command was conditional upon the twenty being able to be steadfast against the two hundred. And His words ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾ indicate that this condition is not fulfilled in the case of these people. So the sum of the matter is that the first verse indicated the establishment of a ruling upon a specific condition, and this verse indicated that this condition is absent in the case of this group. Therefore that ruling was not established, and on this interpretation no abrogation occurred at all.

If they say: His words ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ mean: let the twenty steadfast be set against the two hundred. On this interpretation, abrogation is necessary.

We reply: Why is it not permissible to say that the meaning of the verse is: if twenty steadfast men come to be against two hundred, then let them occupy themselves with fighting them? The sum is that the wording of the verse came in the form of a statement, and we departed from this outward meaning and took it as a command. As for the condition, we have left it on its outward meaning. Its implied sense is: if there come to be among you twenty described as steadfast in resisting two hundred, then let them occupy themselves with resisting them. On this interpretation, there is no abrogation.

If they say: His words ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ imply that this obligation was directed at them before this obligation.

We reply: We do not concede that the word "lightening" indicates that a heavier obligation existed before it. The custom of the Arabs is to grant a dispensation with such speech, as in His words, when granting a free man permission to marry a slave woman: ﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:28]. There is no abrogation there; rather it is the permission to marry a slave woman for one who cannot afford to marry free women. So it is the same here. The fuller explanation is that these twenty were in a position where it could be said that the condition was fulfilled in them, so that obligation was binding upon them. Then, when Allah made clear that this condition was not fulfilled, and that He knew there were weak ones among them who could not bear it, they were relieved of that fear. Thus it is correct to say: Allah has lightened [the burden] for you.

[Page 156]

Among what indicates the absence of abrogation is that He mentioned this verse alongside the first verse, and it is not permissible for the abrogating text to be placed alongside the abrogated one.

If they say: The consideration in abrogating and abrogated texts is the time of revelation, not the recitation, for the latter may come before or after. Do you not see that in the case of the waiting period for widowhood, the abrogating text comes before the abrogated one?

We reply: Since it is not permissible for the abrogating text to exist alongside the abrogated one in actual existence, it must likewise not be permissible in mention, except by a compelling proof, and you have not mentioned any such proof. As for his words concerning the waiting period for widowhood, that the abrogating text precedes the abrogated one, we say: Abu Muslim denies every kind of abrogation in the Qur'an, so how can this objection be imposed on him? This is the explanation of Abu Muslim's view. I say: if a consensus (ijma') of the community, established before Abu Muslim, on the absolute occurrence of this abrogation is proven, then there is nothing to be said against it. But if this decisive consensus was not reached, then we say that Abu Muslim's view is correct and sound.

* * *

**The second issue:** Hisham argued, in support of his position that Allah the Exalted does not know particulars (al-juziyyat) except at the moment they occur, by His words ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾. He said: The meaning of the verse is "Now Allah has come to know that there is weakness among you." This implies that His knowledge of their weakness did not come about except at this time.

The theologians (al-Mutakallimun) replied that the meaning of the verse is: Before a thing occurs, He does not know it as existing and actual; rather He knows that it will come into being. But when it comes into being and occurs, He knows it as having come into being and occurred. So His words ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness among you﴾ mean: Now the knowledge of its occurrence and coming into being has been attained, whereas before that, what was present was the knowledge that it would occur or would come into being.

* * *

**The third issue:** ʿAsim and Hamzah read ﻋَﻠِﻢَ ﺃَﻥَّ ﻓِﻴﻜُﻢْ ﺿَﻌْﻔًﺎ with a fatha on the dad (ḍaʿfan), and in ar-Rum (30:54) they read it likewise, while the rest read both with a damma (ḍuʿf). Both are sound dialects: *ḍaʿf* and *ḍuʿf* are like *makth* and *mukth*. Hafs differed from ʿAsim on this letter and read both with a damma, and said: "I did not differ from ʿAsim in anything of the Qur'an except in this letter."

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The ruling that has become settled by the implication of this verse is that every adult Muslim who is legally responsible and faces two polytheists, whether slave or free, is forbidden to flee as long as he has a weapon with which to fight. If no weapon remains with him, he may flee. If three men fight him, flight becomes permissible for him, though steadfastness is better.

Al-Wahidi related in *al-Basit* that the army of Mu'tah, numbering three thousand, stood firm against two hundred thousand of the polytheists, in succession under their commanders: Zayd ibn Harithah, then Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, then ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah. Of them, a hundred thousand were Romans and a hundred thousand were al-Musta'ribah, who were Lakhm and Judham.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** His words ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ state that victory occurs only by the permission of Allah. Here "permission" (al-idhn) means will (al-irada), and this supports our position in the question of the creation of acts and the will of created beings.

Know that He concluded the verse with His words ﴿And Allah is with the steadfast﴾, and what is meant is what He mentioned in the first verse: ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal 8:65]. So He made clear at the end of this verse that Allah is with the steadfast. The intended meaning is that if the twenty are steadfast and hold their ground, then My support and My success are with them and accompany them. This indicates the soundness of Abu Muslim's view, namely that this ruling was not abrogated but remains established as it was. If the twenty are able to withstand the two hundred, that ruling remains; and if they are not able to withstand them, then the ruling mentioned here no longer applies.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verses 67–68 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre in the land. You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to teach another ruling from the rulings of raiding and jihad concerning the Prophet ﷺ. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr read "takūna" (تَكُونَ) with the ta', while the rest read it with the ya'. As for Abu 'Amr's reading with the ta', it is according to the wording of "al-asra" (الأسرى), for although what is meant is masculine (men), its wording is feminine. As for the reading with the ya', it is because the verb precedes, and "al-asra" are masculine in meaning, and there is a separation between the verb and its subject. Each one of these three, when it stands alone, requires the verb to be masculine, as in your saying: "jā'a al-rijālu" (the men came), "ḥaḍara qabīlatuka" (your tribe attended), and "ḥaḍara al-qāḍiya imra'atun" (a woman attended the judge). So when these things combine, the masculine is more appropriate. The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: it has been read "lin-nabiyyi ﷺ" with the definite article, and "usārā" and "yuthakhkhina" with the doubled letter (shadda).

The second issue: It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was brought seventy captives, among them al-'Abbas, his paternal uncle, and 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib. He consulted Abu Bakr about them, and he said: "They are your people and your family; spare them, perhaps Allah will accept their repentance, and take from them a ransom with which you may strengthen your companions." Then 'Umar stood and said: "They denied you and drove you out; bring them forward and strike their necks, for these are the leaders of disbelief, and Allah has made you independent of ransom. Enable 'Ali to take 'Aqil, and Hamza to take al-'Abbas, and enable me to take so-and-so, a relative of ours, and we shall strike their necks." Then he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah softens the hearts of some men until they are softer than milk, and indeed Allah hardens the hearts of some men until they are harder than stones. And your likeness, O Abu Bakr, is the likeness of Abraham, who said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], and the likeness of Jesus in his saying: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]. And your likeness, O 'Umar, is the likeness of Noah, who said: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26], and the likeness of Moses when he said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts﴾ [Yunus: 88]." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined to the saying of Abu Bakr. It is narrated that he said to 'Umar: "O Abu Hafs" — and that was the first time he gave him this kunya — "you command me to kill al-'Abbas?" So 'Umar began saying: "Woe to 'Umar, may his mother be bereaved of him."

It is also narrated that 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah advised that a fire with much firewood be kindled over them, and al-'Abbas said to him: "You have severed your kinship."

It is narrated that he ﷺ said: "Do not release any of them except for a ransom or the striking of the neck." Then Ibn Mas'ud said: "Except Suhayl ibn Bayda', for I heard him mention Islam." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fell silent, and my fear intensified. Then he said afterwards: "Except Suhayl ibn Bayda'."

And from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the people: "If you wish, kill them, and if you wish, take ransom from them, and a number equal to them of you will be martyred." They said: "Rather, we take the ransom," and so a number of them were martyred at Uhud. The ransom for the captives was twenty ounces, and the ransom of al-'Abbas was forty ounces.

And from Muhammad ibn Sirin: their ransom was a hundred ounces, and an ounce is forty dirhams or six dinars.

It is narrated: "When they took the ransom, this verse was revealed. 'Umar entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found him and Abu Bakr weeping. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me, for if I find (a reason for) weeping I will weep, and if I do not find it I will feign weeping.' He said: 'Weep over your companions in their taking of the ransom. Their punishment was presented to me, as near as this tree' — pointing to a tree near him — 'and had a punishment descended from the sky, none would have been saved from it except 'Umar and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.'"

This is what is said concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.

* * *

The third issue: Those who object to the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, have held to this verse in several respects:

The first respect: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is explicit that this matter is forbidden and prohibited by Allah the Exalted. Then this matter has occurred, and two things indicate it:

The first: the saying of the Exalted after this verse: ﴿O Prophet, say to those in your hands of the captives﴾ [al-Anfal: 70].

The second: the narration we have mentioned indicates that he, peace be upon him, did not kill those disbelievers, but took them captive, so the sin was necessary from this aspect.

The second respect: He, the Exalted, commanded the Prophet, peace be upon him, and all his people on the day of Badr to kill the disbelievers, and that is His saying: ﴿So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. So when they did not kill but took captives, taking captives was disobedience.

The third respect: the Prophet ﷺ ruled to take ransom, and taking ransom was disobedience. Two things indicate this:

The first: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter.﴾ The commentators have unanimously agreed that what is meant by "the goods of this world" here is taking ransom.

The second: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ They have unanimously agreed that what is meant by "what you took" is that ransom.

The fourth respect: the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr wept, and the Messenger ﷺ stated explicitly that he wept only because he ruled to take ransom, and that indicates it was a sin.

The fifth respect: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the punishment has drawn near its descent, and had it descended, none would have been saved from it except 'Umar," and that indicates a sin. This is the sum of the ways in which these people have held to this verse.

As for the answer to the first respect they mentioned: the saying ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre in the land﴾ indicates that taking captives was legislated, but on condition that a massacre in the land precedes it. By "massacre" is meant killing and intense terrorizing. There is no doubt that the Companions killed a great multitude on the day of Badr, and it is not a condition of the massacre in the land that all people be killed. Then, after the great slaughter, they took a group captive, and the verse indicates that after the massacre it is permissible to take captives. So this verse is clearly indicative that that taking was permitted by the ruling of this verse. How then can this verse be used to argue that that taking was a sin and disobedience? This statement is confirmed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿until when you have inflicted a massacre upon them, then bind them firmly, and afterwards either grace or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

If they say: According to what you have explained, the verse indicates that that taking was permissible, and bringing about what is permitted and legislated does not warrant the punishment being attached to it; so why did God mention after it what indicates punishment? We say: The reason for this is that the "massacre in the land" is not bound by a known, fixed measure. Rather, the intent of it is to increase killing to the degree that causes terror to fall into the hearts of the disbelievers, and that they not dare to fight the believers. Reaching the killing to this specific limit is undoubtedly left to ijtihad (independent reasoning). So perhaps it became dominant in the estimation of the Messenger, peace be upon him, that that measure of killing which had preceded was sufficient for achieving this aim, though the matter was not so; thus this was an error occurring in ijtihad in a case where there is no explicit text. And "the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." So it was fitting that punishment be attached to the mention of this statement for this cause, even though that is never at all a sin or disobedience.

As for the answer to the second respect they mentioned, we say: the apparent meaning of the saying of the Exalted ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ is that this address was indeed with the Companions, since the Muslims agree that he, peace be upon him, was not commanded to directly undertake the killing of the disbelievers himself. And if this address is specific to the Companions, then when they abandoned killing and proceeded to taking captives, the sin was issued from them, not from the Messenger ﷺ. It is related that when the Companions defeated the disbelievers and killed a great number of them, and the disbelievers fled, the Companions went after them and moved far from the Messenger and took those people captive. The Messenger did not learn of their proceeding to take captives until after the Companions returned to his presence. He, peace be upon him, neither took captives nor commanded taking captives, and so this objection is removed.

If they say: Granted that the matter is so, yet when they brought the captives to his presence, why did he not command their killing, in compliance with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾?

We say: The saying ﴿So strike﴾ is an obligation specific to the state of war, when the disbelievers are occupied with fighting. As for after the war has ended, this obligation did not encompass that state. The conclusive proof of this is that he, peace be upon him, consulted the Companions about how he should treat them. Had that text encompassed that state, then, in the presence of the decisive text, he would have been abandoning its ruling and seeking that ruling from consultation with the Companions, and that is impossible. Furthermore, the saying ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ is a command, and a command conveys only a single instance, and it is established by consensus that this meaning was obligatory during the state of fighting, so it must remain without indication of what lies beyond the time of fighting. And this answer is sufficient.

As for the answer to what they mentioned third, namely their saying: he, peace be upon him, ruled to take ransom, and taking ransom is prohibited, we say: We do not grant that taking ransom is prohibited.

As for the saying ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾, we say: this does not indicate your claim, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: the purpose of this verse is the occurrence of reproach for taking captives for the aim of taking ransom, and that does not indicate that taking ransom is prohibited absolutely.

The second: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is better that we take the ransom so that the army may be strengthened by it for jihad," and that indicates that they sought that ransom only to strengthen themselves for the religion, whereas this verse indicates the blaming of one who sought ransom for the sheer aim of worldly goods, and neither of the two parts has any connection to the second. These two answers are themselves the two answers to their holding to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾

As for the answer to what they mentioned fourth: the weeping of the Messenger, peace be upon him, may be due to the fact that some of the Companions, when they opposed the command of Allah regarding killing and occupied themselves with taking captives, merited punishment, so the Messenger, peace be upon him, wept out of fear of the punishment descending upon them. It may also be, as we have mentioned, that he, peace be upon him, exerted ijtihad as to whether the killing that had occurred had reached the level of "massacre" which Allah commanded in His saying: ﴿until He has inflicted a massacre in the land﴾, and error occurred in that ijtihad, and "the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near," so he wept for this reason.

As for the answer to what they mentioned fifth: that punishment descended only because those people opposed Allah's command to kill and proceeded to take captives at the time when they were obligated to be occupied with killing. This is the completion of the discussion of this issue, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: in explaining the difficult words in this verse.

As for the saying ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾, one may say: how is it fitting to introduce the word "kāna" (كانَ) upon the word "yakūna" (يَكُونَ) in this verse?

Al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb), commentary on surah 8, verses 67–68 (part 2 of 2):

The answer: His words ﴿ma kāna﴾ ("it is not for") mean negation and exoneration, i.e., what is obligatory and what is fitting is not that this meaning (mentioned) should apply to him. A parallel to this is ﴿mā kāna lillāhi an yattakhidha min walad﴾ ("It is not for God to take a son," Maryam 35). Abu 'Ubayda said: it means that this was not for any Prophet, so it is not for you either. As for the one who reads "mā kāna lil-nabiyyi," its meaning is that this ruling was not fitting to occur for this Prophet, namely Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Asra" is a plural, and "usara" is a plural of plural. He said: I do not know of anyone who read "asara," though it is permissible, as we have quoted from the author of al-Kashshaf, who related that some people recited it that way.

As for His words ﴿ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ ("until he has thoroughly subdued the land"), there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Wahidi said: "al-ithkhān" (thorough subduing) in anything is an expression for its strength and intensity. It is said: "Disease has overwhelmed him" (athkhanahu al-maraḍ) when the disease's power over him intensifies; likewise, "wounds have overwhelmed him" (athkhanahu al-jirāḥ). "Thakhāna" is thickness, so everything thick is "thakhīn." Thus His words ﴿ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ mean: until he becomes strong, intensified, dominant, exceeding, and subduing. Then, many exegetes said that what is intended by it is that he should go to the extreme in killing his enemies. They said: We interpreted the wording this way because dominion and state are only strengthened and intensified through killing. The poet said:

"The lofty nobility is not free from harm
until blood is spilled upon its sides."

Also, because abundant killing necessitates the strength of dread and the severity of awe, and this prevents boldness and the undertaking of what is not fitting. For this reason God, exalted is He, commanded this.

The second discussion: the word "ḥattā" denotes the endpoint (of a period). So His words ﴿mā kāna li-nabiyyin an yakūna lahu asrā ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ indicate that after thorough subduing in the land is achieved, it is permissible for him to proceed to taking captives.

As for His words ﴿turīdūna ʿaraḍa l-dunyā﴾ ("you desire the goods of this world"), what is meant is ransom. He called the benefits and enjoyments of the world "ʿaraḍ" (fleeting goods) because they have no permanence or continuance; it is as if they appear and then vanish. For this reason the theologians called accidents "aʿrāḍ," since they lack the permanence of substances: they occur upon substances and depart from them while the substances remain. Then He said: ﴿wa-llāhu yurīdu l-ākhira﴾ ("and God desires the Hereafter"), meaning: He, exalted is He, does not desire what leads to worldly felicities that appear and vanish, but desires what leads to the everlasting, enduring otherworldly felicities, protected from change and cessation.

Al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi used this verse to refute the view of those who say: nothing occurs from the servant except that God wills it. Because this capture occurred from them in this manner, and God explicitly stated that He does not will it, but wills from them what leads to the reward of the Hereafter, which is obedience, rather than what involves disobedience.

The Sunnis answered them by saying: God did not will that this capture from them be an act of obedience, lawful and permitted. The negation of willing that this capture be obedience does not entail the negation of its being willed in terms of existence. As for the philosophers, they say: a thing is willed accidentally (bi-l-ʿaraḍ) and disliked essentially (bi-l-dhāt).

Page 161

Then He said: ﴿wa-llāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm﴾ ("and God is Mighty, Wise"). The meaning is that if you seek the Hereafter, your enemy will not overcome you, because God is Mighty, not subdued or defeated, and Wise in managing the interests of the world. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this ruling applied only on the day of Badr, because the Muslims were few; when they grew in number and their authority became strong, God revealed afterward concerning captives: ﴿ḥattā idhā athkhantumūhum fa-shuddū l-wathāq, fa-immā mannan baʿdu wa-immā fidāʾan ḥattā taḍaʿa l-ḥarbu awzārahā﴾ ("until, when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind them firmly; then either afterward release them as a favor or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens," Muhammad 4).

I say: this statement may give the impression that His words ﴿fa-immā mannan baʿdu wa-immā fidāʾan﴾ go beyond the ruling of the verse we are interpreting; but the matter is not so, because both verses are consistent, for both indicate that thorough subduing must come first, and after it the taking of ransom.
