And from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the people: "If you wish, kill them, and if you wish, take ransom from them, and a number equal to them of you will be martyred." They said: "Rather, we take the ransom," and so a number of them were martyred at Uhud. The ransom for the captives was twenty ounces, and the ransom of al-'Abbas was forty ounces.

And from Muhammad ibn Sirin: their ransom was a hundred ounces, and an ounce is forty dirhams or six dinars.

It is narrated: "When they took the ransom, this verse was revealed. 'Umar entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found him and Abu Bakr weeping. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me, for if I find (a reason for) weeping I will weep, and if I do not find it I will feign weeping.' He said: 'Weep over your companions in their taking of the ransom. Their punishment was presented to me, as near as this tree' — pointing to a tree near him — 'and had a punishment descended from the sky, none would have been saved from it except 'Umar and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.'"

This is what is said concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.

* * *

The third issue: Those who object to the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, have held to this verse in several respects:

The first respect: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾ is explicit that this matter is forbidden and prohibited by Allah the Exalted. Then this matter has occurred, and two things indicate it:

The first: the saying of the Exalted after this verse: ﴿O Prophet, say to those in your hands of the captives﴾ [al-Anfal: 70].

The second: the narration we have mentioned indicates that he, peace be upon him, did not kill those disbelievers, but took them captive, so the sin was necessary from this aspect.

The second respect: He, the Exalted, commanded the Prophet, peace be upon him, and all his people on the day of Badr to kill the disbelievers, and that is His saying: ﴿So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. So when they did not kill but took captives, taking captives was disobedience.

The third respect: the Prophet ﷺ ruled to take ransom, and taking ransom was disobedience. Two things indicate this:

The first: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter.﴾ The commentators have unanimously agreed that what is meant by "the goods of this world" here is taking ransom.

The second: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾ They have unanimously agreed that what is meant by "what you took" is that ransom.

The fourth respect: the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr wept, and the Messenger ﷺ stated explicitly that he wept only because he ruled to take ransom, and that indicates it was a sin.

The fifth respect: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the punishment has drawn near its descent, and had it descended, none would have been saved from it except 'Umar," and that indicates a sin. This is the sum of the ways in which these people have held to this verse.

As for the answer to the first respect they mentioned: the saying ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre in the land﴾ indicates that taking captives was legislated, but on condition that a massacre in the land precedes it. By "massacre" is meant killing and intense terrorizing. There is no doubt that the Companions killed a great multitude on the day of Badr, and it is not a condition of the massacre in the land that all people be killed. Then, after the great slaughter, they took a group captive, and the verse indicates that after the massacre it is permissible to take captives. So this verse is clearly indicative that that taking was permitted by the ruling of this verse. How then can this verse be used to argue that that taking was a sin and disobedience? This statement is confirmed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿until when you have inflicted a massacre upon them, then bind them firmly, and afterwards either grace or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

If they say: According to what you have explained, the verse indicates that that taking was permissible, and bringing about what is permitted and legislated does not warrant the punishment being attached to it; so why did God mention after it what indicates punishment? We say: The reason for this is that the "massacre in the land" is not bound by a known, fixed measure. Rather, the intent of it is to increase killing to the degree that causes terror to fall into the hearts of the disbelievers, and that they not dare to fight the believers. Reaching the killing to this specific limit is undoubtedly left to ijtihad (independent reasoning). So perhaps it became dominant in the estimation of the Messenger, peace be upon him, that that measure of killing which had preceded was sufficient for achieving this aim, though the matter was not so; thus this was an error occurring in ijtihad in a case where there is no explicit text. And "the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." So it was fitting that punishment be attached to the mention of this statement for this cause, even though that is never at all a sin or disobedience.

As for the answer to the second respect they mentioned, we say: the apparent meaning of the saying of the Exalted ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ is that this address was indeed with the Companions, since the Muslims agree that he, peace be upon him, was not commanded to directly undertake the killing of the disbelievers himself. And if this address is specific to the Companions, then when they abandoned killing and proceeded to taking captives, the sin was issued from them, not from the Messenger ﷺ. It is related that when the Companions defeated the disbelievers and killed a great number of them, and the disbelievers fled, the Companions went after them and moved far from the Messenger and took those people captive. The Messenger did not learn of their proceeding to take captives until after the Companions returned to his presence. He, peace be upon him, neither took captives nor commanded taking captives, and so this objection is removed.

If they say: Granted that the matter is so, yet when they brought the captives to his presence, why did he not command their killing, in compliance with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾?

We say: The saying ﴿So strike﴾ is an obligation specific to the state of war, when the disbelievers are occupied with fighting. As for after the war has ended, this obligation did not encompass that state. The conclusive proof of this is that he, peace be upon him, consulted the Companions about how he should treat them. Had that text encompassed that state, then, in the presence of the decisive text, he would have been abandoning its ruling and seeking that ruling from consultation with the Companions, and that is impossible. Furthermore, the saying ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ is a command, and a command conveys only a single instance, and it is established by consensus that this meaning was obligatory during the state of fighting, so it must remain without indication of what lies beyond the time of fighting. And this answer is sufficient.

As for the answer to what they mentioned third, namely their saying: he, peace be upon him, ruled to take ransom, and taking ransom is prohibited, we say: We do not grant that taking ransom is prohibited.

As for the saying ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾, we say: this does not indicate your claim, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: the purpose of this verse is the occurrence of reproach for taking captives for the aim of taking ransom, and that does not indicate that taking ransom is prohibited absolutely.

The second: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is better that we take the ransom so that the army may be strengthened by it for jihad," and that indicates that they sought that ransom only to strengthen themselves for the religion, whereas this verse indicates the blaming of one who sought ransom for the sheer aim of worldly goods, and neither of the two parts has any connection to the second. These two answers are themselves the two answers to their holding to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾

As for the answer to what they mentioned fourth: the weeping of the Messenger, peace be upon him, may be due to the fact that some of the Companions, when they opposed the command of Allah regarding killing and occupied themselves with taking captives, merited punishment, so the Messenger, peace be upon him, wept out of fear of the punishment descending upon them. It may also be, as we have mentioned, that he, peace be upon him, exerted ijtihad as to whether the killing that had occurred had reached the level of "massacre" which Allah commanded in His saying: ﴿until He has inflicted a massacre in the land﴾, and error occurred in that ijtihad, and "the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near," so he wept for this reason.

As for the answer to what they mentioned fifth: that punishment descended only because those people opposed Allah's command to kill and proceeded to take captives at the time when they were obligated to be occupied with killing. This is the completion of the discussion of this issue, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: in explaining the difficult words in this verse.

As for the saying ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾, one may say: how is it fitting to introduce the word "kāna" (كانَ) upon the word "yakūna" (يَكُونَ) in this verse?

Al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb), commentary on surah 8, verses 67–68 (part 2 of 2):

The answer: His words ﴿ma kāna﴾ ("it is not for") mean negation and exoneration, i.e., what is obligatory and what is fitting is not that this meaning (mentioned) should apply to him. A parallel to this is ﴿mā kāna lillāhi an yattakhidha min walad﴾ ("It is not for God to take a son," Maryam 35). Abu 'Ubayda said: it means that this was not for any Prophet, so it is not for you either. As for the one who reads "mā kāna lil-nabiyyi," its meaning is that this ruling was not fitting to occur for this Prophet, namely Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Asra" is a plural, and "usara" is a plural of plural. He said: I do not know of anyone who read "asara," though it is permissible, as we have quoted from the author of al-Kashshaf, who related that some people recited it that way.

As for His words ﴿ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ ("until he has thoroughly subdued the land"), there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Wahidi said: "al-ithkhān" (thorough subduing) in anything is an expression for its strength and intensity. It is said: "Disease has overwhelmed him" (athkhanahu al-maraḍ) when the disease's power over him intensifies; likewise, "wounds have overwhelmed him" (athkhanahu al-jirāḥ). "Thakhāna" is thickness, so everything thick is "thakhīn." Thus His words ﴿ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ mean: until he becomes strong, intensified, dominant, exceeding, and subduing. Then, many exegetes said that what is intended by it is that he should go to the extreme in killing his enemies. They said: We interpreted the wording this way because dominion and state are only strengthened and intensified through killing. The poet said:

"The lofty nobility is not free from harm
until blood is spilled upon its sides."

Also, because abundant killing necessitates the strength of dread and the severity of awe, and this prevents boldness and the undertaking of what is not fitting. For this reason God, exalted is He, commanded this.

The second discussion: the word "ḥattā" denotes the endpoint (of a period). So His words ﴿mā kāna li-nabiyyin an yakūna lahu asrā ḥattā yuthkhina fī l-arḍ﴾ indicate that after thorough subduing in the land is achieved, it is permissible for him to proceed to taking captives.

As for His words ﴿turīdūna ʿaraḍa l-dunyā﴾ ("you desire the goods of this world"), what is meant is ransom. He called the benefits and enjoyments of the world "ʿaraḍ" (fleeting goods) because they have no permanence or continuance; it is as if they appear and then vanish. For this reason the theologians called accidents "aʿrāḍ," since they lack the permanence of substances: they occur upon substances and depart from them while the substances remain. Then He said: ﴿wa-llāhu yurīdu l-ākhira﴾ ("and God desires the Hereafter"), meaning: He, exalted is He, does not desire what leads to worldly felicities that appear and vanish, but desires what leads to the everlasting, enduring otherworldly felicities, protected from change and cessation.

Al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi used this verse to refute the view of those who say: nothing occurs from the servant except that God wills it. Because this capture occurred from them in this manner, and God explicitly stated that He does not will it, but wills from them what leads to the reward of the Hereafter, which is obedience, rather than what involves disobedience.

The Sunnis answered them by saying: God did not will that this capture from them be an act of obedience, lawful and permitted. The negation of willing that this capture be obedience does not entail the negation of its being willed in terms of existence. As for the philosophers, they say: a thing is willed accidentally (bi-l-ʿaraḍ) and disliked essentially (bi-l-dhāt).

Page 161

Then He said: ﴿wa-llāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm﴾ ("and God is Mighty, Wise"). The meaning is that if you seek the Hereafter, your enemy will not overcome you, because God is Mighty, not subdued or defeated, and Wise in managing the interests of the world. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this ruling applied only on the day of Badr, because the Muslims were few; when they grew in number and their authority became strong, God revealed afterward concerning captives: ﴿ḥattā idhā athkhantumūhum fa-shuddū l-wathāq, fa-immā mannan baʿdu wa-immā fidāʾan ḥattā taḍaʿa l-ḥarbu awzārahā﴾ ("until, when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind them firmly; then either afterward release them as a favor or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens," Muhammad 4).

I say: this statement may give the impression that His words ﴿fa-immā mannan baʿdu wa-immā fidāʾan﴾ go beyond the ruling of the verse we are interpreting; but the matter is not so, because both verses are consistent, for both indicate that thorough subduing must come first, and after it the taking of ransom.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had there not been a decree from God that preceded, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took.﴾

Know that the sayings of people regarding the interpretation of this preceding decree have been many, and we will mention them along with the discussions contained in them:

The first saying, which is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah: "Had there not been a decree from God that preceded, O Muhammad, concerning the permissibility of the spoils for you and your community, the punishment would have touched you." This view is problematic, because the permissibility of spoils and of ransom (fida') — was it established at that time or was it not established at that time? If the permissibility and the permission were established at that time, then it is impossible for punishment to be sent down upon them, because what was already permitted beforehand does not incur punishment for its doing. And if we say that the permission was not established at that time, then that act was forbidden at that time. The most that can be said is that it was in God's knowledge that He would later rule its permissibility, but this does not undermine its being forbidden at that time.

If they say: that it is of a nature that it will become lawful afterward necessitates lightening the punishment.

We say: if that is the case, then it is impossible for punishment to be sent down because of it, and that prevents the warning through that punishment.

The second saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: ﴿Had there not been a decree from God that preceded﴾ that I do not punish except after a prohibition, I would have punished you for what you did; and He, exalted is He, had not prohibited you from taking the ransom. This too is weak, because we say: the upshot of this view is that no legal proof was found that required the prohibition of that ransom. So is there a rational proof that necessitates its prohibition or not? If we say there was, then God, exalted is He, has clarified its prohibition through that rational proof, and it is not possible to say that He did not clarify that prohibition. And if we say that there is nothing in reason or in revelation that requires the prohibition, then it is impossible that the prohibition was established, for otherwise that would be a charge of what cannot be borne. And when the prohibition was not established, the permission was established; and when the permission was established, how is it possible to order punishment for doing it?

The third saying: some people said: God's judgment had already preceded that He would not punish anyone of those who witnessed Badr with the Prophet (ﷺ). This too is problematic, because it entails saying that they were not forbidden from disbelief, sins, fornication and wine, and were not threatened with punishment for these vile acts; and that necessitates the lapsing of obligations from them, which no sensible person would say. Moreover, if that were so, how would God seize them in that very place, in that very incident, and how would He direct this severe punishment upon them?

The fourth saying: "Had there not been a decree from God that preceded concerning the one who commits a sin in ignorance, that He does not hold him accountable for it, the punishment would have touched them." This is of the same kind as what preceded.

Know that people have said much on this matter, and the reliable approach in this chapter is that we say: As for our position, we say: it is permissible that God pardons major sins. So His saying ﴿Had there not been a decree from God that preceded﴾ means: had He, exalted is He, not judged in eternity to pardon this incident, a great punishment would have touched them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54], and of his saying: "My mercy precedes My wrath." As for the view of the Mu'tazilah, they do not permit the pardoning of major sins, so its meaning would be ﴿Had there not been a decree from God that preceded﴾ that whoever abstains from major sins, his minor sins become forgiven; otherwise a great punishment would have touched them. This ruling, although it is established with respect to all Muslims, nonetheless the good deeds of the people of Badr were great: their acceptance of Islam, their submission to Muhammad (ﷺ), and their advancing to fight the disbelievers without weapons or equipment. So it is not far-fetched to say that the reward they deserved for these acts of obedience was greater than the punishment they deserved for this sin, and therefore this sin became forgiven. Had we supposed the occurrence of this sin from the rest of the Muslims, it would not have become forgiven. By virtue of this degree of difference, the people of Badr obtained this distinction.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as lawful and good﴾. It is narrated that they had refrained from the spoils and did not stretch out their hands toward them, so this verse was revealed. It was also said that it refers to the permissibility of ransom.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of the fa' in His saying ﴿So eat﴾?

We say: the implied meaning is: I have already permitted the spoils for you, ﴿so eat of what you have taken as lawful﴾. "Lawful" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the spoil, or as an attribute of the verbal noun, i.e., "eating that is lawful." ﴿And fear God; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ The meaning: fear God, so do not proceed to acts of disobedience after this; and know that God is Forgiving of what you proceeded to in the past of error, Merciful toward what you committed of transgression and disobedience. So His saying ﴿fear God﴾ points to the future, and His saying ﴿indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ points to the past state.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 8, verse 70:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, say to those captives in your hands: If Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you. Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they intend to betray you, they have already betrayed Allah before, so He gave you power over them. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise.﴾

Know that when the Messenger took the ransom from the captives, and taking their wealth from them was difficult for them, Allah revealed this verse to win their hearts, saying: ﴿O Prophet, say to those captives in your hands...﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: It was revealed concerning al-Abbas, Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and Nawfal ibn al-Harith. Al-Abbas was a captive on the day of Badr, and he had with him twenty uqiyyas of gold, which he had brought out to feed the people. He was one of the ten who had guaranteed the food for the people of Badr, and the repentance had not reached him before he was captured. Al-Abbas said: "I was a Muslim, but they forced me." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If what you mention is true, then Allah will reward you. As for the outward of your affair, it was against us." Al-Abbas said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah to return that gold to me, and he said: 'As for the wealth you came out with to help against us, no.'" He said: "The Messenger also charged me with ransoming my nephew Aqil ibn Abi Talib for twenty uqiyyas, and the ransom of Nawfal ibn al-Harith..."

[p. 163]

al-Harith. Al-Abbas said: "O Muhammad, you have left me to beg from Quraysh." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Where is the gold that you gave to Umm al-Fadl at the time of your departure from Makkah, when you said to her: 'I do not know what will befall me; if some calamity happens to me, then it is for you, and for Abdullah, Ubaydullah and al-Fadl'?" Al-Abbas said: "How could you know that?" He said: "My Lord informed me of it." Al-Abbas said: "I testify that you are truthful, and that there is no god but Allah, and that you are His servant and His Messenger. By Allah, no one knew of it except Allah, and I gave it to her in the darkness of the night. I had been doubtful about your affair, but now that you have informed me of this, there is no doubt." Al-Abbas said: "Allah replaced it for me with something better: I now have twenty slaves, and the least of them trades with twenty thousand, and He gave me Zamzam, which I would not want to exchange for all the wealth of the people of Makkah. I am hoping for forgiveness from my Lord." It is also related that "there came to the Messenger of Allah the wealth of Bahrain, eighty thousand. He performed ablution for the noon prayer and did not pray until he had distributed it, and he ordered al-Abbas to take from it. He took as much as he could carry, and he would say: 'This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope for forgiveness.'"

The exegetes differed over whether the verse was revealed concerning al-Abbas alone or concerning all the captives. Some said it was concerning al-Abbas alone, and others said it was revealed concerning all of them, and this is the more correct view, because the apparent meaning of the verse requires generality from six aspects:

First: His saying: ﴿to those in your hands﴾.

Second: His saying: ﴿captives﴾.

Third: His saying: ﴿in your hearts﴾.

Fourth: His saying: ﴿will give you﴾ (good).

Fifth: His saying: ﴿than what was taken from you﴾.

Sixth: His saying: ﴿and He will forgive you﴾.

Since these six expressions indicate generality, what is the cause for restricting it? At most one can say: the occasion of revelation of the verse is al-Abbas. But the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specificity of the occasion.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: this good must necessarily mean faith, and resolve to obey Allah and His Messenger in all obligations, and repentance from disbelief and from all sins. It includes the resolve to support the Messenger and repentance from fighting against him.

The second issue: Hisham ibn al-Hakam argued for his view that He, Exalted is He, does not know a thing except at the time of its occurrence, by this verse, because His saying: ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾ is a condition, and "He will give you..." is the consequent. The condition is the occurrence of this knowledge, and a condition and its consequent can only exist in the future, and this necessitates that the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, is originated.

The answer: although the apparent wording may imply what Hisham mentioned, when the proof has shown that the knowledge of Allah cannot be originated, it is necessary to say: He mentioned the knowledge and intended by it the known, in the sense that the occurrence of knowledge indicates the occurrence of the known.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you, and He will forgive you﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the author of "al-Kashshaf" said: al-Hasan read ﴿مِمّا أخَذَ مِنكم﴾ with the verb in the active voice (akhadha, "He took") rather than the passive (ukhidha, "it was taken").

The second issue: the exegetes have several views about this good:

The first view: what is meant is the replacement for what was taken from them in this world. Al-Qadi said: because He, Exalted is He, conjoined to it the matter of the Hereafter with His saying: ﴿and He will forgive you﴾, so what came before must mean the benefits of this world.

One might say: His saying ﴿and He will forgive you﴾ means the removal of punishment, and on this basis it is not unlikely that the good mentioned here also means reward and bounty in the Hereafter.

The second view: what is meant by this good is the reward of the Hereafter, since His saying ﴿and He will forgive you﴾ means in the Hereafter, so the good which precedes it must also be in this world.

The third view: it is to be understood as covering all of these.

If it is said: If you take the good to mean the goods of this world, do you say that every captive who was sincere has been given by Allah better than what was taken from him?

We say: That is how it must be by the ruling of the verse. However, we do not know who is sincere in his heart so that the question might be directed at us concerning him, nor do we know to whom Allah has given knowledge. We know that a little of this world together with faith is greater than much of this world together with disbelief.

Then He said: ﴿Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, which is an emphasis on what was mentioned before, His saying ﴿and He will forgive you﴾. The meaning: how could He fail to fulfill the promise of forgiveness, when He is Forgiving and Merciful?

Regarding His words, ﴿And if they intend treachery against you, then they had already betrayed Allah before,﴾ there are several issues:

The First Issue: Concerning the interpretation of this treachery, there are several views.

The first: The intended meaning is treachery in religion, which is disbelief. That is, if they disbelieve in you, then they had already betrayed Allah before.

The second: The intended meaning of treachery is withholding the ransom they had pledged.

The third: It is narrated that when he (ﷺ) released them from captivity, he took a pledge from them that they would not return to fighting him or to allying with the polytheists. This is the custom regarding one who is released from confinement and captivity. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they intend treachery against you﴾, meaning the breaking of this pledge, ﴿then they had already betrayed Allah before.﴾ The intended meaning is that they used to say, ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾ [Yunus: 22], and ﴿If You give us a righteous one, we will surely be among the thankful﴾ [al-A'raf: 189]. Then, when they reached blessing and were freed from calamity, they broke the pledge and violated the covenant. This does not preclude that the whole of it is included, although this last view is the more apparent.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So He empowered [him] over them.﴾ Al-Azhari said: It is said amkanani al-amr, yumkinuni, so he is mumkin, and the object of al-imkan (empowerment) is omitted; the meaning is: so He empowered the believers over them. The meaning is that they betrayed Allah by what they undertook of fighting the Messenger on the Day of Badr, so Allah empowered [the believers] over them, by killing and capturing, and that is the utmost of empowerment and victory. Thus Allah alerted by this that they had already tasted the consequence of what they did there. If they return, the empowerment over them would be established and present. In this there is good news for the Messenger (ﷺ) that he will be empowered over everyone who betrays him and breaks his pledge.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Knowing,﴾ meaning of their inner secrets and their hearts, ﴿Wise,﴾ who recompenses them for their deeds.

[Page 165]

﴿Those who disbelieve are allies of one another. If you do not act accordingly, there will be turmoil in the land and great corruption.﴾ ﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the cause of God, and those who gave shelter and aid, they are the true believers. For them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ ﴿Those who believed afterward, emigrated, and struggled alongside you, they are of you. Yet blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of God. Indeed God is Knowing of all things.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed those who believed, emigrated, and struggled with their wealth and their selves in the cause of God, and those who gave shelter and aid, these are allies of one another. As for those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them whatsoever until they emigrate. If they seek your help in religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help, except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant. God is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve are allies of one another. If you do not act accordingly, there will be turmoil in the land and great corruption.﴾ ﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the cause of God, and those who gave shelter and aid, they are the true believers. For them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ ﴿Those who believed afterward, emigrated, and struggled alongside you, they are of you. Yet blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of God. Indeed God is Knowing of all things.﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, divided the believers in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) into four categories, and mentioned the ruling for each of them. The explanation of this division is that the Messenger (peace be upon him) first had his prophethood manifested in Mecca, and he called people there to the religion. Then he moved from Mecca to Medina. When he emigrated from Mecca to Medina, the believers became of two types: some of them agreed with him in that emigration, and some of them did not agree with him in it but remained there.

As for the first category, they are the first emigrants (muhajirun), and He described them by His saying: ﴿Indeed those who believed, emigrated, and struggled with their wealth and their selves in the cause of God﴾. We said that what is meant by them is the first emigrants, because He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Those who believed afterward and emigrated﴾. Once this is established, it becomes clear that these people are described by these four attributes:

The first of them: they believed in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and they accepted all the obligations that Muhammad (ﷺ) conveyed, and did not rebel. His saying ﴿Indeed those who﴾ conveys this meaning.

The second attribute: His saying ﴿and emigrated﴾, meaning they left their homelands and abandoned their relatives and neighbours seeking the pleasure of God. It is well known that this condition is a severe one. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Kill yourselves or leave your homes﴾ [al-Nisa’: 66], making leaving homelands equivalent to killing oneself. So these people, in the first rank, abandoned the old religions seeking the pleasure of God, exalted is He, and in the second rank they abandoned relatives, friends, homelands and neighbours for the pleasure of God, exalted is He.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿and struggled with their wealth and their selves in the cause of God﴾. As for struggle with wealth, when they left their homelands their houses, dwellings, estates and farms were lost and remained in the hands of the enemies. Also, they needed to spend much money because of that resolve. Furthermore, they used to spend their wealth on those expeditions. As for struggle with the self, they went forward to fight at Badr without equipment, provision or preparation, against enemies described as numerous and fierce. That indicates that they removed their desires for life and gave their selves in the cause of God.

[Page 166]

As for the fourth attribute: they were the first of people to advance in these deeds and to commit to these conditions, and this precedence has a great effect in strengthening the religion. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal [to those who did so later]; they are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. Yet God has promised each the best﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. And He said: ﴿The foremost, the first of the emigrants and the helpers, and those who followed them in goodness, God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100]. Precedence is only a cause of merit because their advancing in these deeds necessitates others following their example, so that becomes a cause of strength or perfection. For this meaning God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever gives life to one soul, it is as if he had given life to all of mankind﴾ [al-Ma’idah: 32]. And he (peace be upon him) said: “Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection.” It is a habit of people that their motives are strengthened by what they see of their like in matters of religion and worldly life, just as trials become lighter on their hearts through sharing them. Thus it is established that the existence of these four attributes in the first emigrants indicates the utmost excellence and the highest distinction, and that this necessitates acknowledging that they are the leaders of the Muslims and their masters.

As for the second category of believers present in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), they are the Helpers (ansar). This is because when he (peace be upon him) emigrated to them with a group of his companions, had they not given shelter, aided, and spent their selves and wealth in serving the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in attending to the affairs of his companions, the purpose would never have been accomplished. It must be that the status of the emigrants is higher in excellence than that of the Helpers, for several reasons:

The first of them: they were the foremost in faith, which is the chief of virtues and the emblem of distinctions.

The second: they bore hardship and affliction for a long, long time, and for an extended period at the hands of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they endured it. This condition did not occur for the Helpers.

The third: they bore the harms arising from leaving homelands, family and neighbours, which did not happen to the Helpers.

The fourth: opening the door to accepting the religion and the sharia from the Messenger (peace be upon him) occurred only through the emigrants, and the Helpers followed them and imitated them. We have mentioned that he (peace be upon him) said: “Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection.” So it is necessary that the follower be of lower rank than the one followed. Therefore the sum of these conditions necessitates giving precedence to the first emigrants over the Helpers in virtue, rank and distinction. For this reason, wherever God mentions these two groups, He mentions the emigrants before the Helpers, and in this order their mention came in this verse.

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned these two categories in this verse, He said: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾. The scholars differed about what is meant by this guardianship (wilayah). Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn ‘Abbas and all the exegetes that what is meant is guardianship in inheritance. They said: God made the cause of inheritance emigration and support rather than kinship, and a relative who believed but did not emigrate did not inherit, because he did not emigrate and did not support. But know that the word wilayah does not indicate this meaning, because this word indicates closeness, as we have established in several places in this book. It is said: “The ruler is the guardian of whoever has no guardian,” and this does not imply inheritance. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed the friends of God, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62], and this does not imply inheritance either. Rather, wilayah implies nearness, so it is possible to interpret it as other than inheritance, namely that some of them honour others, are concerned with their affairs, and are specially assisted and supported by them. The aim is that they be one hand against the enemies, and that each one’s love for the other take the place of his love for himself. When the word can bear this meaning, interpreting it as inheritance is far from the indication of the word, especially since they say that this ruling has become abrogated (mansukh) by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿Blood relatives are closer to one another﴾. And what need compels us to interpret the word with a meaning that the word does not indicate!

[Page 167]

Then the ruling that it has been abrogated by another verse mentioned with it is extremely far-fetched, unless a consensus (ijma‘) of the exegetes had been reached that this is the intended meaning. In that case it would be necessary to adopt it. However, the claim of consensus is far-fetched.

* * *

The third category among the believers of the Messenger’s time (peace be upon him) are the believers who did not agree with the Messenger in emigration and remained in Mecca. They are the ones referred to in His saying: ﴿Those who believed but did not emigrate﴾. God explained their ruling from two aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿You have no guardianship over them whatsoever until they emigrate.﴾ Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the guardianship negated in this context is the guardianship affirmed in the category discussed earlier. Whoever interprets that guardianship as inheritance holds that the guardianship negated here is inheritance, and whoever interprets that guardianship as all the other considerations mentioned holds the same here. Those who maintain that what is meant by this guardianship is inheritance argued: it is not permissible that what is meant by it be guardianship in the sense of support, and the evidence for this is that He followed it with His saying: ﴿If they seek your help in religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help﴾, and there is no doubt that this refers to allegiance in religion, and the conjoined item is distinct from the item it is conjoined to, so what is meant by the guardianship mentioned must be something distinct from the meaning of support. This argument is weak, because we have interpreted that guardianship as honour and esteem, which is distinct from support. Do you not see that a person may support some of the protected non-Muslims in some important matters, and may support his slave and female slave in the sense of assistance, yet he does not hold guardianship over them in the sense of honour and reverence? So this argument falls.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they emigrate﴾.

Know that His saying: ﴿You have no guardianship over them whatsoever﴾ may give the impression that, since they did not emigrate with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), their guardianship was completely cancelled. God removed this impression by His saying: ﴿You have no guardianship over them whatsoever until they emigrate﴾, meaning that if they emigrated, that guardianship would return and be obtained. The purpose of this is to encourage emigration and make it desirable, because when a Muslim hears that God, exalted is He, says: if he cuts off emigration, the guardianship between him and the Muslims is severed, and if he emigrates, that guardianship is obtained and restored in the most complete form, there is no doubt that this makes him desirous of emigration. The purpose of emigration is the multiplication of Muslims and their gathering, the mutual assistance of some of them for others, the attainment of harmony and strength, and the avoidance of division.

The third issue: Hamzah read ﴿min wilayatihim﴾ with a kasrah on the waw, while the others read it with a fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with a fatha makes it from support and kinship. He said: the guardianship that has the status of governorship is with a kasrah, to distinguish between the two meanings. It is also permissible to read it with a kasrah, because in one group’s guardianship of another there is a kind of craft, like fulling and tailoring, so it is with a kasrah. Abu ‘Ali al-Farisi said: the fatha is better, because guardianship here is from religion, and the kasrah is for political authority.

The second ruling of this third category is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they seek your help in religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the ruling on severing guardianship between that group of believers, He clarified that what is meant is not a complete boycott as in the case of the disbelievers. Rather, these believers who did not emigrate, if they seek your help, then help them and do not forsake them. It was narrated that when the verse ﴿You have no guardianship over them whatsoever until they emigrate﴾ was revealed, al-Zubayr stood up and said: “Shall we not then help them in a matter if they seek aid from us?” And the verse was revealed: ﴿If they seek your help in religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help﴾.

[Page 168]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾. The meaning is that it is not permissible for you to help them against those people, since the covenant prevents that.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who disbelieve are allies of one another﴾. Regarding this there are issues:

**[p. 169]**

**The first issue:** Know that this ordering which God has observed in this verse is extremely fine, because He mentions here three categories. The first are the believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and they are the best of people, and He made clear that some of them must be allies to one another. The second category are the believers who did not emigrate. For them, because of their faith, there is virtue and honour, and because they did not emigrate, they are in a lowly state. Therefore their ruling must be an intermediate ruling between exaltation and humiliation. That is, the allegiance affirmed for the first category is denied for this category, except that they are such that if they seek the help of the believers and ask them for aid, the believers will help them and assist them. This ruling is intermediate between exaltation and humiliation. As for the disbelievers, they have absolutely nothing that necessitates any of the causes of excellence, so it is necessary that the Muslims be completely cut off from them in every respect, so there is no allegiance or support between them in any way. It is thus evident that this ordering is extremely fine.

**The second issue:** Some scholars said: His words ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾ indicate that disbelievers inherit from one another despite the difference of their religions, just as the people of one religion do. Thus a Magian inherits from a pagan, and a Christian inherits from a Magian, because God Most High said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾.

Know that this statement is correct only if we interpret *wilayah* (allegiance) as inheritance, and this has already been discussed. Rather, the truth is that the disbelievers of Quraysh were in extreme enmity toward the Jews. When the call of Muhammad ﷺ appeared, they supported and aided one another in harming him and fighting him. So this is what the verse means. The complete verification of this is that kinship is the cause of union, and a thing is drawn toward its like. The polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, when they shared in enmity toward Muhammad ﷺ, this aspect became the cause of their joining with one another and drawing near to one another. This indicates that they did not undertake that enmity for the sake of religion, because each of them was in the utmost rejection of the religion of the other. Rather, this is among the clearest proofs that that enmity was purely from envy, transgression, and obstinacy.

Then, when God Most High had explained these rulings, He said: ﴿Unless you do this, there will be fitnah (turmoil) on earth and great corruption﴾. The meaning is: if you do not do what I have commanded you in these detailed matters mentioned above, there will arise fitnah on earth and great corruption. The explanation of this fitnah and corruption is in several aspects:

First: If the Muslims were mixed with the disbelievers at a time when the Muslims were weak and few in number, and the disbelievers were strong and numerous, then that mixing might become a cause for a Muslim to join the disbelievers.

Second: If the Muslims were scattered, a great assembly of them would not appear, and that would become a cause for the disbelievers to become bold against them.

Third: If the gathering of the Muslims is increasing in number and equipment every day, that becomes a cause for greater eagerness among them for what they are in, and for the desire of the dissenter to join them.

**[p. 169]**

Know that when He Most High mentioned this third category, He returned to mention the first and second categories once more, saying: ﴿Those who believed and emigrated and struggled in the way of God, and those who gave shelter and helped—those are the believers in truth; for them is forgiveness and generous provision﴾.

Know that this is not a repetition, because He mentioned them first to clarify their ruling, which is the allegiance of some of them to others. Then He mentioned them here to clarify the magnification of their status and the elevation of their rank. Its explanation is in two aspects:

First: Repetition indicates greater attention to their condition, and this indicates nobility and honour.

Second: He Most High praised them here in three ways:

The first: His words ﴿those are the believers in truth﴾. His words ﴿those are the believers﴾ indicate restriction, and His words ﴿in truth﴾ indicate emphasis in describing them as being rightly guided and firmly established on the path of religion. The matter in reality is so, because whoever is not rightly guided in his religion does not bear abandoning former religions, does not part from family and homeland, does not give up self and wealth, and is not among those who hasten and compete in these conditions.

The second: His words ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾. The indefiniteness of the word *maghfirah* (forgiveness) indicates completeness, just as the indefiniteness in His words ﴿and you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 96] indicates the completeness of that life. The meaning is: for them is complete and perfect forgiveness from all sins and consequences.

The third: His words ﴿and generous provision﴾, and what is meant by it is the lofty and noble reward.

The summary: He Most High explained their condition in this world and in the Hereafter. As for this world, He described them with His words ﴿those are the believers in truth﴾. As for the Hereafter, what is intended is either the repelling of punishment or the attainment of reward. The repelling of punishment is what is meant by His words ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾, and the attainment of reward is what is meant by His words ﴿and generous provision﴾. These lofty felicities were obtained only because they turned away from bodily pleasures, so they left family and homeland and gave up self and wealth. That is an indication that there is no path to attaining felicities except by turning away from these bodily things.

* * *

The fourth category of believers in the time of Muhammad ﷺ are those who did not agree with the Messenger in emigrating, but after that they emigrated to him. This is what is meant by the words of God Most High: ﴿And those who believed afterwards and emigrated and struggled with you, those are of you﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** They differed about the meaning of His words ﴿afterwards﴾. Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: after Hudaybiyyah, which is the second emigration. It was said: after the revelation of this verse. It was said: after the day of Badr. The more correct view is that what is meant is those who emigrated after the first emigration, and these are the followers in good conduct, as He said: ﴿And those who followed them in good conduct—God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ [Al-Tawbah: 100].

**The second issue:** The more correct view is that emigration ceased with the Conquest of Mecca, because from then on Mecca became a land of Islam. Al-Hasan said: emigration is never discontinued. As for His, peace be upon him, saying: "There is no emigration after the Conquest," what is meant is the specific emigration, for it ceased with the Conquest and with the strength of Islam. But if it happens at some time that the believers are in a land where they are few in number, and the disbelievers have might because of their presence among them, and the Muslims emigrate from that land and move to another land where the might of the disbelievers weakens, then emigration becomes obligatory for them according to what al-Hasan said, because the same cause for emigration from Mecca to Medina has arisen among them.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿those are of you﴾ indicate that the rank of these people is below the rank of the earlier Emigrants, because He joined these people to them and made them of them in a context of honouring. Were it not that the first category is more noble, this meaning would not be valid. This is the explanation of these four categories which God Most High mentioned in this verse.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of God﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Those who said that what is meant by His words ﴿those, some of them are allies of others﴾ is the allegiance of inheritance said: this verse abrogates (*naskh*, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) that, because God Most High explained that inheritance was by means of support and emigration, and now that has been abrogated, so inheritance is obtained only by means of kinship. His words ﴿in the Book of God﴾ mean the shares mentioned in Surah al-Nisa. As for those who interpreted that verse as support, love, and honouring, they said: since that allegiance could be understood as allegiance by means of inheritance, God Most High clarified in this verse that the allegiance of inheritance is obtained only by means of kinship, except what the evidence specifies. So the purpose of this statement is to remove this misunderstanding. This is better, because multiplying abrogation without necessity or need is not permissible.

**The second issue:** Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with them all, cited this verse in his letter to Abu Jaʿfar al-Mansur as evidence that the Imam after the Messenger of God ﷺ is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. He said: God Most High's words ﴿and those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another﴾ indicate the establishment of allegiance, and there is nothing specific in the verse regarding the establishment of this priority. Therefore it must be understood in its entirety, except what the evidence specifies. In that case, the Imamate is included in it. And it is not permissible to say that Abu Bakr was among the people of blood relationship, because it is reported that "he, peace be upon him, gave him the chapter of Bara'ah to convey to the people. Then he sent ʿAli after him and commanded that the one to convey it should be ʿAli, and said: 'None should convey it except a man from me.'" That indicates that Abu Bakr was not of them. This is the way of deducing from this verse.

The answer: If this indication is valid, then al-Abbas would have a better claim to the Imamate, because he was closer to the Messenger of God than ʿAli. Abu Jaʿfar al-Mansur answered him in this way.

**The third issue:** The followers of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, cited this verse regarding the inheritance of distant kindred (*dhawu al-arham*). Our companions answered them that His words ﴿and those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another﴾ are general regarding the matter in which this priority occurs. When He said ﴿in the Book of God﴾, its meaning is in the ruling which God has explained in His Book. Thus this priority became restricted to the rulings which God has explained in His Book, and those rulings are nothing but the inheritance of the male agnatic relatives (*ʿaṣabāt*, those who inherit by male lineage without a fixed share). So it is necessary that what is meant by this general term is only that, and it does not extend to the inheritance of distant kindred.

Then He said at the end of the surah: ﴿Indeed, God is Knowing of all things﴾. What is meant is that these rulings which I have mentioned and detailed are all wisdom, rightness, and benefit, and there is nothing in them of futility or falsehood, because one who knows all that is known does not judge except with what is right. Its parallel is that when the angels said: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30], He answered them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30], meaning: since you know that I am knowing of all that is known, know that My ruling is free from error, and so it is here. And God knows best.

The commentary on this surah is complete, and all praise and thanks are due to God, as He is worthy of them. On Sunday in Ramadan of the year six hundred and one, in a village called Baghdan. We ask God for deliverance from terrors and the hardship of the times, and from the plots of the people of rebellion and abandonment, for He is the King, the Judge. And His blessings and peace be upon the beloved of the Most Merciful, Muhammad the Chosen, the possessor of miracles and proof.
